Provoked, he sent Bacchides, his closest friend, with a very great force, ordering him to kill Judas and those with him. Coming into Judaea, he sent to Judas and his brothers inviting them to peace. They did not trust him. But some of the people received oaths from Bacchides and came to him; and he, despising the oaths, killed sixty of them and so checked the impulse of the rest to come to him. He ordered all in the country to obey the high priest Alcimus. Having done this he returned to Antioch.

Alcimus, speaking to each to please him and winning over all, quickly gathered a large force, most of them exiles and impious men, by whom he killed those who sided with Judas; and Judas on the other side destroyed those who acted for Alcimus. Alcimus stirred up Demetrius against Judas. So the king sent Nicanor again with a very great force, ordering him not to spare the nation. He went and tried to seize Judas by trickery and invited him to peace; Judas gave and received pledges and received Nicanor with his force. Nicanor, greeting him and talking with him, gave his men a signal to seize Judas. The man, seeing the plot, leapt away to the Jews and escaped. When the ambush was discovered, Nicanor fought an open battle and won. After that Judas fled to the citadel of Jerusalem. Nicanor threatened the people that if they did not hand Judas over to him, he would throw down the temple. Judas spoke to the thousand men with him and roused them to valour, engaged the enemy and won, many falling, and Nicanor himself; the rest fled, and all were destroyed as they were caught. And so for a little while the Jews

## 4.22

had rest from wars. When the high priest Alcimus, also called Jakeim, was struck by a blow sent from God and so his life broke off after four years as high priest, the people gave the high priesthood to Judas. Judas, hearing that the Romans had great power, and had subdued the Galatians, Iberians, Carthaginians and Libyans, the whole of Greece and the kings Perseus, Philip and Antiochus, sent asking for friendship, and asked them to write to Demetrius not to make war on the Jews. The senate agreed to friendship and consented to an alliance with the Jews.

Demetrius, learning of the death of Nicanor and the loss of the army, sent Bacchides again. He hurried against Judas, who was camped in a village with a thousand men. They, afraid of the army with Bacchides, advised him to withdraw and save himself. When he said, "May the sun never see me do this, turn my back on the enemy," many of those with him fled. Engaging Bacchides, he fought on equal terms for a long time; but towards sunset, bearing down with the bravest on the right wing, where Bacchides was, he broke through the phalanx and put it to flight. Those on the left came up and surrounded Judas. He stood and fought with those with him, and after killing many he too fell at last; and when he fell those with him fled. He died having adorned the high priesthood for three years, a noble man, ready to do and suffer anything for the freedom of the nation.

When he was dead, Bacchides entrusted the care of the country to those of the Jews who had become impious and broken the ancestral customs. They afflicted their countrymen in every way, and seizing those who sided with Judas they brought them to Bacchides, who first tortured them and then put them to death. So the surviving companions of Judas persuaded his brother Jonathan and appointed him general of the Jews. Bacchides sought to kill Jonathan by trickery; but he fled into the desert with his brother Simon and their companions. Bacchides set out against them; and Jonathan sent his brother John to the Nabataean Arabs, for they were friends, to deposit the baggage with them. As he went, the sons of Amaraeus ambushed him and killed him with those following him, and plundered what they were carrying. Bacchides attacked Jonathan on the sabbath, thinking he would not fight because of the law. But he said that their lives were at stake and drew up against him; after killing many and charging at Bacchides to strike him, and missing, he leapt into the river with his companions and swam across. Bacchides returned to the citadel in Jerusalem, and taking the sons of the leading men of Judaea as hostages he shut them up in the citadel.

Jonathan took care to avenge the murder of his brother John. When the sons of Amaraeus were celebrating a wedding and bringing the bridegroom and bride from one town to another with a lavish procession, he lay in ambush on a mountain with those about him, attacked those in the procession, killed them all and plundered everything they were carrying. Jonathan and Simon with their men lived in the marshes of the river. Bacchides, leaving a garrison in Judaea, returned to Demetrius. Since the nation was quiet from then on for two years, Jonathan and those about him lived in the country without fear. So the impious Jews sent to King Demetrius, saying that if someone were sent against Jonathan he would be caught without trouble. And the king sent Bacchides. He came into Judaea, and though he tried hard he could not seize Jonathan, so he killed fifty of the leading men among those who had made the report to the king about Jonathan, as having lied. Jonathan, Simon and their men withdrew into the desert, where he built towers and waited. Bacchides came and besieged him. Jonathan, leaving his brother Simon there, slipped out secretly himself, gathered many from the country and by night attacked Bacchides and his army. He killed many himself, and Simon many, he too having slipped out from the strongholds, and they burned the siege engines as well. Despondent at this, Bacchides wished to withdraw, but sought a seemly reason for withdrawing. Jonathan, learning this, sent an embassy about friendship, so that each side might give back to the other the captives they held. Bacchides accepted the embassy and made peace. They swore not to march against each other again, and exchanged the captives. Bacchides returned and no longer came against Judaea, and Jonathan, having security, directed the affairs of his countrymen and punished the impious.

## 4.23

Alexander, the son of Antiochus Epiphanes, took Ptolemais by betrayal and so alarmed Demetrius that he gathered his forces and sent to Jonathan about goodwill and alliance. He allowed him to raise an army, and permitted him to take back the boys whom Bacchides had shut up in the citadel as hostages. Receiving the king's letter, Jonathan came to Jerusalem, read it in the hearing of the people and the guards, took the boys from the citadel and gave each back to his parents, and himself stayed in Jerusalem renewing the city and rebuilding its walls. Alexander also wrote to Jonathan, calling him to alliance, making him his friend, granting him the high priesthood and sending gifts. Jonathan, receiving the letter, put on the high priest's robe at the feast of tabernacles, four years having been completed since his brother Judas died, gathered a force and prepared arms. Alexander engaged Demetrius and won; Demetrius fell with his horse into a deep marsh hard to get out of, where the enemy surrounded him and he fell covered with wounds, having killed many himself. He reigned eleven years.

Alexander, taking over the kingdom of Syria, betrothed to himself the daughter of Ptolemy Philometor. When the wedding was being celebrated he wrote to Jonathan to come to Ptolemais. Coming, he was honoured both by Ptolemy and by Alexander. When Demetrius, the son of the dead Demetrius, sailed from Crete to Cilicia with a heavy force, Alexander was anxious; he hurried to Antioch to make things safe there, and left Apollonius Daus as governor of Syria. He sent to Jonathan, saying it was unjust that he alone did not submit to the king, challenged him to battle and taunted the nation with cowardice. Provoked by this, the high priest joined battle with Apollonius, won, killed many of the enemy, took cities of Syria and returned to Jerusalem with much booty. King Alexander, learning this, sent to Jonathan saying he rejoiced at the defeat of Apollonius, since he had fought against his friend and ally against his wishes.

Ptolemy Philometor, going to Alexander's aid with a naval and land force, came to Ptolemais and was almost in danger, Alexander having plotted against him through one of his friends, Ammonius. Escaping the plot, he asked for Ammonius for punishment; but Alexander would not give him up. From this Ptolemy knew that Alexander was party to the plot, gave up the alliance and dissolved the marriage tie. For taking his daughter away from him, he sent to Demetrius, promising to ally with him, give him his daughter in marriage and set him on his father's throne. Demetrius gladly accepted the marriage and the alliance. Ptolemy was eager to persuade the people of Antioch to receive Demetrius; and he easily achieved what he was eager for, since the people of Antioch hated Alexander both because of his father, who had broken the law against them, and because of Ammonius; and they quickly drove him out of Antioch. Driven out of there, he went to Cilicia, and the people of Antioch declared Ptolemy king and made him put on two diadems, as ruler of Syria and Egypt. But he, able through his understanding to reckon the future, so as not to seem to the Romans, who were already very powerful, an object of envy, persuaded the people of Antioch to receive Demetrius.

When Alexander came against Syria with a large army and ravaged the land of Antioch, Ptolemy, with Demetrius, to whom he had already given his daughter in marriage, marched against him; Alexander was defeated and fled to Arabia, and Ptolemy, thrown from his horse when it was frightened by an elephant's trumpeting and threw him, received many wounds on the head as the enemy surrounded him; rescued with difficulty by his bodyguards, he lay for four days neither understanding nor speaking. Coming to on the fifth day, and receiving the head of Alexander, sent to him by the chief of the Arabs, he was pleased at his destruction, and he too died a little later.

## 4.24

Demetrius Nicanor, taking over the kingdom of Asia after Alexander had reigned five years, began to destroy Ptolemy's soldiery, forgetting both the kinship and the alliance. The soldiers beat off his attempt and withdrew to Alexandria, but he took the elephants. Jonathan the high priest was besieging the citadel of Jerusalem, which held Macedonian guards and some of the impious Jews; some of these came out by night and reported the siege to Demetrius. He came with a force against Jonathan, and when he was at Ptolemais he wrote to him to come to him. Jonathan did not stop the siege, but taking the priests and elders of the people and bringing much money he came to Demetrius. Courting him with this, he was honoured by him and had his high priesthood confirmed.

When Demetrius, since no war was pressing, cut the soldiers' pay, and so was hated by them, a general of Alexander called Trypho, learning of their hatred of him, came to Malchus the Arab, and asked for Alexander's son Antiochus, who was being brought up with him, saying he would restore his father's rule to him; and he gave him up. Demetrius sent to Jonathan asking for an alliance and promising him many favours. He sent him three thousand men, by whom, when the people of Antioch rose against him out of the hatred they nursed because they were badly treated by him, he routed them, burned the city and killed many of them, until they were forced to lay down their arms and surrender to him. So the revolt was ended, and he sent the Jews back to Jonathan, giving them gifts and acknowledging his gratitude to him. But later he broke his promises too and threatened him with war. And he would have carried out his threats had not Trypho returned from Arabia to Syria, put the diadem on Antiochus, then a youth, and joined battle with Demetrius, those soldiers who had left Demetrius because of the cut in their pay coming over to him. Trypho, getting the better in the battle, took Antioch and the elephants. Demetrius went off to Cilicia, and the boy Antiochus called Jonathan to an alliance.

He agreed to be friend and ally, undertook to make war on Demetrius and set to work at once. First he made many cities go over to Antiochus, causing them to revolt from Demetrius; then, leaving his brother Simon in Judaea, he advanced against Demetrius's generals. Simon besieged Bethsura, a place in Judaea held by Demetrius's men, who, hard pressed by the siege, received pledges and left the place; and Simon put a garrison of his own in it. Jonathan engaged Demetrius's generals, put them to flight, killed about two thousand and returned to Jerusalem. He also sent an embassy to Rome to renew the former friendship they had with the nation; and the senate confirmed again what had been decreed before. On their way back the envoys came to Sparta too, having been instructed by Jonathan to do so. The Spartans received the envoys kindly and passed a decree of friendship and alliance with the Jews.

But the generals of Demetrius, eager to retrieve their defeat, came against Jonathan with a greater force. He met them swiftly. Losing heart to face him in open battle, they fled by night. At daybreak Jonathan, learning of the flight, pursued but did not overtake them; but going into Arabia and attacking the Nabataeans he drove off much booty from there, took captives and returned. Gathering the people, he advised them to renew the walls of Jerusalem and set up again whatever of the enclosure of the temple had been pulled down. When the advice pleased all, he set to the work himself, and sent his brother Simon to secure the country.

Demetrius came to Mesopotamia to take over Babylon and the upper satrapies. For the Greeks and Macedonians living there promised to surrender themselves to him and help him make war on Arsaces, the king of the Parthians. And so they received him. But engaging Arsaces, he lost his whole army and was himself captured. Trypho, learning how things stood with Demetrius, plotted against Antiochus, intending to kill him and take the rule for himself. But he feared Jonathan, who was a friend of Antiochus, and he was eager first to capture him by deceit and then to attack Antiochus's affairs. So he went to Scythopolis, where Jonathan met him with forty thousand fighting men. He approached him deceitfully, receiving him with gifts and honours, wishing to remove all suspicion so as to take him off his guard. He advised him to dismiss his army and come himself with a few to Ptolemais with him, to take over the city and all the strongholds there. Jonathan, suspecting nothing, sent the army back and went with only a thousand men. Shut up in Ptolemais, he was taken alive, and those with him were killed.

Those in Jerusalem, learning this, fell into fear because of the surrounding nations, which, learning of Jonathan's capture, had stirred against the Jews. Simon spoke to the multitude, encouraged it, and was chosen leader by it; gathering the fighting men of the people he saw to the walls of the city and took thought for everything for the safety of affairs. Trypho came into Judaea, bringing Jonathan in chains. Simon met him with a force; and he sent to him saying that if he wished his brother to be released, he should give a hundred talents of silver and two of Jonathan's sons as hostages. Simon understood Trypho's wickedness, but so as not to be blamed for being unwilling to save his brother, he sent both the money and the boys. Trypho took them but did not keep the agreement, and went up towards Jerusalem with the army. Simon kept pace with him, always camping opposite. A heavy fall of snow prevented him from reaching Jerusalem; he turned to Syria, and as he went he killed Jonathan.

Simon, when his brother Jonathan died after four years of the high priesthood, was himself put forward as high priest by the multitude, and no longer paid tribute to the Macedonians. Under him the nation prospered greatly; they mastered the surrounding nations and destroyed many of the cities, so that they might not be bases for their enemies. And the hill on which the citadel had been built, which was very high, they brought down to a plain in three years of constant labour, so that the sanctuary might stand above it.

## 5.1

Trypho put to death Antiochus, who was also called the God, after he had reigned four years, being his guardian. He gave out that he had died, and promised the soldiers money if they made him king. They, hoping to gain much, chose him as ruler. Having taken the kingdom, Trypho put off his pretence; and the soldiery, hating him, went over to Cleopatra, the wife of Demetrius, who was shut up in Seleucia. While Antiochus, called the Saviour, who was the brother of Demetrius, was wandering and hemmed in on all sides because of Trypho, Cleopatra sent to him, inviting him to marriage and the kingdom; for she feared that the people of Seleucia would give the city to Trypho. So Antiochus came to Seleucia and set out against Trypho, defeated him and drove him out of upper Syria, besieged him when he fled to a fortress, and invited the high priest Simon to friendship. He accepted the invitation and supplied food to those besieging Trypho. Trypho fled from there and came to Apamea, where he was besieged, captured and put to death, after reigning three years.

Antiochus, forgetting what Simon had done for him, sent Cendebaeus, ordering him to ravage Judaea and seize Simon. Simon faced him and won. And he spent the rest of his life in peace, having ruled Judaea for eight years. He died the victim of a plot by Ptolemy, his son-in-law. Simon's wife and two of his sons were seized and put in chains, but the third, John, who was also called Hyrcanus, escaped, and was received by the people of Jerusalem because of his father's benefits, while they drove Ptolemy off when he came.

Taking over the ancestral priesthood, Hyrcanus marched against Ptolemy, who was in a fortress called Dagon. He was winning in the siege, but was defeated by pity for his mother and brothers; for Ptolemy brought them up on the wall and tortured them in full view. His mother, however, begged him not to grow soft because of her. While the siege was dragging on in this way, the seventh year came, in which the Jews are accustomed to rest. And because of this Ptolemy, freed from the war, killed Hyrcanus's mother and brothers and fled to Zeno called Cotylas, the [a gap in the text].

Antiochus, angry with Simon for what he had suffered, came against Judaea, overran the country and besieged Hyrcanus; he raised very high towers on the north side of the city and attacked the wall from them. But he achieved nothing, because of the courage of those within, the strength of the walls and the abundance of water from rain that had just fallen. Hyrcanus, afraid that their necessities would run short, chose out only the fighting men of the multitude and drove the rest out of the city; Antiochus would not let them go away from there, and so they died waiting outside the walls. Those within, pitying them, took them in again. When the feast of tabernacles came, Hyrcanus sent to Antiochus asking for a truce of seven days because of the feast. He gave the truce and sent a lavish sacrifice with offerings; and because of his piety towards God they called him the Pious. Knowing Antiochus's reverence for God, Hyrcanus sent an embassy asking for their ancestral constitution to be restored to them. He said that if they handed over their arms, agreed to pay tribute for the other cities apart from Judaea, and received a garrison, he would stop the war and do the rest they asked. The Jews accepted the rest, but would not consent to the garrison, and instead gave hostages and five hundred talents of silver. When Antiochus gave way on these terms, the siege was raised. Hyrcanus opened the tomb of David and took three thousand talents of silver from it. Making friendship with Antiochus, he received him into the city, and set out with him when he marched against the Parthians; there Antiochus, making war on Arsaces, perished himself with the greater part of his army.

## 5.2

His brother Demetrius became successor to the kingdom of the Syrians, Arsaces having released him when Antiochus attacked the Parthians. After the death of Antiochus, Hyrcanus took many of the cities of Syria and others of Idumaea. Having subdued the Idumaeans, he allowed them to live in the country if they were circumcised and followed Jewish customs. They, for the sake of their homes, submitted to circumcision and the rest. Demetrius, having decided to march against Hyrcanus, was checked, since the Syrians and the soldiers hated him for his wickedness and sent to Ptolemy Physcon to give them one of the kin of Seleucus to take up the kingdom. He sent Alexander called Zebinas. When battle was joined between him and Demetrius, Demetrius was routed and fled to Ptolemais; not received by his wife Cleopatra, he ran away to Tyre, where he was captured and, after much suffering, put to death. Alexander, taking over the kingdom, made friendship with Hyrcanus. When Antiochus Grypus, the son of Demetrius, rose against him, he was defeated in battle and perished.

This Antiochus, having become king of Syria, fought for many years over the kingdom with his brother Antiochus, called Cyzicenus because he was brought up at Cyzicus. He was the son of Antiochus, the brother of Demetrius, who died among the Parthians, so that he was a half-brother of Antiochus Grypus; for Cleopatra had married the two brothers, Demetrius first and Antiochus afterwards, as has been written, and bore Antiochus Grypus to Demetrius, and Antiochus Cyzicenus to Antiochus the Saviour, Demetrius's brother. While these were fighting each other, Hyrcanus kept quiet, and despising the Antiochi he revolted, giving them nothing any more; and at leisure he reaped the fruits of Judaea, so as to gather a boundless amount of money. He also marched against Samaria and besieged it through his sons Aristobulus and Antigonus. When famine pressed the city, the Samaritans called Antiochus Cyzicenus to their aid. He engaged Aristobulus's men and was defeated; then, gathering a host again, he ravaged Hyrcanus's country, to force him in this way to raise the siege. But losing many of those with him he went off to Tripolis. Hyrcanus took Samaria and wiped it out entirely. It is said that on the day on which his sons were fighting Antiochus, he himself, as high priest, burning incense alone in the temple, heard a voice saying that his sons had just defeated Antiochus; and coming out he told the multitude what he had heard. And so it happened.

Having prospered, Hyrcanus was envied by the Jews, and most hated by the Pharisees. These are one of the sects among the Jews, of which there are three. These Pharisees hold that there is fate, but that some things are also in our power to happen or not to happen. The Essenes hold that fate is master of everything and that everything befalls men from it. The Sadducees reject fate, and place everything in our own power, teaching that we are the cause of our own good things and choose the worse of ourselves through folly. The Pharisees, who had been friendly to Hyrcanus before (for he had been their disciple), happened for some reason to come to enmity with him. They had very great power with the multitude. Hyrcanus attached himself to the party of the Sadducees, breaking with the Pharisees, and set out to abolish the observances they had handed down. For the Sadducees said that only what is written must be held as law, and what comes from tradition need not be kept. For this Hyrcanus was hated by the Pharisees. Having lived happily for thirty-one years, he died, leaving five sons. It is said that he was also granted prophecy, and foretold of his two elder sons that they would not remain masters of affairs.

## 5.3

When Hyrcanus died, Aristobulus succeeded to the rule; and deciding to change it into a kingship, he put on a diadem, four hundred and eighty-one years after the people returned from Babylon to Jerusalem. He imprisoned his other brothers and his mother, who disputed the rule with him, but loved Antigonus, the next after him, and held him worthy of equal honour. His mother he starved to death, and he did away with his brother Antigonus too, trusting slanders. For when Antigonus returned brilliantly from a campaign, Aristobulus was ill; and while the feast of tabernacles was being kept, Antigonus went up to the temple with the armed men about him, splendidly adorned. Those slandering him to his brother said that he had not come to the feast like a private man but with royal splendour, and that, having come up with so great a bodyguard of soldiers, he was plotting against him.

Aristobulus, taking thought both for his own safety and for his brother, set his bodyguards in a dark underground passage, ordering them to spare his brother if he came unarmed, but to kill him if he came with his arms; and he sent to Antigonus bidding him come unarmed. But Aristobulus's wife and those who conspired with her against Antigonus persuaded the man sent to tell Antigonus: "Your brother, hearing that you have had new armour made, asks you to come armed, so that he may see it." He, suspecting nothing, went in full armour, and coming to Strato's Tower, where the place was dark, he was killed by the bodyguards. A certain Judas, an Essene by race, who foretold many things truly, seeing Antigonus pass by the temple then, cried out, praying to die, since he had been proved false while Antigonus lived; for he had foretold that he would die that day at Strato's Tower, and that was six hundred stades away, so that it was impossible for Antigonus to get there, the day already declining. While Judas was saying this, it was reported that Antigonus had been killed in the underground passage, which was itself also named Strato's Tower, the same name as Caesarea on the coast.

Such was the end of Antigonus; and justice for the murder of his brother at once pursued Aristobulus. His insides were destroyed and he brought up blood; one of his servants, carrying it out, slipped at the place where Antigonus had been slaughtered, which still had stains of his blood, and spilled it, so that the blood of both was mingled. When those who saw it cried out, Aristobulus, learning what had happened, groaned and was moved to tears, and said: "So I was not to escape God's notice in such impious daring deeds." And after saying more he died, having reigned a year.

## 5.4

Salome, his wife, who was also called Alexandra, released her husband's brothers (for Aristobulus had kept them in chains) and made king Jannaeus, also called Alexander, who was senior in age and most moderate. Taking over the kingdom, he killed one of his brothers who was plotting revolt, but honoured the other, who lived without ambition. Having made some wars against certain peoples, in some winning and in others even being defeated, he finally took up arms against his own countrymen too, who had risen against him. For during a feast, when he went up to the altar to sacrifice, the multitude pelted him with citrons (it being the custom at the feast of tabernacles to hold wands of palm and citrons in their hands) and poured insults on him. Provoked by this, Alexander killed about six thousand of them. Then, joining battle with the Arabs and being defeated, he came in flight to Jerusalem; and when the nation attacked him in his misfortune, he fought against it for six years (for he maintained Pisidians and Cilicians) and killed no fewer than fifty thousand. For this he was hated still more, so that when he asked what must happen to end their hostility, the multitude shouted that he should die. After this too the Jews fought Alexander, and very many perished. He shut up the most powerful of them in a city and besieged them, and mastering them he brought them to Jerusalem. And feasting with his women in full view, he did a most savage deed, crucifying eight hundred of them, and slaughtering their children and wives before their eyes while they were still alive. This cruel deed persuaded his opponents, about eight thousand, to flee. And from then on Alexander enjoyed quiet.

Then Antiochus called Dionysus marched against Judaea. In a hard battle with the Jews, Antiochus died in the war while winning and helping the part of his army that was in difficulty. When he had died his army fled and perished of hunger. After Antiochus, Aretas reigned over Coele Syria; he marched against Judaea, defeated Alexander in battle and withdrew on terms.

After this Alexander took many cities of the Idumaeans, Cilicians, Phoenicians and Syrians, and having completed the third year on the campaign he returned, the Jews receiving him eagerly because of his success. Then, falling ill from drink and struggling for three years with a quartan fever, he did not give up his campaigns. The queen, seeing him now despaired of, lamented for herself and the children. He advised her to hide his death from the soldiers until she had taken the place (for he happened to be besieging one), and then, coming to Jerusalem as if from a victory, to give the Pharisees a share of power. For they could make the nation well disposed to her; and he said that he himself had offended the nation because of them, since they had been outraged by him. "So," he said, "send for their leaders and allow them to treat my body as they wish, since I insulted them greatly, and promise to do nothing against their judgement. If you speak so, I shall be buried lavishly and you will rule securely." Having given his wife this advice he died, having ruled twenty-seven years and lived forty-nine. Alexandra did everything according to her husband's advice, made the Pharisees well disposed to herself, secured the kingdom, and gave her husband a burial more splendid than those of the kings before him.

## 5.5

Alexander had two sons, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus; Hyrcanus was sluggish in character and unsuited to managing affairs, but the younger was energetic. Their mother made Hyrcanus high priest because of his lack of ambition, entrusted everything to the Pharisees, ordered the multitude to obey them, and she herself had the name of the kingdom, while the Pharisees had the power. The country was quiet, the Pharisees alone troubling it and urging that those who had advised Alexander to destroy the eight hundred be killed. They slaughtered one at first, and after him others one after another, until the powerful men came to the palace, and Aristobulus with them (for he was not pleased with what was being done), and by saying much and lamenting those already destroyed they moved those present to pity for those in danger and to tears. Aristobulus blamed his mother for this; but she did not know what to do.

At this time Tigranes was reported to have invaded Syria with a great army and to be about to come to Judaea. This frightened both the nation and the queen, and they sent him many valuable gifts and envoys while he was besieging Ptolemais. He accepted them and made fair promises. Just as he had sacked Ptolemais, it was reported to him that Lucullus had set out for Armenia, and for this reason he withdrew to his own country.

When the queen fell gravely ill, Aristobulus slipped away secretly and went to the forts where his father's friends had been stationed, only his wife knowing of the deed, and he was received by them. When his mother learned of his flight, and that he had won over all the forts, she and the nation were in great alarm; and they put his wife and children in the fortress above the temple. Hyrcanus and the elders of the Jews, learning that in fifteen days Aristobulus had mastered twenty-two places, gathered much money and assembled an army, begged the queen to give her opinion about Aristobulus. She said she no longer cared about affairs, as she was already dying, and left them to do what they judged best. Not long after she died, having reigned nine years and lived seventy-three.

As soon as Alexandra was dead, Aristobulus made war on his brother, and many of Hyrcanus's soldiers deserted to Aristobulus. He fled to the citadel, where Aristobulus's wife and children had been shut up before. Coming to terms, the brothers ended their enmity, on the basis that Aristobulus should reign and Hyrcanus live without office. Confirming the agreement with oaths, they withdrew, the one to the palace and Hyrcanus to Aristobulus's house.

But an Idumaean named Antipater, a friend of Hyrcanus, seditious and energetic and having much money, talking secretly with the powerful men of the Jews and slandering Aristobulus to Hyrcanus as planning to kill him, persuaded him to flee to Aretas, the king of the Arabs. Hyrcanus sent Antipater to Aretas to obtain pledges that he would not hand him over to his enemies if he came to him. Having received pledges, Antipater returned, and taking Hyrcanus with him by night he brought him to Aretas at the place called Petra. Hyrcanus begged him to bring him back to Judaea and restore him to the kingdom, promising, if this happened, to give him the country and the twelve cities which his father Alexander had taken from the Arabs. Aretas marched against Aristobulus and won the battle. Many deserted to Hyrcanus, and Aristobulus fled to Jerusalem. The Arab attacked the temple and besieged Aristobulus, the people too siding with Hyrcanus, and only the priests remaining with Aristobulus.

There was a certain Onias, a just man dear to God, who once, when there was a drought, prevailed on God by prayer and ended the lack of rain; the Jews asked him to pray against Aristobulus and those with him. He would not agree. When he was forced, he said: "O God, king of all, since both those standing with me are yours and the besieged priests are yours, I pray you neither to help these against those, nor those against these." At once they surrounded the man and stoned him. Not long after God exacted punishment from them for their impiety, when a violent wind blew and destroyed the crops of the country.

## 5.6

Scaurus, sent into Syria by Pompey while he was making war on Tigranes in Armenia, received envoys from both Aristobulus and Hyrcanus, each asking for his alliance. Receiving four hundred talents from Aristobulus, he sided with him. He ordered Aretas to withdraw or be judged an enemy of the Romans, and so raised the siege. When it had been raised, Aristobulus marched against Aretas and Hyrcanus, engaged them and won. Not long after, when Pompey came to Damascus, envoys came from many places and from Judaea, bringing a great gift from Aristobulus, a golden vine worth five hundred talents. Josephus says he saw it in Rome, dedicated to Jupiter on the Capitol. And again Antipater came to him on behalf of Hyrcanus, and Nicodemus on behalf of Aristobulus. He ordered the disputants themselves to come.

When the Jews and their leaders had come to Damascus, the people asked not to be ruled by kings; for it was their ancestral custom to be ruled by the high priests, and these, being of that family, had changed the rule into a kingship. Hyrcanus accused his brother, saying that though the rule had been allotted to him by right of seniority, it had been taken from him by his brother, and he strung together many other charges against him. More than a thousand of the most reputable Jews spoke with him as he said this, Antipater having arranged it. Aristobulus put forward Hyrcanus's own nature as the cause of his losing the rule, being idle and so easily despised; he himself, he said, had taken it on of necessity, for fear that it might pass to others; and he was called by the same title as his father. Pompey judged that Aristobulus had used force, but speaking mildly to them at the time he ordered them to keep quiet for the present, and promised to settle everything when he came to the country.

Aristobulus, however, did not wait, but went off to Judaea. Angered, Pompey marched against him. When he took refuge in a fortress called Alexandrium, Pompey ordered him to come to him. Since his friends asked him not to make war on the Romans, he came down, pleaded his case and returned to where he had come from. When Pompey ordered him to hand over the fortresses and write to the commandants in his own hand (for they were forbidden to give them up otherwise), he obeyed, but withdrew in vexation to Jerusalem and prepared for war. While Pompey was marching against him, the death of Mithridates was reported to him, brought about by his son Pharnaces. When Pompey was near Jericho, where the balsam is grown, the finest of perfumes, which oozes out like sap when the shrubs are cut with a sharp stone, Aristobulus came to him and begged him to stop the war, offering money and receiving him into Jerusalem to do as he wished. Pompey pardoned him and sent Gabinius for the money and the city. But since Aristobulus's soldiers would not let the agreement be carried out, Gabinius came back with nothing done. So Pompey came against the city, having put Aristobulus under arrest.

Those within were not of one mind. Some thought they should receive Pompey, Aristobulus's party the opposite; and these seized the temple and prepared for a siege. The others handed the city and the palace over to Pompey. He camped inside and besieged the temple. When it was taken about the third month, the enemy burst in and slaughtered those in it; but they went on no less with the service and the sacrifices. Everything was full of slaughter; for some of the Jews were slaughtered by the Romans, others by one another, or threw themselves down from the heights. Pompey and some of those about him went into the inner sanctuary of the temple, which may not be entered, and saw what was not to be seen by others than the high priests. But out of piety he touched none of the offerings or the money in it. The next day he ordered the temple to be cleansed and the lawful sacrifices offered, handed the high priesthood to Hyrcanus, executed with the axe those responsible for the war, and made Jerusalem tributary to the Romans. Pompey, going away to Rome, took Aristobulus in chains with him, and his children. He had two daughters and as many sons, of whom the elder, Alexander, escaped and later overran Judaea, since Hyrcanus was unable to stand against him.

## 5.7

When Gabinius came to Syria, he sent Mark Antony against Alexander with an army. In the battle the Romans killed about three thousand of the enemy and took no fewer alive. When Alexander fled to a fortress called Alexandrium, he besieged it. So Alexander sent to Gabinius asking pardon, and handed over the fortresses he held. The high priest Hyrcanus was brought back to Jerusalem by Gabinius. But Aristobulus escaped from Rome, came to Judaea and tried to fortify Alexandrium, which had just been razed. Gabinius sent men to stop him or even seize him. Many of the Jews flocked to Aristobulus, most of whom were unarmed. These Aristobulus sent away, but kept with him those who were armed, about eight thousand. When battle was joined between them and the Romans, the Jews were defeated and fled; some were killed and the rest scattered. Aristobulus took refuge in Machaerus with his son Antigonus, who had escaped from Rome with him. Two days later he was wounded and captured, and was brought as a prisoner to Gabinius with his son Antigonus, and was sent back again to Rome and kept in chains, having been king and high priest for three years.

Gabinius went off to Egypt. Returning from there he found Aristobulus's son Alexander overrunning the country with a great army and killing all the Romans he met. Engaging him near Mount Tabor, when he led thirty thousand Jews, he killed about ten thousand. Having settled affairs in Jerusalem as Antipater wished, and having done other great deeds as general, he left for Rome, handing over the command to Crassus. This Crassus came into Judaea and took all the money in the temple, which Pompey had not touched, two thousand talents, and stripping the temple of its ornament he plundered it all, amounting to eight thousand talents of gold. He also took a beam of beaten gold made of three hundred minas. The mina among the Jews weighs two and a half pounds. Taking these, he set out against the Parthians, and perished with his army. Cassius, fleeing from there to Syria, also went up into Judaea.

Antipater had great influence with him, and with the Idumaeans, among whom he married a wife from Arabia named Cypros, by whom he had four sons, Phasael and Herod, Joseph and Pheroras, and a daughter Salome. Some time later Gaius Julius Caesar, having taken Rome after Pompey and most of the senate fled from it, released Aristobulus and sent him to Syria with an army. But Pompey's partisans forestalled him and killed Aristobulus with poison. Scipio, on instructions from Pompey, beheaded Aristobulus's son Alexander.

After Pompey's death Antipater made himself useful in many ways to Caesar while he was at war in Egypt, so that Caesar used him for the whole war; there he even happened to be wounded. Antigonus, the son of Aristobulus, came to Caesar then and begged him to pity him, cast out from his rule, and reminded him of his father and how he had died because of him. Antipater was present and answered. Since his words seemed the stronger, Caesar confirmed the high priesthood to Hyrcanus and appointed Antipater procurator of Judaea. When Caesar went away to Rome, Antipater set affairs in Judaea in order. Seeing that Hyrcanus was slow and sluggish, he appointed Phasael, the eldest of his sons, general of Jerusalem and the surrounding parts, and set Herod, the next after him, who was very young, over Galilee.

Herod, being noble in spirit, made his office an occasion for displaying his valour; he seized and killed the bandit chief Ezekias, who was plundering the neighbouring parts of Syria with a great band, and very many of those with him; and from this he was loved by the Syrians. Because of this he also became known to Sextus Caesar, who was a kinsman of the great Caesar and governor of Syria. Phasael emulated his brother. All this made Antipater receive royal honour from the nation. The men in office among the Jews envied Antipater and his sons for this, and feared them, seeing Herod violent, bold and in love with tyranny; and they accused Antipater to Hyrcanus and stirred him against him and his sons, saying that they were not stewards of the kingdom's affairs but masters. For Herod had killed Ezekias and many of those with him, though the law forbade putting a man to death, even if he was wicked, unless he had first been condemned by the Sanhedrin. Hyrcanus was roused to anger by this. The mothers of those murdered by Herod inflamed his anger further, begging that he be made to answer for what he had done. Moved, Hyrcanus summoned Herod to stand trial. He came with a band sufficient for him, so as not to go to trial bare and unguarded.

Coming into the Sanhedrin with the band, he terrified everyone, and no one dared to accuse him, but they were at a loss what to do. But one man named Sameas, a just man and bold as a lion, said: "Men, I know of no one who has been summoned to trial who has stood before us like this, nor, I think, do you; but everyone who is to be judged stands here in the guise of one who fears; while the excellent Herod, on trial for murders, stands with armed men round him, to kill us if he is condemned according to the law. But I would not blame Herod, but you, who have given him such licence. Know, then, that God is just, and that this man, whom you now wish to acquit for Hyrcanus's sake, will one day punish you and Hyrcanus himself." The account as it proceeds will show that this came to pass. Hyrcanus put off the trial to another day, and secretly advised Herod to slip out of the city. He went away, and the members of the Sanhedrin were indignant. When Sextus sold the generalship of Coele Syria to Herod for money, not much time passed before Herod came with an army, angry with Hyrcanus that he had been summoned to trial at all. His father and brother prevented him from attacking Jerusalem.

## 5.8

So things stood in Judaea; but affairs in Syria had been thrown into confusion for this reason. Caecilius Bassus, one of Pompey's partisans, killed Sextus Caesar by a plot and took control of affairs himself. When the generals of Julius Caesar set out against Bassus, Antipater fought on their side through his sons, remembering the benefits he had received from Caesar. While time was being spent in the war, Marcus came from Rome to Sextus's command. And Caesar was killed in Rome by Brutus and Cassius and their party. When war broke out over Caesar's death and the men in power scattered in different directions to gather armies, Cassius came to Syria, and going round it he gathered arms and soldiers, taxed most heavily, and exacted seven hundred talents of silver from Judaea, the collection of which Antipater divided between his two sons. Herod, being the first to bring Cassius what had been assigned to him, became his close friend. Malichus would have been put to death by Cassius, had not Hyrcanus checked his impulse by winning him over with a hundred talents through Antipater.

When Cassius had left Judaea, Malichus plotted against Antipater, thinking that if he were destroyed Hyrcanus's rule would be secure. This did not escape Antipater, who took precautions for himself; and Malichus denied it on oath. Marcus, the general in Syria, would almost have put Malichus to death, had not Antipater interceded with him and saved him. Cassius and Marcus, gathering an army, entrusted its charge to Herod, making him general of Coele Syria and promising to declare him king of Judaea after the war, which was then joined against Antony and the young Caesar. Then Malichus, bribing Hyrcanus's cupbearer, killed Antipater with poison; for they were both dining with Hyrcanus. When Antipater's sons learned of the plot, Malichus denied it. Herod wished to avenge his father's murder at once, but Phasael preferred to pursue Malichus by guile, so that they might not cause a civil war. So they pretended to believe Malichus's denial.

When a feast came at Jerusalem, Herod came to the city with an army; but Hyrcanus, persuaded by Malichus, tried to keep him from entering the city, on the pretext that a foreign crowd must not mingle with the people while they were purified. Paying no heed to his words, he entered the city by night. Malichus still kept up his pretence, weeping for Antipater and calling on him as a friend, but secretly he kept a guard on his person. When Cassius took Laodicea, both went to him. Herod was planning for Malichus to pay the penalty there; but Malichus, suspecting the matter, since his son was a hostage in Tyre, planned to steal him away secretly, set off for Judaea and seize the rule. Herod, suspecting Malichus's intention, sent ahead secretly to Tyre and persuaded the tribunes to go out against Malichus and kill him; for Cassius had already instructed them to help Herod in a just deed. They met him near the city and stabbed him to death. Hyrcanus was speechless with fear. When he came to himself he asked how Malichus had been killed; and hearing that it was at Cassius's command, he praised the deed, saying he was a wicked man and a plotter against his country.

## 5.9

When Cassius had left Syria to go against Antony, Herod distinguished himself on various occasions; and he met Antigonus, the son of Aristobulus, in battle just as he had set foot on the edge of the land of the Jews, defeated him and drove him out of its borders. So when he came to Jerusalem the people and Hyrcanus crowned him. He was also betrothed to Hyrcanus's granddaughter, the daughter of Alexander, the son of Aristobulus. He had before another wife, a commoner called Doris, by whom he had a son, Antipater, the eldest of his children.

When Antony and Caesar had defeated Cassius and Brutus at Philippi, Caesar went off to Gaul, and Antony to Asia. When he was in Bithynia, embassies met him from every side. Jews came too, accusing Phasael and Herod. When Herod came to make his defence, Antony treated him with honour, and the accusers were not even given a hearing, Herod having bought this from Antony with money. When Antony came to Ephesus, Hyrcanus sent him a golden crown, and asked that the Jews whom Cassius had taken captive, not by the law of war, be set free, and that the land Cassius had taken from them be restored. Judging the request just, he ordered it to be carried out. After this, when Antony came to Syria and was in the grip of his love for Cleopatra, a hundred of the most powerful men of the Jews came to him and accused Herod and those about him, with Hyrcanus also present. Antony asked Hyrcanus which of them led the nation better; and he said Herod and his brother, being related to them by marriage. So Antony, being well disposed to them because of his ties of guest-friendship with their father, named them both tetrarchs and entrusted the affairs of the Jews to them; and he put ten of the accusers in chains and would have killed them, had not the brothers begged them off. Again a thousand met Antony near Tyre. He, already won over by gifts, ordered the local governor to punish the Jews as rebels. Herod advised them to go away quickly, so as not to meet with great harm. When they would not listen, the Romans ran out, killed some and wounded many; and the rest escaped and kept quiet. When the people shouted against Herod, Antony, provoked, put the prisoners to death.

Antigonus promised Pacorus, the king of the Parthians, to give a thousand talents and five hundred women if they took the rule from Hyrcanus and handed it to him and killed Herod and his party. Because of this the Parthians marched against Judaea to bring Antigonus back; Herod's men engaged them often and won. The Parthian general came into the city with a few horsemen, as if to calm the strife, but in truth to help Antigonus. Phasael entertained him, and he persuaded Phasael to go as envoy to Barzapharnes. Hyrcanus and Phasael went off as envoys, though Herod did not agree; and the general escorted them. Barzapharnes received them sincerely at first, but then plotted against them. Phasael and those with him were suspicious of the barbarians, and learned that they were secretly guarded by them at night. They were told that they would have been seized already, had not the barbarians put it off until Herod had been taken by the Parthians there, lest he learn what had happened to them and escape. Some advised Phasael to ride away at once, and Ophellius even promised ships for the flight, for the sea was near. But he did not wish to leave Hyrcanus. So they were seized and put in chains.

Herod, learning this, took the armed men he had by night, with his mother, his sister, the girl betrothed to him, the daughter of Hyrcanus's daughter, the mother of this bride and all the household, and went off towards Idumaea, escaping the enemy's notice. When the carriage overturned on the road and his mother was in danger of dying, he almost killed himself. Recovering his mother and giving her such care as the crisis allowed, he pressed on more urgently towards the fortress of Masada. On the way he fought both the Parthians pursuing him and the Jews who attacked him in turn, and won and prevailed. But since the crowd following him was large, and the fortress of Masada, to which they were hurrying, was not enough to receive them all, he dismissed most of them, giving them provisions, and with those who were lightly equipped and his closest kin he reached the fortress. Leaving there the women and the household with sufficient provisions, he himself set off for Petra in Arabia. At dawn the Parthians plundered all the rest of the people of Jerusalem's goods and the palace itself, keeping away only from the money of Hyrcanus, which amounted to eighty talents; and the Parthians ravaged the country.

## 5.10

So Antigonus, brought back into Judaea in this way, received Hyrcanus and Phasael as prisoners. Fearing that the people would restore the kingdom to Hyrcanus, he cut off his ears, since the law requires those who are to be priests to be whole. Phasael, knowing he was about to be slaughtered, dashed his head against a rock, since his hands were bound, and so took himself out of life and robbed the enemy of the pleasure of killing him. Before he quite expired, hearing that his brother Herod had escaped the enemy, he died content, leaving an avenger behind him to punish his enemies.

Herod hurried to Malchus, the king of the Arabs, whom he had benefited before, to get money from him as ransom for his brother; for he had not yet learned what had happened to him. When Malchus sent word to him by some men to go back, since the Parthians had told him not to receive him, he answered that he had come to cause no trouble, but to talk about most necessary matters. With these words he went off to Egypt, and as he went he heard what had happened to his brother. Malchus repented and sent men to bring Herod back; but he was far away. Brought to Egypt and going on from there to Rome, he told Antony what had befallen him and Phasael, how Antigonus had been brought into the kingdom by the Parthians on a promise of money and women, and everything else he had done and suffered. Pity for Herod's change of fortune came over Antony. And Caesar, for other reasons and to please Antony, who was deeply grieved for Herod, was the more ready to help. So they brought Herod before the senate and told of the benefits his father had done and spoke of his own goodwill towards the Romans; they accused Antigonus and called him an enemy, both on other grounds and because he had received his rule from the Parthians, disregarding the Romans. Antony added that it was also useful for the war against the Parthians that Herod should be king. This pleased all, and they voted it.

So he received the kingdom in this way; but Antigonus was besieging Masada all the while. Those inside were so short of water that Herod's brother Joseph was planning to escape to the Arabs with two hundred men; but he was held back when rain fell in the night. Ventidius, the Roman general sent from Syria to keep the Parthians back, came into Judaea, supposedly to help the besieged, but really to get money from Antigonus. Having fulfilled his wish he withdrew, but left Silo with part of the army, so that the bribe might not be detected.

Herod sailed from Italy to Ptolemais, gathered a force and marched against Antigonus. Taking Joppa on the way, so that there might be no stronghold for the enemy, he hurried to Masada to rescue his kin; and taking them he went on towards Jerusalem; the troops with Silo were with him too. He camped outside, and those within, fighting from the wall, kept them off from the towers. Silo made some of his own soldiers cry out against Herod because of the shortage of necessities, and moved the camp as if to withdraw. He did this out of regard for Antigonus, because of the bribe. Herod asked him to stay, and going out he brought in a great quantity of provisions, so as to leave Silo no further pretext for withdrawing. They were in plenty, and Herod, coming to Samaria, settled his mother and his other kin there, and went himself to Galilee. He brought over the whole of it except those living in the caves. The caves were in mountains broken on every side and surrounded by sharp rocks. These too he mastered, with difficulty but all the same.

Having settled matters there, the king set out for Samaria, to decide things in battle with Antigonus. Meanwhile, when Pacorus fell in war and the Parthians were routed by the Romans, Ventidius sent Machaeras to Herod as a helper with an army. Herod left his brother Joseph with him, ordering him not to run risks and not to quarrel with Machaeras, and himself hurried to Antony, who was besieging Samosata, a city of the Euphrates region. When Herod drew near, Antony sent the army to meet him, greeted him when he came, and ordered Sossius to help him; and he did as he was told. Joseph, Herod's brother, hurrying towards Jericho, fell in with Antigonus's men, and cut off in rough country he died fighting bravely, and lost the whole army. Antigonus cut off his head and gave it back to his brother Pheroras for fifty talents.

## 5.11

The Galileans revolted and drowned in the lake those who sided with Herod, and much in Judaea was thrown into revolt. This was reported to Herod, and his brother's death, at Daphne by Antioch. As he hurried on, when he was in Galilee, the enemy met him. Defeated, they were shut up in a stronghold, and he hurried to Jericho, wishing to take vengeance on them for his brother. Antigonus sent a general named Pappus with a force against Samaria, giving his enemies the impression that he was making war from a surplus. Herod came against Pappus, engaged the enemy and prevailed, and followed them as they fled into the village, killing those he caught. When the houses were full of armed men and many had fled up onto the roofs, he pulled down the roofs of the houses and overcame them. As the roofs were pulled down, the rooms below were seen to be full of soldiers, whom they killed by throwing stones down on them. This broke the spirit of the enemy; and Herod would have come to Jerusalem at once with the army and finished the whole business, had not a severe winter held him back.

Then, in the evening, King Herod went into a small room to bathe, and stripped and was bathing, with one boy attending him. In the inner room some of the enemy had taken refuge, armed, and were hiding there out of fear. While the king was bathing, one came out with a drawn sword, and after him another and then a third, armed alike, striking no one out of fear, and glad if they themselves were saved. Such was the danger Herod escaped. The next day he cut off the head of Pappus, who had already been killed, and sent it to his brother Pheroras in return for the head of Joseph; for this Pappus was the one who had killed him with his own hand.

When the winter ended he came to Jerusalem and camped very close to the city; and leaving there men to prepare for the siege, he went himself to Samaria to marry the daughter of Alexander, who had already been betrothed to him, as has been told. After the wedding he came from Samaria; and Sossius came too with an army. They gathered at the wall of Jerusalem, raised mounds, brought up siege engines and shook the wall. Those within resisted, led by desperation rather than forethought. First twenty picked men climbed the wall, then centurions of Sossius. The first wall was taken in forty days, the second in fifteen. When the outer temple and the lower city were taken, the Jews fled into the inner temple and the upper city. These too were taken, and everything was full of slaughter.

Antigonus, mindful neither of his present fortune nor of his past, came down from the fortress and fell at Sossius's feet. He, without pitying him for his change of fortune, laughed at him, called him Antigone, and kept him in chains. When the allies rushed to view the sanctuary and the holy things in the temple, King Herod held them back, some by entreaty, some by threats, and some even by arms, and stopped the plundering in the city, promising to pay each man's wages himself from his own means. So, having saved the rest of the city, he fulfilled his promises. To Sossius himself he gave most royal gifts. He left Jerusalem taking Antigonus in chains to Antony. Herod, afraid that Antigonus, if brought to Rome, would plead his case before the senate, showing himself to be of royal descent and Herod a private man, and that even if he himself had wronged the Romans, the kingdom belonged to his children, persuaded Antony with much money to put Antigonus to death. So he was killed, and the rule was taken from the family of the Hasmonaeans, after lasting a hundred and twenty years, and passed to Herod the son of Antipater, who was of a private family and a common house.

## 5.12

Having in this way taken on the rule of all Judaea, Herod brought over those who sided with him and punished those who opposed him. He honoured above all Pollio the Pharisee and Sameas his disciple; for while the siege was going on these advised receiving Herod. This Sameas, as has already been said above, had foretold to Hyrcanus and the judges that if Herod survived he would pursue them all. He killed forty of the leading men of Antigonus's party and took their property, and there was no end to the evil.

Hyrcanus, a captive among the Parthians, met with kindness from Phraates, the king of the Parthians, and released from his chains he was allowed to live in Babylon, where there was a multitude of Jews, who honoured Hyrcanus as high priest and king. Learning that Herod had taken over the kingdom, he thought of moving to him, both because of the marriage tie and thinking that he would remember that he had saved him from danger when he was on trial for murder. The Jews in Babylon asked him to stay, since he was honoured by them as high priest and king, and because even if he went he could not hold the high priesthood, having been mutilated in body by Antigonus. They tried to stop him, but he would not be persuaded, both longing to return himself and being urged by Herod. Herod sent an embassy and gifts to Phraates too, asking him not to prevent him from repaying his benefactor. His eagerness was not for Hyrcanus's sake; but because he did not rule by right, he feared changes that would have reason on their side, and he hurried either to put Hyrcanus out of the way or meanwhile to have him in his hands. When the Parthian allowed his departure, Hyrcanus came and was treated with every honour by Herod, called father, given the first place at feasts and deceived in every way, so that he might not perceive that he was being plotted against.

Herod, wary of appointing any of the notable men high priest, sent for a priest of the more obscure from Babylon, named Ananel, and gave him the high priesthood. Alexandra, Herod's mother-in-law, who had a son by Alexander the son of Aristobulus, very beautiful in his youth, called Aristobulus, took the slighting of her son hard; and she wrote to Cleopatra to ask Antony for the high priesthood for the boy. When Antony was slow over the request, Dellius came to Judaea, and seeing Aristobulus he admired him, and no less Mariamme, the king's wife; and he persuaded Alexandra to send portraits of both her children to Antony; for if he saw them, he said, she would not fail to obtain anything she asked. So she sent the portraits to Antony; but he was ashamed to send for the girl, since she was married to Herod, and at the same time he avoided slanders with Cleopatra. He wrote to Herod to send the boy, adding, "if it does not seem burdensome". Herod, judging it against his interest that Aristobulus, being most beautiful and of preeminent birth, should come to Antony, who was most powerful among the Romans and ready for love affairs and easily drawn to pleasures, wrote back that if the youth left the country, everything would be filled with disturbance.

So he excused himself to Antony; and gathering his friends he blamed Alexandra for plotting to have him deprived of the rule. "But I will not," he said, "be unjust because of this; but now I give the priesthood to the youth; for it was because he was still quite a child that I made another high priest before." When he said this, joy and fear together seized Alexandra: joy at the honour to her son, fear at Herod's suspicion. Weeping, she defended herself, saying that she had been eager about the priesthood, but had not aimed at the kingdom; and now she accepted the honour for her son, and assured him that she would be obedient in everything.

## 5.13

After talking in this way they parted, as if all suspicion had been removed. When the high priesthood had been given to the boy Aristobulus, the affairs of the household seemed to have been healed. But Alexandra was suspect to Herod, and he required her to live in the palace and do nothing on her own authority, and some kept careful watch on her. She was enraged, preferring to endure anything rather than live in slavery and fear; and she begged Cleopatra to help, telling her the state she was in. Cleopatra told her to run away to her with the boy. So she prepared two coffins as if for carrying out dead bodies, and was going to put herself and her son into them, having ordered the servants who were in the secret to carry them out by night and take them to the sea, where a boat had been prepared for them to sail to Egypt. Herod learned this from one of her servants, let her go on until the attempt, and caught her in the very act of flight. He overlooked the offence out of fear of Cleopatra, and not out of kindness.

He had decided to put the youth out of the way. So when he was seventeen, he went up to the altar to sacrifice at the feast of tabernacles, robed as high priest. An impulse of goodwill towards him came over the multitude because of his beauty, the size of his body and the dignity of his family; they rejoiced and were overcome at once, and uttered words of acclamation mingled with prayers. Moved by this, Herod held all the more to his purpose against the youth. When the feast was over, after a banquet, he made much of the youth, played the young man and joked with him to please him. They swam in the pools; and Herod's friends, who were in the secret, swimming with them as if in play, did not stop pressing Aristobulus down and ducking him until they drowned him. So he perished before he had completed his eighteenth year, and the misfortune was felt by all as their own. Alexandra, understanding the cause of his death too, was gripped still more by grief, but held out for fear of other evils. Herod did everything to remove suspicion, weeping, appearing distraught and making a show of a lavish funeral. Alexandra was softened by none of this, but wrote to Cleopatra of her son's death by Herod's plot; and she urged Antony to avenge the boy's murder.

So Antony sent ordering Herod to come to Laodicea and defend himself. He, fearing the charge and Cleopatra's hostility, as he went left his uncle Joseph as steward of affairs there, ordering him secretly that if anything happened to him at Antony's hands, he should at once kill Mariamme, so that when he was dead she might not be kept for another because of her beauty. So Herod went away; and Joseph, managing the government and constantly meeting Mariamme and Alexandra, told them of the king's love for Mariamme. When they spoke ironically about his words, he was led on to reveal the secret of his orders too. This drove the women to still greater desperation. A rumour also arose among those hostile to Herod that Antony had killed him. Meanwhile letters came from Herod telling of the honour Antony paid him, how he sat with him in judging cases and dined with him, and that he received these honours even though Cleopatra was harsh to him in slander. When these letters arrived, the false rumour ceased.

## 5.14

When King Herod, having escorted Antony on his way against the Parthians, returned to Judaea, at once his sister Salome and their mother accused Alexandra and Mariamme. Salome even brought a charge against her own husband, that he had lain with Mariamme; he was Joseph, the steward of the affairs of the kingdom. She said this mostly out of anger with Mariamme because she taunted them with their low birth. Herod was at once disturbed, and in his jealousy questioned Mariamme privately. When she swore it was not so, he relaxed his anger, was overcome by love, and assured her of his affection for her. She said: "It was not the act of a loving man to order that I too should be killed if any harm came to you from Antony." These words disturbed Herod, and he cried out that Joseph's love for her was clearly proved by this. For he would not, he said, have revealed the secret if no great intimacy had joined them. And he would have killed his wife at once had he not been enslaved by love of her. Joseph, without even letting him come into his sight, he ordered to be put to death, and Alexandra, as the cause of everything, he put in chains and kept under guard.

Antony, corrupted by love of Cleopatra, or rather by her drugs, was enslaved to her wishes. She had poisoned her brother, to whom the kingdom belonged, and killed her sister Arsinoe through Antony; and she pressed Antony to assign Judaea and Arabia to her. He, ashamed of the open injustice, but forced to please her because of his love and her spells, cut off parts of both countries and with these appeased her greed. Antony marched to Armenia, and she on her way back was in Judaea, where Herod met her. When she had become familiar with Herod she invited him to her bed, being incontinent in lust and perhaps feeling some love for him, or, which is more likely, contriving their intercourse as the start of a trap against the man. Herod rejected her words, but courted her with gifts and escorted her on her way to Egypt.

In the seventh year of Herod's reign the land of the Jews was shaken by an earthquake such as never before; there was great loss of cattle, and about thirty thousand people were buried in the fallen houses. When Herod had farmed the tributes of the lands assigned to Cleopatra from Arabia and Judaea, the Arab behaved unfairly over payment of the tax. So the king decided to march against the Arab, and being permitted by Antony he engaged him many times and at last won, and was chosen by the Arabs to lead their nation. He returned home, having won a great name by his exploits and full of pride.

Just after Caesar had defeated Antony in the battle of Actium, Herod's affairs were thrown into confusion and almost despaired of. For there was no hope, after so great a friendship with Antony, that he would not be harmed by Caesar. So, having in mind to remove Hyrcanus, he thought the attempt more to his advantage then, so that a man more worthy to obtain his kingdom might not survive. Herod had this in mind, but something that happened spurred him on to the deed further. Alexandra, being a contentious woman, did not stop urging her father to go over to Malchus, who held Arabia. He at first rejected her words, but as she pressed him he at last wrote a letter to Malchus about receiving them, and gave it to one of his friends, Dositheus. He handed the letter to Herod, and Herod asked Dositheus to deliver the letter to Malchus and bring back his reply. When Dositheus had done this, the Arab wrote back that he would receive Hyrcanus himself and all those with him. Receiving this letter, Herod sent for Hyrcanus and questioned him about his agreement with Malchus; when he denied it, he showed the letters to the Sanhedrin and put the man to death. Many say that the affair of Hyrcanus was a pretext of Herod's, who wished to put him out of the way, and they take as proof the man's gentleness or simplicity, and that even in his youth he had shown no rashness or recklessness; he was then eighty-one years old.

## 5.15

Herod, hurrying to Caesar, placed his mother, his sister and all his family at Masada, and took his wife Mariamme with her mother Alexandra to Alexandrium, setting over them as guards, under pretext of honour, Joseph the treasurer and Soemus the Ituraean, who were most faithful to him, ordering them that if they heard anything bad about him they should at once kill them both, and keep the kingdom for his sons and his brother Pheroras. Having given such orders, he hurried to Rhodes to Caesar. Landing there, he took off his diadem, but laid aside nothing else of his dignity, and in talking with Caesar he showed the greatness of his spirit, neither turning to supplication nor giving an account of what he had done with any reserve. So he won Caesar over not a little, and Caesar restored the diadem to him and treated him with honour. Having thus, beyond hope, had his kingdom made more secure, he escorted Caesar on his way to Egypt, giving most generous gifts to him and his friends; and he returned to Judaea with greater honour and confidence, and found his household in turmoil.

For Mariamme and Alexandra, thinking (as was the case) that they had been shut up in Alexandrium as if under guard, so that they might not have power even over themselves, took it hard, and won over the guards by attentions, especially Soemus, courting him with words and gifts. He gave way little by little and revealed the king's orders to them. They were bitterly disposed at this, Mariamme most of all. For when Herod, as was natural, told the good news of his fortunes first to his wife and embraced her before the others, she groaned at his embraces and seemed vexed at his good fortune, so that the king was disturbed and troubled at the unaccountable hatred, and often set out to avenge her contempt, but was checked because he was held fast by love. Above all he feared that by punishing her he might unawares do himself more harm, if the woman he loved were gone. His mother and sister provoked Herod with slanders, instilling jealousy and hatred in him. And he grew ever worse towards her, since she did not hide her feelings towards him, and he kept turning love into anger. And had he not been hurrying to Caesar in Egypt, who had already won, Antony and Cleopatra being dead, perhaps the terrible thing would have been done at once. As it was, he left the affairs of his household as they were, and coming to Egypt he was granted the greatest honours by Caesar and returned more splendid.

He loved Mariamme most ardently; and she, though in other respects chaste and faithful to him, took advantage of her husband, enslaved by love, and often insulted him, and mocked his mother and sister for their low birth. The hatred broke out into the open on this occasion. At midday the king went into his bedroom to rest and called Mariamme; and she came in and reviled him for having killed her grandfather and her brother. The king was angry at this. Salome, seizing the moment, having first bribed the cupbearer to accuse Mariamme, persuaded him to go to the king then and tell him what she had taught him. He said that he had been courted with gifts by Mariamme, who was urging him to give the king a love potion; it was some drug whose power, he insisted, he did not know. Hearing this, the king was moved still more to anger, and tortured his wife's eunuch, who was most faithful to her. He neither knew nor said anything about what he was being tortured for, but said that the woman's hatred had arisen from the words Soemus had told her. He had not yet finished speaking when Herod cried out loudly: "Soemus would never have made light of my orders, unless he had had some intimacy with my wife." So he ordered Soemus to be killed at once; and gathering his closest kin, he accused his wife of potions and drugs, and was angrily disposed against her. Those present, seeing him so, condemned her to death.

As she was being led away to death, her mother Alexandra, now afraid for herself too, and making a show of ignorance of what Mariamme was accused of, leapt out and called her daughter wicked and ungrateful to her husband, and said she was suffering justly. She was neither disturbed at this nor made any answer, but went to her death with a calm bearing and noble spirit, showing her high birth even at the last.

## 5.16

So she died, Salome having hastened her death; and Herod was then all the more inflamed with love for her, and often called on her and lamented unseemly. His passion so mastered him that he even ordered his servants to call Mariamme. At last he gave himself to solitude, and, being distraught in it, he fell into a terrible illness: it was an inflammation and a pain at the back of the neck and a derangement of the mind. While he was ill in this way, Alexandra in Jerusalem, learning of the king's illness, tried to gain control of the two fortresses about the city. Learning this, Herod at once ordered her to be put to death; and having himself barely escaped the danger of his illness, he was harsh and hard to please and ready for punishments and murders; and there were murders not only of the many but even of his closest friends. He also transgressed the ancestral customs and corrupted the old order with foreign practices. At this the multitude was troubled and angry. Ten of the citizens conspired, hid daggers under their cloaks and went into the theatre by agreement, to kill either Herod himself or at least many of those about him. They were found out, and not even denying the plan but showing their swords, they endured every torture and were put to death. A little later some people seized the man who had informed against them, cut him limb from limb and threw him to the dogs. Herod found them and punished them with their whole households. But the anger of the multitude remained.

Then most terrible sufferings befell the country, famine, and diseases of the body from unaccustomed diet caused by the lack of food, and on top of all these, plague. Herod, eager to help in the crisis, neither had money, having already spent it for display on the adornment of cities, nor did the neighbouring lands have grain, since the same scarcity prevailed in them too. Deciding meanwhile to help as he could, he broke up the ornaments in the palace into coin, sent to Egypt and bought grain from there. When it was brought, he distributed grain to those who could prepare their food themselves; and for those who because of old age or some other weakness could not prepare food for themselves, he provided by appointing bakers and supplying them with ready food. This not only changed the minds of those who had been angry with him before, but turned them to goodwill. Having thus recovered his rule after it had been damaged, he no less relieved the neighbours who were suffering equally from the calamity, so that ten thousand kors of grain were given outside his realm, and about eighty thousand within his own kingdom. A kor, according to Josephus, is worth ten Attic medimni. This generosity and the timeliness of the favour changed the Jews from hostility to affection, and won him renown among outsiders.

He also contrived a marriage for himself out of amorous desire. A priest in Jerusalem, Simon, had a most beautiful daughter; Herod fell in love with her. Since Simon was unsuitable for a marriage alliance because of his obscurity, he took the high priesthood from Jesus the son of Phabes, who held it then, made Simon high priest and married his daughter. With everything going as it should, he surrounded himself with security from outside, dealing skilfully with cities and courting the powerful, so that everything increased for him in every way. Through his ambition in this and his courting of Caesar and of the most powerful Romans, he transgressed the customs and debased the laws, founding cities and raising temples, not in the land of the Jews but outside it, excusing himself to the Jews that he did these things by command and not of his own accord, and doing favours to Caesar and the Romans by departing from his ancestral customs out of honour to them. For he set up statues and carved images, and built cities, broad harbours sheltered from the waves, costly palaces and splendid residences.

## 5.17

While so engaged, he sent his sons Alexander and Aristobulus to Rome to meet Caesar.
