Caesar received them kindly, and gave Herod the right to assign the kingdom to whichever of his sons he wished, added more land, and associated him with the governors of Syria, ordering them to do everything with his consent. Having enjoyed such good fortune, he asked Caesar for a tetrarchy for his brother Pheroras, and remitted a third of the tribute to those in his kingdom, as he said, so that they might recover from the barren years, but as others thought, to heal the multitude's hostility to him; for they took it hard that their customs were being changed. So he took away their liberties, always giving them orders, forbidding meetings, watching their walks and their ways of life and punishing most severely those caught; both in the city and on journeys there were men watching those who came together. Some say that he himself sometimes put on the dress of a private man and mingled with the crowds by night, testing what they thought about his rule. Those who were defiant he pursued in every way, and he required the multitude to confirm their loyalty to him by oaths. Most gave way, but those who were displeased he made away with altogether. He also tried to persuade Pollio the Pharisee and Sameas and most of their fellow disciples to swear. They were neither persuaded nor punished, because the king respected Pollio.

Those called Essenes were also released from this compulsion; this is a body that follows a Pythagorean way of life. He honoured them because of Manaemus. He was one of them, a man good in other respects and foreseeing the future, who, seeing Herod still a boy going to school, addressed him as king of the Jews. He said he was a private person. Manaemus smiled, slapped him gently and said: "But you will be king, and complete your reign most happily; and remember these blows of mine. You will be best if you love justice, piety towards God and fairness towards the citizens. But I do not know that you will be such." When Herod became king, he sent for Manaemus and asked about the length of his rule. When he was silent, and Herod himself asked whether there would be ten years of his reign, or twenty, or thirty, he did not set a limit to the end of the term; and Herod, content with this too, dismissed Manaemus with a handclasp and for his sake honoured all the Essenes.

In the eighteenth year of his reign he decided to rebuild the temple, raise it higher and make it more magnificent. The multitude hesitated at the undertaking. He said he would not pull down the temple before he had prepared everything he needed for the work. When everything had been prepared, he pulled it down, laid other foundations and raised the temple a hundred cubits long and twenty more in height. It was built of white, strong stones, each about twenty-five cubits long, eight high and about twelve broad. On the north side a well-defended angular citadel had been walled in, exceptional in strength, which the kings who were also high priests, of the family of the Hasmonaeans, had built and called the Baris, so that the high priest's robe might be stored in it. Herod rebuilt this Baris too, stronger, for the safety of the temple, and named it Antonia in memory of Antony. The temple itself and everything about it were built in eight years. It is recorded that at the time when the temple itself was being raised (for it was built in one year and six months), it did not rain by day, but the rains came at night, so that the works were not hindered.

Trying to check wrongdoing, Herod made a law that housebreakers should be sold for export out of the country; which was burdensome as a punishment for the sufferers, and not least a breaking of the laws. For to be slaves to foreigners and forced to live by their customs was, so far as it lay with them, the destruction of their religion. For the laws ordered thieves to be sold if they could not repay fourfold what they had stolen, but not to foreigners, only to their own countrymen, so that they might neither fall away from their religion nor be slaves for their whole life, but gain release after six years. This was part of the slanders against him and of the multitude's ill will towards him.

## 5.18

At that time Herod went to Italy, to talk with Caesar and see his sons, who were living in Rome; he was received kindly by Caesar, and took his sons, now that they had completed their studies, to bring them home. When they returned, they became admired both for the bearing of their souls and for the beauty of their looks, and were envied by Salome, the king's sister, and by those who had destroyed their mother with slanders. Already they were preparing against them the weapons by which they had brought down the woman who bore them, spreading the story that the youths were unfriendly to their father because of their mother's murder, and contriving as far as they could to make hatred grow in the father towards his sons. For a while, however, the father was still affectionate towards them, gave them a share of honour, and when they came of age he married them to wives: Aristobulus to Salome's daughter Berenice, and Alexander to Glaphyra, the daughter of Archelaus, king of the Cappadocians.

This fed Salome's hostility to the young men all the more, and she won over all who had helped her bring about Mariamme's death. Since the young men too gave some handles, through remembering their mother and through desire for power, they abused Salome and Pheroras, the hostility of these towards them increased, and malicious slanders against them went forward, taking their grounds from the young men themselves. For when the foul Salome spoke ill of them and their mother and provoked them to talk, they described their mother's end as pitiable and called themselves wretched for being forced to live with her murderers. This happened while the king was abroad. As soon as he returned, these words were brought to him by Pheroras and Salome, who said that a great danger hung over them, since the young men openly threatened to avenge their mother's murder. Herod was disturbed, as others reported this too. In this state of mind he decided, to bring the young men down, to take into favour another son, named Antipater, born to him while he was still a private man; and he chose to honour him so as to check the boldness of Mariamme's sons, who would learn that the succession to the kingdom was not owed to them alone or of necessity. So he brought in Antipater as a kind of reserve.

He, being clever, once he had gained freedom of speech, had one aim, to keep close to his father and estrange him from his brothers by slanders. And they still gave openings, weeping as though dishonoured, calling on their mother and saying openly that their father was not just. Antipater's people maliciously reported this to Herod with additions and made his hostility to them greater. Wishing to humble Mariamme's sons, the father gave Antipater more honour; and at last he brought his mother in too. He commended him to Caesar, writing on his behalf, and sent him to Rome with many gifts, so that everything already seemed to rest with him, and the youths seemed to have been pushed altogether out of the rule.

Antipater, afraid that while he was abroad his father might become more lenient towards Mariamme's sons, did not stop writing continually to his father against his brothers even while abroad, and stirring him to hostility, until he brought him to the point of sailing to Rome and accusing his sons there before Caesar. Going to Rome with his sons, he presented them to Caesar and charged them with madness, saying they hated their father and were planning to kill him and so take the kingdom. While their father was still speaking the young men were in tears, and at last wailing, fearing that if they kept silent they would seem through a guilty conscience to have no defence. When they saw goodwill from Caesar, and of the others some weeping with them and all grieving with them, Alexander set about dissolving the charges, addressing his words to his father. When he had spoken very persuasively, Caesar, who had not believed the slanders against them even before, was still more changed, and kept looking at Herod, seeing that he too was somewhat confounded. The audience was in suspense. Caesar said that the young men, even if they seemed far from the slanders, had erred in this very thing, that they had not shown themselves such to their father that no such talk could arise about them; and he urged Herod to be reconciled to his sons, putting away all suspicion; for he judged it unjust even to think these charges against his sons credible. Giving such advice, he nodded to the young men to fall at their father's feet. As they set out to do so, their father anticipated them and embraced them weeping, taking each in his arms.

Then they thanked Caesar and went away together, and Antipater with them, pretending to be glad at the reconciliation. The next day Caesar gave Herod authority over the kingdom, to appoint whichever of his sons he chose as successor, or to divide it among them all, but after his death; while he lived he did not allow the division, but wished him to remain master both of his sons and of the kingdom. As he returned, Archelaus, Alexander's father-in-law, met Herod in Cilicia, rejoicing with him at the reconciliation of his sons. From there Herod came to Judaea, called an assembly, told what had been done on his journey, ended his speech with admonition to his sons, and announced that he was leaving the kingdom to his sons, first to Antipater, and then to those of Mariamme. With these words he dismissed the gathering.

## 5.19

In disposition he was most generous and beneficent to others, but oppressive and most unjust to his subjects, and to his kin and friends an implacable punisher. The causes of this were love of glory and love of power. For through love of glory, if he was likely to win remembrance hereafter or praise at present, he did not spare expense; and being lavish, he pressed his subjects with heavy exactions and was harsh to them. Through love of power, if he suspected anyone of aiming at the rule or of stirring anything against it, he treated him like an enemy; and so he punished kinsmen and friends unsparingly, wishing to be honoured alone. A proof that he wished to make money from every quarter because of his lavishness is that, having heard that Hyrcanus, who reigned before him, had opened the tomb of David and taken three thousand talents of silver, he opened the tomb at night and went in, taking his most trusted friends, so that what was done might not get out. He found no money, that is, silver, but many treasures of gold ornament, which he took away entirely. He was eager to go further in among the coffins in which the bodies of the kings David and Solomon had been laid away. When he tried to force his way in, two of his guards were destroyed, a flame, as the story goes, meeting them from within, and he went out in terror.

Because of this attempt his household affairs seemed to grow worse; for the affairs of the royal court were like a civil war. Antipater was always waging war against his brothers, being clever, entangling them in charges through others, while often defending them himself, so that, seeming well disposed to them, he might be unsuspected by his father in his schemes and seem the only one who cared for his safety. He was everything to his father, while Mariamme's sons were always worse disposed and, through their high birth, did not bear the dishonour, being thrust aside and given a lower place. And the wives: Glaphyra, the daughter of Archelaus, who was married to Alexander, hated Salome, both because of her disposition towards her husband and because of Salome's daughter, who was married to Aristobulus; Glaphyra treated her arrogantly and resented her equal rank.

A cause also arose which brought Pheroras, the king's brother, into suspicion and hatred with his brother. The king's daughter had been betrothed to him, but he, overcome by a slave woman and madly in love with her, paid no attention to his brother's daughter, but devoted himself to the slave. Herod was vexed at this and married the girl to a son of Phasael; and after a time he blamed his brother for what had happened before and asked him to take his second daughter, thinking that his love for the slave had already faded. He sent away the slave, by whom he had a child, and agreed to take the king's daughter after thirty days. But when the appointed time had passed he was so mad with love for the slave that he broke what had been agreed and went back to living with the first. This drove Herod wild; and always some new thing falling on him did not let him rest.

Salome, being hostile to Mariamme's sons, persuaded her own daughter, who was married to Aristobulus, not to be well disposed to her husband, but to report to her whatever he said in private. She said that the young men remembered their mother and loathed their father, and threatened, when they gained the rule, to make Herod's sons by his other wives village clerks, and to shut up the women so that they would not even see the sun. This was reported to the king through the vilest Salome. He heard it with pain, but tried to set things right; and when his sons defended themselves he grew easier.

## 5.20

Pheroras threw affairs into confusion again, telling Alexander that he had heard Salome say that Herod was in love with Glaphyra. Alexander was disturbed at the words out of jealousy, and not bearing the pain he reported to his father what Pheroras had said. Herod, deeply moved and unable to bear the falseness of the slander, was distraught; he sent for Pheroras and said: "Vilest of men, by saying such things against us, do you think you have put words into my son's soul, or a sword into his right hand?" Pheroras said that Salome had persuaded him to it, and that the words were hers. She denied it, tore her hair and beat her breast, but because of the malice of her character she was not believed. At last the king sent away both his brother and his sister, and praised his son for his self-control and for bringing the words to him.

Something else happened that again raised disturbances in the king's household. He had eunuchs whom he favoured for their beauty, one appointed to pour his wine, one to serve his dinner and one to put him to bed. It was reported that they had been bribed by Alexander. Put to torture, the eunuchs admitted that they had had relations with the young man, but said they knew of nothing else by Alexander against his father. When the torturers increased the lashes, they said that Alexander had hostility and hatred towards his father, and urged them to give Herod up because of his age and attach themselves to him, since the kingdom would come round to him even if his father did not wish it, both because of his birth and because of the goodwill of the commanders and friends. Hearing this, Herod was terrified, had suspicions and hatred towards everyone, and forbade many of his friends even to come to the palace. Antipater was the cause of it all.

First, then, Herod examined under torture all those he thought loyal to Alexander, whether they knew of anything dared against him; and they died having nothing to say. But one, unable to bear the tortures, said that Alexander, when praised for the size of his body, his accurate shooting with the bow and the rest, used to say that whatever good had been given him by nature or added by training turned to his misfortune; for his father was vexed at his good qualities. He added that Alexander had planned with Aristobulus to kill their father while hunting and flee to Rome to seek the kingdom. Letters of Alexander to his brother were also found, saying that their father was not acting justly in preferring Antipater. On this he seized Alexander and put him in chains. He was eager to get some greater proof against his son too, so as not to seem to have chained him rashly. So he tortured and killed many, even of those in office, who said nothing such as he expected. When one of the younger men was under compulsion, he said that Alexander had written to his friends in Rome asking to be summoned by Caesar, to inform him that Mithridates, the king of the Parthians, had made friends with his father against the Romans; and that he had a poison prepared at Ascalon. Herod reckoned this a consolation for his rashness. But the poison, searched for at once, was not found.

Because of the excess of his troubles Alexander became contentious, and wishing to take revenge on his enemies so that they might perish with him, he sent letters to his father saying there was no need for torture; for the plot had been planned, and Pheroras and his most trusted friends shared in it; and Salome had come to him at night and lain with him against his will; and that all had come together so that, with him out of the way, they might be rid of always expecting to be destroyed.

Archelaus, the king of the Cappadocians, learning this and anxious for his daughter and his son-in-law, came, and skilfully set about remedying the troubles, condemning the young man, calling Herod lenient, and saying he would dissolve the marriage. As Archelaus said this, Herod gave way in his harshness and was moved to grief and tears, and begged him not to dissolve the marriage, but to relax his anger at the young man's offences. Archelaus, seeing Herod already softened, turned the charges onto others, and especially onto Pheroras. Pheroras turned to Archelaus, so that he might be his mediator with Herod. Archelaus advised him that it was better to go to his brother himself and entreat him, admitting that he was the cause of everything; for so he would soften the harshness of his anger; and he promised to be present and help. Pheroras was persuaded. Alexander was freed from the charges, and Archelaus reconciled Pheroras to Herod.

## 5.21

Some time later Herod's affairs with his sons and household grew much worse. Eurycles, a man of Lacedaemon not undistinguished there, but a most wicked man in his purposes, visited Herod, gave him gifts, received more, and became a friend of the king above all. He lodged at Antipater's; and he also went to Alexander, saying he was known to Archelaus too, and so he pretended to honour Glaphyra. When he had become familiar with him, Alexander poured out the tragedy of his situation, told him of his mother's fate, and said it seemed past bearing. He, in his pain, made such remarks to Eurycles, and Eurycles reported everything to Antipater. Antipater rewarded him with gifts and asked him to tell the words to his father. He so disposed the king as to make his hatred irrevocable. He went off having made his money, and Herod was so enraged against his sons that he no longer needed slanders, but himself pried into their affairs and watched everything.

Two of the king's bodyguards, who had been dismissed in his anger, rode with Alexander and his companions and received gifts from him. Suspecting them, Herod at once put them to torture. They held out at first, and then reported that Alexander was persuading them to kill Herod while he was hunting. The commandant of Alexandrium too was examined, as having promised to receive the young men in the fortress. He admitted nothing, but his son agreed that this had happened, and produced letters about it, apparently in Alexander's hand. So Herod no longer had any doubt about his sons' plot, while Alexander insisted that the little letter had been forged by Antipater. Then the young men were put under guard, and had the disgrace and fear of condemned men.

Aristobulus, thinking that his mother-in-law Salome shared his grief and hated the man who believed such things, said: "This warns of danger for you too, since you have been slandered over your hope of marrying Syllaeus." She at once brought these words to her brother. He ordered both sons to be put in chains and kept apart from each other, and each to write down what they had planned against their father. They wrote that they had neither thought of nor contrived a plot against their father, but had planned flight, and this from necessity, since their life was suspected and full of fear.

Then, when an envoy came from Archelaus, Herod brought Alexander out in chains and asked about the flight in the envoy's hearing, where and how they had decided to go away. He said they had agreed with Archelaus that he would send them on from there to Rome, but had thought of nothing else wrong or harmful against their father. When this had been said, the king gave letters to Caesar to two of his men, and ordered them, putting in at Cilicia on their voyage, to meet Archelaus and reproach him for having joined his sons in the plot. Archelaus defended himself, saying that he had agreed to receive the young men for the good of both them and their father, but not to send them to Caesar. The bearers of the letters, reaching Rome, gave them to Caesar. He wrote back that he was grieved for the sons, but gave Herod full authority. If they had done anything impious, he should proceed against them as parricides; but if they had thought of flight, he should admonish them otherwise and do nothing irreparable. He advised him to gather a council near Berytus, taking the governors, Archelaus the king of the Cappadocians and all others he knew to be eminent in rank, and consider with them what was needed.

## 5.22

On receiving this letter Herod summoned to the council those he wished, leaving out Archelaus out of enmity, or because he thought he would oppose his purpose. When the governors and the others had gathered, the king accused his sons and read out what they themselves had written; in which nothing else was written than that they planned to flee, and some abuse of him containing reproaches because of their ill will. At last, saying that the authority had been given him both by nature and by Caesar, he added an ancestral law, which ordered that if parents accused a child and laid their hands on his head, the bystanders must stone him and so kill him. This, he said, he could have done himself in his own country and kingdom, but he had waited for their judgement. When Herod had said this, the members of the council confirmed his authority, though the young men had not even been brought before the council. Some condemned Herod's sons, but not to death; the greater number declared that they should be punished with death too. With that the council broke up. Herod came to Tyre, bringing his sons. When they came to Caesarea, everyone was in suspense, waiting to see how he would proceed against the young men. They were distressed at what was happening, but it was not safe either to say anything for them or to hear another say it; they bore the excess of their feeling in pain, but in silence.

A soldier named Tero, whose son was of Alexander's age and his friend, said much to the crowd, and speaking boldly asked to meet the king alone. When Herod allowed it, he said: "Where has that outstanding mind of yours gone? What is this desertion by friends and kin? Will you not consider what is being done, if you destroy two young men born to you of a queen, foremost in every virtue, leaving yourself in old age dependent on one son and on kinsmen whom you have yourself so often condemned to death? Will you not reflect that even the silence of the crowds comes from the greatness of their grief, and that the whole army feels pity for the unfortunate and hatred for those who are bringing this about?" At first the king heard this not without feeling. But Tero, using an unmeasured, soldierly freedom of speech, disturbed Herod. He was stirred by the soldiers' indignation, and ordered Tero to be bound and kept under guard. Trypho, the king's barber, seized the moment too, saying that he had often been urged by Tero to cut the king's throat with his razor; for he would be among the first with Alexander. Having said this he too was arrested. Tero, his son and the barber himself were put to torture. As Tero held out under the tortures, his son, seeing his father in a bad way, said he would tell the king the truth if he would free his father and himself from torture. Receiving pledges, he said there was an agreement that Tero would attack the king with his own hand. With these words he freed his father from the torment. Herod, with no doubt any longer left in his soul about killing his children, at last carried out his purpose. Alexander and Aristobulus were taken to Sebaste and strangled with a cord on their father's order. Bringing before the crowd three hundred of the officers who were under accusation, with Tero and his son and the barber, he accused them; and the people pelted them with whatever came to hand and killed them.

For Antipater, who had brought about his brothers' end, attaining the kingdom became harder, since hatred had grown against him in the nation, and above all in the army. For the time, however, he shared the rule with his father and was trusted by him. Herod sent Alexander's wife back to her father, and brought up the dead men's children with great care. Alexander had two sons by Glaphyra, and Aristobulus three sons and two daughters by Berenice. A son, Herod, was also born to the king by the high priest's daughter. For nine wives lived with the king, it being an ancestral custom to have several at the same time. They were Antipater's mother and the high priest's daughter, by whom, as has been said, a son of the same name was born to him. He was also married to one daughter of his brother, and to a cousin with her, that is, a first cousin; for the ancients called first cousins *anepsiai*, as one can find in many places, both in Plutarch and in the books of law. Among Herod's wives was also one from the nation of the Samaritans, whose children were Antipas, Archelaus and a daughter Olympias. Cleopatra of Jerusalem too was counted among his wives; and her children were Herod and Philip. Pallas was among his wives too, who had borne him a son Phasael. Besides the rest Phaedra and Elpis lived with him. Herod also had two daughters by Mariamme, and by Phaedra and Elpis daughters were born to him, Roxane and Salome.

## 5.23

This, then, was Herod's family; but affairs looked to Antipater alone. He was feared by all, not so much for his power as for the wickedness of his ways. Pheroras courted him most of all and was courted in return. Salome opposed them, always the opposite of what her name signified: for it showed that the one so called was a sign of peace and peaceable, but she was very warlike and stirred others to fights and quarrels and the estrangement of kin. Watching the intimacy of Antipater and Pheroras, she told Herod that their goodwill was for his harm. When they learned of Salome's slander, in public they made a show of hatred and abuse towards each other, but in secret kept up their concord. They did not escape Salome, who tracked down everything and reported to the king their secret meetings, drinking parties and private councils. He himself understood much of it.

The Pharisees had made friends with the women's quarters. They were men who prided themselves greatly on exactness in the ancestral law and worked against the king; when all had sworn to be loyal to Caesar and to King Herod, they were not persuaded, being more than six thousand; and being well disposed to Pheroras's wife, they foretold that God had decreed an end to Herod's rule, and that it would be allotted to Pheroras and his descendants. Nor did this escape Salome's malice, and it was at once reported to the king. Those of the Pharisees convicted of this were put to death, as were the eunuch Bagoas, one Carus, outstanding for bodily beauty and Herod's favourite, and others about the king, as accomplices. Then the king held a council, accused Pheroras's wife and listed many charges, and at last turned his words to Pheroras and said: "You ought even before this to have sent the woman away of your own accord for these things. Now at least, if you lay claim to kinship with me, refuse to live with her." He answered that he would choose to die rather than be deprived of his wife while alive. On this Herod forbade Antipater and his mother to associate with Pheroras or to meet the women. They agreed, but met each other and caroused together when they had the chance. Antipater, suspecting his father's anger, wrote to his friends in Rome to write to Herod to send Antipater to Caesar. So Antipater was sent to Rome with gifts, carrying also Herod's will, which gave the rule to him, or, if he died first, to Herod, the son born of the high priest's daughter. Herod ordered Pheroras, since he would not give up his wife, to leave. He went off to his tetrarchy, swearing not to come back until he learned that his brother had died. So when the king fell ill and summoned him, he did not obey, so as not to break his oath. Later, when Pheroras fell ill, Herod came to him unasked, and when he died honoured him.

The death of Pheroras became the beginning of troubles for Antipater, the divine punishing him for the murder of his brothers. Two freedmen who had been held in honour by Pheroras asked Herod not to leave his brother unavenged, destroyed as he had been by poison. This seemed credible and moved the king to an inquiry, and women, slave and free, were tortured. The others held out and kept silent, but one woman said nothing else, but called on God that Antipater's mother might fall into such torments, as the cause of these evils. This moved Herod to a wider search; and the women, subjected to harsher tortures, made everything known: the carousals and secret meetings, and words Antipater had spoken to Pheroras's women, his hatred for his father, his laments to his mother that his father's life had been drawn out so long that he would not even enjoy the pleasures of the kingdom, if ever it came to him, because of the old age already upon him; and the women told much else that touched his father too. Now condemning Antipater on this, the king took from his mother Doris all her finery, worth many talents, and sent her away. Most of all Herod was spurred against his son by Antipater, his steward, who among other things said under torture that Antipater had given Pheroras a poison, with orders to give it to his father during his own absence, so that being away he would be unsuspected; and that Pheroras had given it to his wife to keep. The wife admitted it, and going away to fetch the poison threw herself from the roof, but did not die. When she had recovered the king questioned her again, and she swore to tell everything as it had been done. She said she had received the poison from her husband, prepared by Antipater against his father himself. "But when Pheroras fell ill, after you came yourself and tended your brother, he, seeing your goodwill, said to me: 'Bring the poison, wife, and burn it before my eyes.' And I at once did as he ordered, putting most of it in the fire, but keeping a little for myself, so that I might use it if evils came on me from you after Pheroras's death." She brought out the box and the poison before them all. The king's wife, the high priest's daughter, was also accused as knowing of everything; he at once cast her out, struck her son from the will, which had named him to reign, took the high priesthood from his father-in-law Simon son of Boethus, and appointed another, Matthias son of Theophilus.

## 5.24

Meanwhile Bathyllus, a freedman of Antipater, arrived from Rome bringing poison to Antipater's mother and to Pheroras. Under examination he said it had been sent so that, if the first had not taken hold of the father, he might at least be dispatched with this. He also brought letters from Herod's friends in Rome accusing Archelaus and Philip, who were living in Rome for their studies, of perhaps reproaching their father for the murder of their brothers, and of fearing for themselves too. This was done for Antipater at great cost. Herod, hiding his anger, ordered him not to delay; and bringing complaints against his mother, promised to drop them for his sake when he arrived. Antipater received these letters in Cilicia. At Tarentum he learned of Pheroras's death and took it hard, not out of goodwill, but because he had died before killing Herod, as he had promised. When he put in at the harbour called Sebastos, named so after Caesar, he was already in plain trouble, since no one came up to him or greeted him. He reached Jerusalem while Varus, the governor of Syria, was sitting with Herod, having been called to advise on the matter in hand. He went into the palace still wearing purple. Those at the doors let Antipater in, but kept out his friends. He was already alarmed, seeing what he had come to, when his father too pushed him away as he came up to embrace him, calling him the murderer of his brothers and a plotter against his life, and said that Varus would hear the case and judge it the next day. He went away in such trouble, and his mother and his wife met him; she was a daughter of Antigonus, who had reigned before Herod. Learning everything from them, he prepared for the trial.

The next day Herod and Varus sat in council. Their friends on both sides came, and Herod's kin, and the informers about Antipater's schemes, and slaves of Antipater's mother bringing a letter of hers telling him not to come back, since everything had become known to his father, and that the only refuge left him was Caesar, and not to fall into his father's hands. When Antipater fell at his father's feet and begged him to hear him and so give his verdict, Herod ordered him brought into the middle, and himself lamented the conduct of his sons, and that his old age had come round to Antipater; he said he was amazed how Antipater had gone to such lengths, being written down as successor to the rule and able to do everything while Herod lived, and in return for this stirring up his kin to murder him. As he said this he burst into tears. Nicolaus of Damascus, at the king's bidding, accused Antipater, telling everything in order. Many others also spoke against Antipater of their own accord. When Nicolaus had finished speaking, Varus ordered Antipater to make his defence. But he lay on his face, calling on God to bear witness that he had done no wrong. Since Antipater said nothing but his appeal to God, Varus ordered the poison to be brought into the middle. When it was brought, one of those condemned to death was ordered to drink it, and on drinking he died at once. Varus rose and left the council, and Herod at once put Antipater in chains and sent letters about him to Caesar in Rome.

## 5.25

At that time a little letter sent by Antiphilus to Antipater was also seized, saying: "I have sent you Acme's letter, not sparing my own life. For you know that I am in danger again from two households, if I am found out. Good luck to you in the business." The king looked for the other letter too. Antiphilus's slave insisted he had received no other. But someone, seeing that the slave's inner tunic had been sewn over, guessed that the note was hidden there; and so it was. So they took the letter, which ran: "Acme to Antipater. I have written your father such a letter as you wished, and making a copy of one to my mistress as if sent by Salome, I have sent it; when he reads it I know he will punish Salome." The letter to Herod was this: "I make it my business that nothing done against you escapes you. Having found a letter of Salome to my mistress against you, I have sent you a copy of it, at risk to myself but to your benefit." Acme was a Jew by birth, a slave of Julia, Caesar's wife, and she did this bought by Antipater for a great sum of money. Herod was eager at once to kill Antipater as the stirrer of great troubles, and Salome urged him on, beating her breast and asking him to kill her if he found any proof worth trusting of the charges against her; but he restrained himself and sent for his son, telling him to answer without fear. He laid the blame for everything on Antiphilus. Herod again sent letters to Caesar accusing Antipater, setting out also how far Acme had been found to share in the crime; and he sent the copies of her letters too.

Meanwhile the king fell ill and wrote a will, giving the kingdom to the youngest of his sons, out of hatred for Archelaus and Philip because of Antipater's slanders. Despairing of life, being about seventy years old, he grew savage; the reason was that he thought himself despised, and everyone glad at his misfortunes. He was driven to this by the following. Herod had done many things against the law, one of which was the golden eagle set up by the great gate of the temple. The law forbids setting up images or making figures of living things. Judas and Matthias, the most learned of the Jews and dear to the people for their teaching of the young, urged them to pull down this eagle. For even if anyone came into danger for it, they said, blessed is he who will die for the laws. While they were spurring on the young men with such words, a report came that the king had died. At once, at midday, they pulled down the eagle and hacked it to pieces with axes. Many of the young men were arrested, with Judas and Matthias, the leaders of the bold deed and the trainers of those who did it, and they were brought to Herod. He asked if they had dared to pull down his offering. The men said: "It is done; and you should not wonder if we put the laws that Moses left us, taught by God, before your decrees." He sent the prisoners to Jericho, and calling the Jews in office, lying on a couch, he reminded them of his benefits to them and of his building of the temple, and cried out that they insulted him even while he still lived by pulling down his offerings, so that in seeming they insulted him, but in truth they committed sacrilege. They, fearing his cruelty, said that those who had dared this deserved punishment. The king dealt more mildly with the others; but he took the honour from Matthias the high priest and appointed another to the priesthood, Joazar, his own wife's brother; and Matthias who had raised the sedition, and some of the rioters, he burned alive.

## 5.26

But his disease grew ever more bitter, as he paid the penalty for his crimes. A slow fire ravaged his insides; there were ulcers of the bowels, and pains especially of the colon, and a watery, transparent swelling about the feet, a disorder of the belly, and a rotting of the privy parts that bred worms; and besides these he could breathe only sitting upright, with a foul smell and constant gasping, and there were convulsions in every limb. Even in so bad a state he still hoped to live, and did not refuse to try any remedy. He crossed the Jordan and used the hot springs at Callirrhoe, which besides their other virtue are also good to drink. There the doctors put him into a tub full of oil, and he seemed to faint away. Recovering, he was carried to Jericho, where on top of everything black bile took hold of him.

As he was dying he thought of an unholy deed. At his order the more distinguished men from the whole nation came there, and he shut them all up in the hippodrome and charged his sister Salome and her husband Alexas, when he himself gave up the ghost, to kill all those shut in, "so that the people," he said, "may not rejoice at my death or applaud, but with each mourning their own, I too shall seem to be mourned, and my departure may be honoured with many tears." He laid this charge on them weeping and wailing, and they promised not to disobey the order. Meanwhile letters sent by those in Rome arrived, reporting that Acme had been put to death, and that the matter of Antipater was left to his father's judgement. Hearing this, Herod was glad and revived a little. But as his pains grew great he refused food; and asking for an apple and a knife, he meant to kill himself. He would have carried out his plan, had not someone foreseen it and held his right hand. When he cried out loudly there was wailing and a great uproar, as though the king were gone. Antipater, as if he were already dead, took heart and asked the jailer to release him, promising great things. The jailer told the king what he intended. He shouted, and sent men to kill him at once. He changed his will again, giving Antipas a tetrarchy, Galilee and Peraea, assigning the kingdom to Archelaus, allotting Gaulanitis, Trachonitis, Batanaea and Paneas as a tetrarchy to Philip, his son and Archelaus's full brother, and granting Jamnia, Azotus and Phasaelis to his sister Salome. Having done this, and leaving gifts of many talents to Caesar and to his wife Julia, he died on the fifth day after he had killed Antipater, having reigned thirty-four years after he killed Antigonus, and thirty-seven after he had been declared king by the Romans.

Salome and Alexas, before his death became known, sent away those shut in the hippodrome, saying the king ordered them to go off to their fields and look after their own affairs. This was the greatest benefit they did the nation. Then the king's death was made public, and the will was read, which allotted the kingdom to his son Archelaus. Ptolemy, who had been entrusted with the king's signet ring, said that the will could be confirmed only through Caesar. At once there was a shout of people acclaiming Archelaus as king. And after this the king's funeral was carried out with great expense.

## 6.1

So Herod paid his debt to nature. Archelaus went up to the temple, was acclaimed, sat on a golden throne and greeted the multitude. When the army would have put the diadem on him, he did not accept it until Caesar had confirmed his father's will; and having sacrificed, he turned to feasting. Some of the Jews gathered and lamented Matthias and those punished with him by Herod for pulling down the golden eagle, raising their wailing loud. When they had come together, they asked Archelaus to avenge the dead by punishing those honoured by Herod, and above all to remove the high priest and appoint another more lawful. Archelaus, though vexed at this, nodded assent to check their impulse, and sent his general to speak to the multitude, saying that this was not the time for these things, but when his rule had been confirmed by Caesar's assent. But they shouted and made an uproar and would not let the general speak, nor would they bear anyone else who set out to speak to them to bring them to reason and turn them from sedition. The feast of Unleavened Bread had just begun, and as a multitude streamed into the temple from every side, they were eager to raise the sedition high. Archelaus, fearing this, sent out a tribune with a cohort to check the impulse of the rioting people. The rioters at once rushed at the soldiers and stoned most of them; a few, and the tribune, escaped wounded. Archelaus, seeing that unless the onrush of the multitude were checked the sedition would end in great harm, sent out his whole army; about three thousand were killed, and the rest were scattered to the mountains. A proclamation was made for all to go home; and they left the feast and went away.

Archelaus sailed for Rome with his mother, entrusting affairs to his brother Philip; and Salome, Herod's sister, went with him. Antipas, Herod's son, also set out for Rome by another way, to lay claim to the kingdom himself, since it had been written down for him in an earlier will; and Salome lifted his hopes. When they reached Rome and stood before Caesar, some spoke for Archelaus, and others for Antipas, accusing Archelaus. Caesar showed a leaning rather towards Archelaus.

Meanwhile it was reported to Caesar that the nation of the Jews had risen and was besieging the Romans there. For at the feast of Pentecost many tens of thousands had gathered from every side, and the Romans were shut in by them, and Sabinus himself; he was the Roman commander. There was a hard battle, and the Romans were winning. So the Jews went round and climbed onto the porticoes outside the temple, and from there, shooting down from above, did the Romans great harm. The Romans set fire to the porticoes and fed it with stuff that naturally raises a flame; quickly it caught the roof, and of those on the porticoes some were carried down with the roof as it broke, the enemy shot down others from all round, others threw themselves into the fire, and others were killed by their own swords; and of those who had gone up on the porticoes not one was saved. The Romans seized the temple treasury; much was plundered by the soldiers, and Sabinus openly saved four hundred talents. Those of the fighters who were left surrounded the palace and threatened to set fire to it and kill everyone, but if they left, they promised safety to the Romans and to Sabinus; and many of the king's men deserted to them. Rufus and Gratus, who had three thousand of Herod's army, men strong in body, joined the Romans. The Jews did not give up the siege, and Sabinus held out under siege.

Besides this, other disturbances took hold of Judaea. Judas, the son of Hezekiah the bandit chief, who had been taken by Herod with great labour, gathered a multitude, made a raid on the palace at Sepphoris in Galilee, seized the arms there and armed his followers, and was feared by everyone. Simon too, a slave of King Herod, but a handsome man, outstanding in size and strength of body, was carried away by the confusion of affairs and dared to put on a diadem. When a multitude gathered round him, he too was proclaimed king, burned the palace at Jericho and other royal houses, and plundered what was in them. But Gratus joined battle with him, destroyed most of the multitude with him, seized Simon himself and cut off his head. Others also arose at that time, harming both the Romans and the king's men.

## 6.2

Varus in Syria, learning of Sabinus's situation, hurried to help those besieged in Judaea. When his whole force had gathered at Ptolemais, he gave part of it to his son and sent him out to fight the Galileans; he engaged them and won. Varus, advancing on Jerusalem with the rest of the army, threw the besieging Jews into panic; and they left the siege half done and went off. When Varus blamed the people of Jerusalem for the war, they said that the multitude had gathered because of the feast, but the war had come from outsiders. Varus sent through the country and searched for those responsible for the revolt, and found some and punished them; two thousand were crucified. Others too, about ten thousand, surrendered themselves to Varus when he moved against them; he sent their leaders to Caesar. Caesar punished only those who, being kin of Herod, had fought alongside the rebels.

Envoys came to Rome from Judaea, and when Caesar had assembled a council, the envoys, supported by about eight thousand of the Jews at Rome, asked for self-government. They turned to accusing Herod of lawless acts; for they called him not a king but a tyrant. Many troubles, they said, had often befallen the nation, but none equalled the troubles he had brought on it. So, thinking that whoever got control of the kingdom would be more moderate than Herod, they had gladly addressed Archelaus as king. But he, afraid that he might be thought no son of Herod if he seemed gentler to the Jews, had made a slaughter of three thousand men in the sacred precinct, "and that, Caesar, before you had even confirmed his rule." Saying this, they asked to be rid of kingship and such rulers, and to become an annex of Syria and be subject to the Roman governors sent there. They asked this; but Archelaus's party in defence cleared the kings, I mean the father and the son, of the charges, and charged the Jews in turn with seditions and revolutions. Caesar did not declare Archelaus king, but gave him half of his father's realm, promising to name him king too if he ruled well; the yearly tribute of the land assigned to him was six hundred talents. The other half he divided in two and shared between Antipas and Philip, Herod's other sons; the land assigned to Antipas paid two hundred talents, and the portion handed to Philip brought in a hundred talents. To Salome, besides what Herod had left her, he gave the palace at Ascalon too; from everything a tribute of sixty talents came in to her.

So these matters were settled. A young Jew made his way into Herod's family, since he looked like Alexander, Herod's son who had been killed. Taking up with a wicked man able to throw affairs into confusion, he called himself Alexander, Herod's son, claiming that others had been killed by some of those sent to kill both brothers, while they themselves had been saved and smuggled away. With such words he deceived those he met, gathered a great deal of money that way, and hurried to Rome. Caesar did not believe that Herod had been easily deceived, and bringing the false Alexander before him, he was not deceived. For he had a face like Herod's Alexander, but he was worn by manual work, and his body had grown harder, not softened by luxury like the other's. So Caesar asked where Aristobulus might be; and when he said he had been left in Cyprus, "so that if anything terrible happened to me, the line of Mariamme might not fail altogether," Caesar took the false Alexander aside alone and urged him to tell him the truth, with his life as the reward. He revealed the trick to Caesar. Caesar, seeing he was strong for hard work, set him among the rowers; and the man who had conspired with him in this he put to death.

Archelaus, on receiving the ethnarchy, took the high priesthood from Joazar son of Boethus and put in his place his brother Eleazar. He married Glaphyra, the daughter of Archelaus, who had been the wife of his brother Alexander and had children by him, though the law forbade marrying brothers' wives who had children by the dead. A little later he drove out Eleazar too and brought in instead Jesus son of See. In the tenth year of his rule he was accused before Caesar by his subjects of having handled affairs cruelly and altogether tyrannically. So Caesar quickly summoned him, and having heard the accusers and him, condemned him to exile, and took his money.

The future was shown to Archelaus in a dream. He thought he saw ten ears of grain, ripe and full of wheat, being eaten by oxen. Some explained the dream one way and some another, but Simon, an Essene by race, said that the vision brought Archelaus a change of fortune, though not for good. The oxen were a sign of hardship, being animals that toil at work, and they showed a change of affairs, because the earth ploughed by them is not left unmoved; the ten ears meant a number of years, since they are filled in the course of a year and the harvest completed; and the time of Archelaus's rule had run out.

Glaphyra, Archelaus's wife, also saw another dream. She, as has been told, was first married to Alexander, Archelaus's brother; after he was killed she was married to Juba, king of the Libyans; and when he too departed this life she became the wife of Archelaus, who sent away Mariamme, his wife, though Glaphyra had children by Alexander. She thought, then, that Alexander stood over her, reproaching her and saying: "Glaphyra, you have proved true the saying that wives are faithless to their husbands. For you were married to me as a virgin and bore children by me, yet forgetting my love you joined in a second marriage; and not even so did you have enough of insulting us, but you laid a third bridegroom beside you, and that my brother. But I shall make you mine again and free you from this shame." She told this to the women she knew, and a little later she died.

## 6.3

The land subject to Archelaus was added to Syria. Quirinius was sent to register Syria, and Judaea itself, which had become an annex of it. The Jews, though at first they took the registration hard even to hear of, then gave way when the high priest Joazar persuaded them. But a man of Gaulanitis, who had taken as his associate Zadok, a Pharisee, filled the nation with wars and banditry, saying that the assessment of property was nothing else but outright slavery. They seemed to have been stirred to set public affairs right, but in truth they were eager for chances of their own gain. From this grew seditions and the murder of many, even of the leading men, some in civil slaughter and some at enemy hands, and famine, the capture and razing of cities, and the burning of the temple.

For there were three ways of philosophy among the Jews from of old, as has been said before, that of the Essenes, that of the Pharisees and that of the Sadducees; this fourth was brought in and newly made by Zadok and Judas. The Pharisees live simply and do not lean to softer ways; they are exact in keeping the laws, give way in honour to the old, and do not boldly contradict what they propose. They teach fate, and allow that men need not yield to its impulses, but resist them with zeal. They grant immortality to souls, and believe in judgements below the earth for the lives men have lived. For this reason they are most persuasive to the people, who use them as interpreters in prayers and the performance of sacred rites. The Sadducees hold that souls are mortal, and say that they perish together with the bodies. They do not observe transgression of the laws, and think it a virtue to contradict their elders and their teachers. If any of them come into office, they go over to the Pharisees' teaching, even against their will; for otherwise they do not seem bearable to the multitude. The Essenes leave everything to God; they hold souls to be immortal; they cling to justice. They send offerings to the temple, but do not sacrifice there, differing from the others over purifications; so, being shut out of the common precinct, they sacrifice by themselves. They turn to the work of farming. They hold their property in common, so that the rich man enjoys no more of his own than the very poorest. They neither bring in wives nor own slaves, thinking the one an injustice and the bringing in of women a cause of strife; living by themselves they serve one another. They choose receivers for the fruits of the land and for what is brought to them from elsewhere. The fourth, of which Judas the Galilean became the leader, agrees with the Pharisees in other things, but a fierce love of freedom is fixed in it; its followers name God alone as leader and master, not bearing to share these names with a man, and not refusing to endure deaths and punishments of many terrible kinds, so as not to depart from their stand.

From this, then, the nation of the Jews began to sicken from folly into madness, Gessius Florus the governor provoking them to it by his outrages. Quirinius, when the registration and the assessments were finished, which took place in the thirty-seventh year after Antony's defeat by Caesar at Actium, took the honour from Joazar the high priest, who had been overthrown by a revolt of the multitude, and appointed Ananus son of Seth high priest. When Quirinius left for Rome, Coponius governed Judaea. His successor was Marcus Ambivulus; and Annius Rufus succeeded Marcus. In his time Caesar, emperor of the Romans, died, having ruled fifty-seven years, six months and two days, for fourteen years of which Antony ruled with him, so that the time of his sole rule was forty-three years, or according to some forty-four. He lived seventy-seven years.

The monarchy passed to Tiberius, the son of Caesar's wife Julia. He sent Valerius Gratus to Judaea as governor; he removed Ananus from the high priesthood and appointed Ishmael son of Phabi, and not long after removed him too and gave the honour of the priesthood to Eleazar, the son of Ananus; and after a year he brought in instead Simon son of Camithus. When he had been priest for the same time, Joseph Caiaphas was his successor.

## 6.4

Gratus, having governed Judaea for eleven years and done these things, went back to Rome; and Pontius Pilate came, taking over the governorship. Herod the tetrarch, who had been counted a friend of Tiberius before his rule, built after Tiberius became sole ruler a city named after him in Galilee on the lake of Gennesaret, calling it Tiberias. Pilate moved an army from Caesarea to winter in Jerusalem, and by night brought into the city standards bearing images of Caesar, though the law forbids the Jews to have images. When what had been done became known, a multitude rushed to Caesarea asking for the images to be moved, and made supplications for five days on this account. Pilate would not yield, saying that Caesar would be insulted by it; and since the multitude did not stop begging, on the sixth day he surrounded them with armed soldiers and threatened them with death unless they stopped their uproar. They threw themselves down on their faces and said they would accept death with pleasure. Pilate, amazed at their nobility and their zeal for keeping the laws, at once took the images back to Caesarea.

Making an aqueduct to bring water into Jerusalem, he spent the sacred money on it. So many gathered and cried out against Pilate, asking him to stop, and some even used abuse against him. He ordered a crowd of soldiers dressed in Jewish clothes, with clubs under their clothes, to go round and surround those making the uproar, and then ordered the Jews to withdraw. When they began to abuse him, he gave the soldiers the signal; and they punished the rioters with blows. They, being unarmed and beaten, had no thought of giving way; but many fell, and the others went away wounded.

At this time our Lord and God Jesus Christ appeared in Judaea, about whom Josephus says this, word for word, in the eighteenth book of the Antiquities: "At this time there lived Jesus, a wise man, if indeed one ought to call him a man; for he was a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of men who receive the truth with pleasure; and he drew to himself many Jews and many of the Greeks too. He was the Christ. And when Pilate, at the accusation of the leading men among us, had condemned him to the cross, those who had loved him at first did not cease. For he appeared to them on the third day alive again, the divine prophets having told these and countless other wonders about him. And even now the tribe of Christians, named after him, has not died out."

This is what Josephus wrote about Christ in the Antiquities. In his treatise to the Greeks, which is entitled Against Plato, on the Cause of the Universe, which Saint John of Damascus also mentions in the book he laboured on, called the Parallels, he says this: "For all, both just and unjust, will be brought before God the Word. For the Father has given judgement to him, and he, fulfilling the Father's will, comes as judge, he whom we call Christ. For it is not Minos and Rhadamanthus who are judges, as you Greeks think, but he whom God the Father has glorified; about whom we have gone into more detail elsewhere for those who seek the truth. He, carrying out the Father's just judgement for each, will prepare what is just for all according to their works. Standing at his judgement, all men and angels and demons will utter one voice, saying: 'Just is your judgement.' The response to this voice brings justice on both, since he grants eternal enjoyment justly to those who have done well, and assigns eternal punishment to the lovers of evil. For these the fire remains unquenched and endless, and a fiery worm that does not die nor destroy the body, but bursts out of the body with unceasing pain, remains." He says other things besides. So, then, Josephus wrote about Christ.

## 6.5

At that time there was in Rome a woman named Paulina, honoured for her distinguished family and her good character, and exceedingly rich. She was graceful in looks and of the age in which women take pride, and she was adorned with modesty. She was married to Saturninus, a man in no way behind her in any good quality. Decius Mundus, a man of great standing among the knights of the time, was taken with love for her and tried her with gifts; for he offered two hundred thousand Attic drachmas for one night. She would not bear it. He was inflamed still more with love, so that he courted death for himself by refusing food. He had a freedwoman of his father's named Ida, skilled in every kind of evil. Seeing the young man in this state, she encouraged him with words and revived him with promises, saying she would need only fifty thousand to bring the deed about for him. Taking the money she asked for, since she saw that Paulina could not be caught by money, but knew that she was most warmly devoted to the worship of Isis (she was then held a goddess by the Romans), she went to some of the priests of that false goddess, and with money persuaded them to deceive Paulina by whatever tricks they could and bring her to bed with Mundus. Charmed by the money, they set about the deed. The eldest of them went to Paulina, met her in private, and said he had come sent by Anubis, since the god, being in love with her, ordered her to come to him. The message seemed to her most welcome, if she was loved by a god; and she shared the news with her husband, and he agreed, knowing his wife's modesty. So she went to the precinct; and when it was time for sleep, a place had been prepared for the woman to sleep inside the temple, and the lamps were put out. Mundus, who had been hidden there, had his fill of her all night, coming to her as Anubis. Then he went away, and she went to her husband and told him of the appearance of Anubis, and boasted to the women she knew of having been thought worthy of a god's company. On the third day after the deed Mundus met her and said: "Paulina, I have kept the two hundred thousand, and you have served me without them. Your insults to Mundus did not touch me at all, once I had taken the name of Anubis." At this the woman understood the outrage, tore her dress, and showed her husband the plot; and he went to Tiberius. The emperor examined what had happened, crucified the priests and Ida, pulled down the temple, sank the statue of Isis in the river Tiber, and punished Mundus with exile, granting him pardon so that he was not punished more heavily because of the violence of his love.

These things were done in Rome; and in Samaria there was a disturbance. A man ordered the Samaritans to gather with him on Mount Gerizim, which they hold the holiest of mountains; and he promised to show them, when they came, the sacred vessels buried there by Moses. They gathered and were in arms. Pilate sent soldiers and killed some, put others to flight, and put to death the leaders among those taken alive. The Samaritans went to Vitellius, governor of Syria, accusing Pilate over the slaughter of their countrymen. Vitellius sent Marcellus to take care of the Jews, and ordered Pilate to go away to Rome to answer before the emperor for what he was charged with. He went away, having governed Judaea for ten years; but before he came near Rome, Tiberius had already died.

Vitellius came to Jerusalem while the feast of the Passover was being held, and was received magnificently. He remitted to the people of Jerusalem the taxes on the fruits of the land, and allowed the high priest's robe to be kept in the temple and to be in the priests' charge as before. At that time it was kept in the tower; for one of the high priests, namely the first Hyrcanus, built a tower close to the temple and lived in it, and kept there the high priest's robe that belonged to him as high priest. The same was done by him and by those after him. Herod, rebuilding that tower more richly, renamed it after Antony, being his friend; and finding the robe in it, he kept it there. Archelaus did this too, and after him the Romans did the same with the robe, which was kept there under the seals of the priests and the treasurers. When a feast came, it was given back to the high priests by the commander of the fort, and one day after the feast it was put back there again. Vitellius gave the robe up to the nation. He removed the high priest Joseph, also called Caiaphas, from the priesthood, and gave it to Jonathan, the son of Ananus the high priest. On Tiberius's orders Vitellius made a treaty with Artabanus, king of the Parthians, who sent his son Darius with many gifts as a hostage. Herod the tetrarch, who was present at the treaty, at once wrote and sent an account of what had happened to Caesar. Then, when Vitellius wrote about these things to Tiberius, he wrote back that he had learned everything from Herod. This moved Vitellius to anger against Herod; he nursed his anger in secret, and took revenge on him when Gaius came to power.

## 6.6

At that time Philip, this Herod's brother, died too, in the twentieth year of Tiberius's rule, having ruled for thirty-seven years. He was quiet in character and moderate to his subjects, making his progresses with a few chosen men; and if anyone came up to him as he went, asking for help, at once his throne was set down on the spot (for the men carrying it followed him), and he sat and heard him, punished the wrongdoers and released those unjustly accused. Since Philip had no children, Tiberius added his realm to the province of Syria.

Herod the tetrarch, setting out for Rome, stayed with his brother Herod, whom the daughter of Simon the high priest had borne to King Herod. Falling in love with Herodias, his brother's wife, the daughter of their brother Aristobulus and the sister of Agrippa the Great, he spoke to her of marriage. She accepted and agreed to move to him if he would cast out the daughter of Aretas. He sailed to Rome on these terms; and when he came back, his wife, the daughter of Aretas, learning of the agreement with Herodias, asked to be sent to the fortress of Machaerus, which was on the border of Aretas's realm and Herod's. Herod sent her, not knowing what she intended; and from there she set off to her father in Arabia, and told him of Herod's purpose towards her. He took this as a ground for enmity; a battle was fought between them through their generals, and Herod's men were beaten and his whole army fell. Herod reported this by letter to Tiberius; and he wrote to Vitellius to make war on Aretas, and either send him to Rome a prisoner if taken alive, or send his head if he was killed.

Some thought that Herod's army had been destroyed by God, since he was paying the penalty for the murder of John, the prophet and baptist. For Josephus wrote this about him too, word for word: "For Herod killed him, a good man, who bade the Jews practise virtue, use justice towards one another and piety towards God, and so come together for baptism; for so the baptism would appear acceptable to him. Herod, fearing that his great power of persuasion over men might lead to some sedition (for they seemed ready to do anything on his advice), thought it far better to forestall him and kill him before any revolt came from him, rather than fall into trouble when a change came and then repent. So because of Herod's suspicion he was sent in chains to Machaerus and killed there; and the Jews thought that the destruction of the army came as punishment for him, God wishing to harm Herod."

Vitellius hurried to make war on Aretas. When he set out to march through the country of the Jews, their leading men begged him not to go through their land; for it was not their ancestral custom for images to be carried through their country, and many images were on the standards. Persuaded, he took the army across through the great plain, and himself went up with Herod to Jerusalem to sacrifice to God. Staying there three days, he removed Jonathan from the high priesthood and put in his brother Theophilus. On the fourth day, when letters were brought to him about the death of Tiberius, he made the multitude swear loyalty to Gaius, and called back the army. They say that Aretas too, having taken the auspices, said that it was impossible for the army to fight; for one of the leaders would die, either the one who ordered the war, or the one ordered, or the one against whom the order had been made.

## 6.7

Vitellius went back to Antioch; and Agrippa, the son of Aristobulus, happened to be in Rome when Tiberius died. A little before the death of his grandfather Herod the Great he had been brought up in Rome, and became a companion of Drusus, the son of Tiberius, and known to Antonia, the wife of the elder Drusus, since his mother Berenice was honoured by her. Agrippa was magnificent and lavish in giving, and when his mother died he spent some of the money on himself, living expensively, some on gifts, and most on Caesar's freedmen. Quickly he was in want. When Tiberius's son died, Tiberius forbade his son's companions to come into his sight, so that he might not be reminded of him through them and stirred to grief. For this reason, then, and because he had run out of money, he went back to Judaea in a bad way. Pressed to pay his creditors his debts, which were many, and having nothing, he thought of killing himself. His wife Cypros understood his intention. She was the daughter of Phasael, the nephew of King Herod, born to him by Salampsio, Herod's daughter, whom he had by Mariamme, the one he killed, as has been told. This Cypros, then, the wife of Agrippa, perceiving his plan, held him back from it, and sent to Herodias, the wife of Herod the tetrarch, who was Agrippa's sister, telling her of her brother's intention, and asking her to help and to call on her own husband to help too. They sent for him and gave him Tiberias to live in, and assigned him some money for his expenses. But after a time a quarrel arose between Herod and Agrippa, and Agrippa moved to Flaccus, governor of Syria, who had been friendly to him since Rome, and lived there, Flaccus receiving him. Agrippa's brother Aristobulus was there too; quarrelling with his brother, he made Flaccus his enemy by slanders; and Agrippa was driven out from there.

Brought to the last extremity of want, he wished to sail to Italy, and asked Marsyas, his freedman, to get him money from somewhere by borrowing. Marsyas went to Peter, a freedman of Berenice, Agrippa's mother; and Peter said that if he made a bond for twenty thousand Attic drachmas, he could take the sum less two thousand five hundred. Agrippa agreed, and taking the loan was about to sail away. But Herennius Capito, the procurator of Jamnia, demanded from him three hundred thousand pieces of silver owed to Caesar, and ordered him to stay on that account. Agrippa pretended to obey, but went off by night. Sailing to Alexandria, he asked Alexander the alabarch to lend him two hundred thousand. He said he would not lend it to him, but lent it to his wife Cypros, because of her love for her husband and her other virtues. When she had received the loan, Agrippa sailed off to Italy, and Cypros went back to Judaea with the children.

Coming to Caesar Tiberius, Agrippa was received kindly. But when a letter from Herennius Capito was brought to Caesar, saying that Agrippa had run away while being pressed for a debt of three hundred thousand, he was angry, and ordered that he should not be allowed to come to him until he paid the debt. Agrippa borrowed and paid the debt, and went in to Tiberius again. Caesar told him to keep company with his grandson and look after him. But Agrippa leaned rather to Gaius, who was the grandson of Antonia, the mother of Germanicus and of Claudius, who became sole ruler after Gaius. By courting him he won his friendship. Once, as the two were driving together, talk arose about Tiberius. Agrippa, calling on the gods, prayed that Tiberius might quickly step down from the rule in favour of Gaius. Eutychus, a freedman of Agrippa, who heard the words, went to Caesar as if to tell him something for his safety. But Tiberius had become slow in everything, and paid no attention even to those who reported something for his own sake. He did not deal quickly with envoys, saying that otherwise, if they went back quickly, others would come, and he would have a crowd about him; nor did he replace the governors and procurators he had sent out with successors, unless they died first. He said he did this out of care for his subjects, so that, having had enough gain in the time, they might be duller towards wrongdoing. Well then. He gave as an example a wounded man whose wounds were covered with flies; someone, pitying him, tried to drive them off, and when he stopped him, the one who was trying to drive off the flies asked the reason; and the wounded man answered: "These, being full of blood, do not trouble me much; but if they were chased away, fresh, hungry ones would come and hurt me more." A further proof of Tiberius's slowness in this is that in twenty-two years of his sole rule he sent the Jews only two men to govern their nation, Gratus and Pilate. Being like this in everything, he did not think Eutychus worth a hearing either.

## 6.8

Agrippa begged Antonia to get Caesar to hear Eutychus. Antonia was held in the highest honour by Tiberius, both as having been the wife of his brother Drusus and for her chastity. For being widowed young she remained a widow and refused a second marriage, though the emperor urged it on her, and she lived her life so as to be above reproach. For this she was honoured by Tiberius, and also because she had been his benefactor, having revealed a plot formed by many powerful men. So, when she asked him to examine Eutychus, he said: "Let the gods know, Antonia, that what will be done will be not by my will, but at your urging." And he ordered Eutychus to be brought. Standing before him, he said: "Gaius and Agrippa, master, were talking together, and Agrippa said: 'If only the day would come when this old man departs and appoints you ruler of the world! For Tiberius his grandson will be no hindrance to us, dying at your hand. And the world would be blessed, and I before it.'" Tiberius thought the words true; and at the same time, keeping a grudge against Agrippa because he had not chosen to look after his grandson but had gone over entirely to Gaius, he ordered one of those standing by to bind him. He was led away in chains still in purple, and stood before the palace leaning on a tree in despair. Others in chains were there too. When a bird flew down onto that tree (the Romans call the bird *bubo*), one of the prisoners, seeing it, asked the soldier guarding him who the man in purple was; and when he learned, he asked the soldier chained to him to go near. On getting his wish, he said: "Young man, I bring you good news of a very quick release from your chains, and of advancement to the greatest rank and power; you will be envied by those who now pity you, and will die in happiness, leaving your wealth to your children. But when you see this bird again, know that your death will then come after five days. When you have prospered according to our prediction, remember us too, so that we may escape the misfortune in which we now are." When he said this he was laughed at then, but later he was seen to deserve wonder.

Agrippa was in chains for six months. Tiberius, failing as his illness grew stronger, ordered Euodus, who was the most honoured of his freedmen, to bring the children to him, so that he could talk to them before his death. He had no children; for his son Drusus had died; but he had by him a grandson, Tiberius Gemellus, and a nephew Gaius, the son of his brother Germanicus, already a young man, schooled in learning and loved and honoured by the people for his father's virtue. So Tiberius ordered the children to be brought in early the next day. His wish was above all to leave the rule to his grandson; but he took it as an omen that the divine wished the rule to come round to whichever reached him first, and he sent ordering his grandson's tutor to bring the boy early. When day had come, he sent Euodus to call in whichever of the children was there; he found Gaius before the room and brought him in to Tiberius. Tiberius, reflecting on the power of the divine, lamented for his grandson as if he were lost. Though troubled by this, he said to Gaius: "My boy, though Tiberius is closer kin to me than you, I myself, both by my own will and by the vote of the gods, put the rule of the Romans into your hands. I ask you not to forget your kinship with Tiberius, but to care for him as a kinsman; for whatever is done against justice does not go unpunished by divine providence." So Tiberius, having declared Gaius successor to the rule, lived on a few days and died, having ruled twenty-two years, seven months and as many days; and Gaius was left as emperor.

## 6.9

The death of Tiberius was announced to the Romans; but they did not believe the report, because they wished so much for the thing. For he had done the Roman nobles very many terrible things, being harsh in anger and punishing even the slightest slips with death. Marsyas, Agrippa's freedman, learning of Tiberius's death, ran to him and said in Hebrew: "The lion is dead." He promised him thanks, if he had brought true news. The centurion, seeing Agrippa joyful, suspected that something new had happened, and asked what the news might be; and Agrippa, having already become familiar with the man, revealed the secret. He shared his pleasure and set out a dinner. While they were feasting, someone came saying that Tiberius was alive. The centurion, afraid because he had been living with a prisoner of the emperor, ordered him to be bound, though he had already loosed him. The next day the report of Tiberius's death was widespread, and letters were sent by Gaius, one to the senate, announcing Tiberius's death and his own succession to the rule, the other to Piso, the prefect of the city, instructing him to move Agrippa from the camp to the house in which he had been before he was bound.

Gaius brought Tiberius's body to Rome and buried it lavishly, and wished to free Agrippa at once; but Antonia prevented it, not out of hatred for the one to be freed, but out of concern for the one who would free him, so that he might not seem to rejoice at the emperor's death by freeing his prisoner so quickly. When a few days had passed he sent for Agrippa, had his overgrown hair cut and changed his clothes, then put the diadem on him and made him king of Philip's tetrarchy, adding the tetrarchy of Lysanias too as an increase; and he exchanged gold for bronze, giving him in place of the iron chain with which he had been bound a golden one of equal weight.

In the second year of Gaius's sole rule Agrippa asked to be allowed to go home, and promised to come back again once he had arranged the affairs of his realm as they should be; and when Gaius allowed it, he sailed. Herodias, his sister, envied her brother his good fortune, especially when she saw him doing business with the crowds with the insignia of kingship; and she stirred her husband to sail to Rome and seek an equal rule for himself. He wished to keep quiet. But his wife pestered her husband more fiercely, urging him to do everything for the kingship, and did not let up until she had brought Herod to her view even against his will. So he set sail for Rome with his wife. Agrippa too prepared to go to Rome, and sent ahead one of his freedmen bringing gifts to the emperor and letters against Herod. They found Gaius at Baiae, a small town in Campania. As soon as Herod came into his sight, Gaius read Agrippa's letters, which accused Herod of an agreement with Sejanus against the rule of Tiberius, and again with Artabanus the Parthian, at that time, against Gaius's own.
