As proof of the charge he gave a store of arms in Herod's armouries, enough for seventy thousand heavy infantry. Gaius was moved by what had been written, and asked Herod if the story about the arms was true. When he admitted it, Gaius, believing in his revolt, took away his tetrarchy and added it to Agrippa's kingdom, and likewise gave his money to Agrippa, and condemned Herod to exile for life. To Herodias, as Agrippa's sister, he gave all the money that belonged to her, and told her she need not share her husband's exile, for Agrippa's sake. She thanked Gaius, but said it was not right, having shared her husband's prosperity, to desert him in his misfortunes.

Gaius handled affairs fairly moderately for the first year and the next, but as he went on he made himself divine and tried to make himself a god. When a quarrel had arisen between the Jews and the Greeks in Alexandria, three from each side came

## 6.10

to Gaius as envoys. Apion, one of the envoys of the Alexandrians, accused the Jews of many things, and in particular that, while all who were under the Romans set up altars and temples to Gaius and honoured him as a god, these alone thought it shameful to honour him with statues and to swear by his name. At this Philo, the head of the Jews' embassy, a man of note and not unskilled in philosophy, was ready to make a defence for his countrymen. But Gaius would not bear it, ordered them to go away out of his sight, and plainly meant to harm them. Philo went out, having been insulted, and said to the Jews with him that they must take heart; for Gaius had raged not against them but against the divine itself.

The emperor, thinking it terrible not to be worshipped as a god by the Jews, sent out Petronius as successor to Vitellius's command, ordering him to invade Judaea with a large force and set up his statue in the temple of God; and if they did not give way willingly, to do it after defeating them in war. Petronius, having taken over the command of Syria, hurried to carry out Caesar's orders. When he reached Ptolemais, many tens of thousands of Jews came to him, begging him not to force them to break their ancestral customs. "If you cannot be moved," they said, "kill us first and so set up the statue." Petronius answered: "If I were doing this of my own accord, your plea to me would be just; but since Caesar has ordered it, I am under every necessity to carry out what he has decided." Saying this he went to Tiberias, to see what the Jews had in mind. Many tens of thousands met him there, begging him not to put them under compulsion or defile the city with a statue. Petronius said: "Will you go to war, then?" They said: "We will not go to war, but we will die before we break our ancestral customs," and offered themselves to be slaughtered. This went on for forty days. Aristobulus, the brother of Agrippa, and others of the chief men begged Petronius not to drive the multitude to desperation, but to write to Gaius of their unbending refusal to receive the statue; for perhaps he would soften and give up his decision; and if he held to his vote again, then he could take the matter in hand himself. Petronius was persuaded and wrote to Gaius about the matter.

King Agrippa, living in Rome, was advancing in his intimacy with Gaius. When he was admired for the lavishness and magnificence with which he entertained the emperor at dinner, he was urged to ask for whatever he wished. He said: "I will ask you for nothing that brings wealth, but for something that will bring you a reputation for piety and me renown. I ask you to give up, for my sake, the setting up of the statue that you order Petronius to place in the temple of the Jews." Gaius, ashamed to seem false before so many witnesses, agreed, and wrote to Petronius that if he had already set up the statue he should not take it down, but if he had not yet set it up, he should not try to do it any more: "for I no longer wish it to be set up, because of Agrippa, a man honoured by me." Gaius wrote this to Petronius before he read Petronius's letters showing that the Jews were being driven to revolt because of the statue. Deeply pained at this, he wrote to Petronius: "Since the gifts of the Jews have counted for more with you than my orders, consider for yourself what you must do about yourself. For I shall make you an example to men now and hereafter, not to set aside an emperor's orders." Petronius did not receive this letter while Gaius was still alive; he received first the letters about his death, and only then Gaius's letter to him.

So Gaius, having been most wicked, perished, killed by a plot. The manner of the plot against him, and by whom he was killed, the narrative will tell when it goes through the affairs of the emperors. When he had been killed, Claudius, who was hiding out of fear, was brought out by the soldiers and proclaimed emperor, Agrippa too having worked hard for his proclamation. As soon as his sole rule was confirmed, he confirmed Agrippa's realm, praised him, and added to it all that King Herod, his grandfather, had ruled. Agrippa also asked Claudius for the kingdom of Chalcis for his brother Herod; and it was given him by Caesar.

## 6.11

At this time the Jews there rose against the Alexandrians. For since Gaius had been ill disposed towards them, in the way that has been told, they had been mistreated by the Greeks in the city while he was sole ruler; but when Gaius died they took heart and were in arms. Claudius wrote to the prefect in Egypt to put down the strife, and at the request of the two kings, Agrippa and Herod, he also sent an edict to Syria, to Alexandria and to all the rest of the world that was subject to the Romans, saying: "Though the Jews from of old were granted equal citizenship with the Alexandrians and the citizens of the other cities, Gaius out of madness humbled them, because the nation of the Jews would not bear to call him a god. But I ordain that the nation shall lose none of its ancient rights because of his folly, and that their former rights shall be kept for them while they abide by the customs of the Jews; the kings Agrippa and Herod, most dear to me, having asked me for this."

He also sent Agrippa off to his kingdom, which had become more splendid. Coming to Jerusalem he offered sacrifices of thanksgiving, and hung up over the treasury the golden chain given him by Gaius, as a proof of the power of God and of the change of fortune, and that great things sometimes fall and the lowly are raised up. Having sacrificed lavishly, he removed Theophilus son of Ananus from the high priesthood, and gave the honour to Simon son of Boethus, whose surname was Cantheras. Simon had two brothers, and his father was Boethus, whose daughter King Herod married, as has been told. He repaid the people of Jerusalem for their goodwill towards him by remitting to them the tax on each house. He appointed Silas commander of the cavalry of his whole army, a man who had shared many of his labours.

Some young men of Dora, reckless and bold, brought a statue of Caesar into the synagogue of the Jews and set it up. This disturbed Agrippa; at once he went to Publius Petronius, governor of Syria, and accused the people of Dora. Petronius sent a centurion and ordered those who had done the bold deed to be brought to him, and wrote to the magistrates of Dora to show the centurion the guilty men, if they did not wish to seem accomplices in the deed. Agrippa took the priesthood from Simon Cantheras and brought Jonathan son of Ananus to it again. But he declined, saying he was content to have held the high priesthood once, and asked that his brother Matthias be advanced to it as worthy of the honour. The king was persuaded and gave the high priesthood to Matthias.

Silas, Agrippa's cavalry commander, trusting in the dangers he had run for him, claimed an untimely freedom of speech, and was tiresome, reminding him of the gloomy times of his fortune and boasting of his own zeal and loyalty then. Agrippa was displeased at his unrestrained frankness; and when Silas did not give way, the king was provoked to anger, and not only removed him from the cavalry command but even put him in chains. In time his anger was blunted, and reckoning how many labours Silas had endured for him, on the day he was celebrating his birthday he invited Silas to feast with him. But he would not obey, saying: "To what honour is the king calling me back, one that will soon be lost? Or does he think I have stopped speaking freely? Now I shall cry out all the more about the dangers I saved him from, the labours I bore winning him safety and honour; for which my reward is chains and a dark prison, which I shall never forget." The king, learning this, and seeing that he was incurably disposed, left him in custody again.

This king was beneficent in his gifts no less than his grandfather Herod; but while Herod showed his generosity to foreigners and not to the Jews, Agrippa was beneficent to all alike and gentle in character. He liked to live constantly in Jerusalem, and kept the ancestral customs purely. There was one Simon in Jerusalem, reputed to be exact in the law; he gathered a crowd and dared to denounce the king while he was away at Caesarea. This did not escape Agrippa. So he sent for Simon and said: "Tell me, what of the things being done is against the law?" He, having nothing to say, begged to be pardoned. And the king, beyond expectation, was reconciled with him and sent him away with gifts. He took the high priesthood from Matthias and gave it to Elionaeus, the son of Cithaerus.

When he had reigned three years over all Judaea, he held games in the city of Caesarea, which was formerly called Strato's Tower. On the second day of the games he put on a robe made of silver and came into the theatre at the start of the day. Lit by the first rays of the rising sun, the silver shone wonderfully, glittering in a way that struck awe in those who gazed at it. At once the flatterers cried out, one from here and another from there, calling him a god and adding: "Be gracious to us; for if until now we feared you as a man, from now on we acknowledge you as greater than mortal nature." The king did not rebuke them, nor reject the impious flattery. Looking up a little later, he saw the bird, the owl, above his head, and understood it then as a messenger of evil, as it had once been the herald of good. He felt a pain to the heart, and a sudden pain of the belly came on him. He said to his friends: "I, your god, am now ending my life; and I who was called immortal by you am hastening to die." As he said this he was overcome by the growing pain, and was quickly carried to the palace. When word went round that he was dying, the multitude at once, with women and children, sat in sackcloth according to the ancestral law and begged God for the king, and all lamented. Agrippa, lying in a high room and looking down on them falling on their faces, was not without tears himself. For five days he was worn down by the pain of the belly and ended his life, having lived fifty-four years and reigned seven, four under Gaius

## 6.12

and three under Claudius. While his death was still unknown to the multitude, Herod his brother, the ruler of Chalcis, and Helcias the cavalry commander agreed together, sent men to Silas, who was their enemy, and murdered him, as if the king had ordered it.

So Agrippa died, leaving a son Agrippa of seventeen years and three daughters: one was married to Herod, her father's brother, and was called Berenice, while the two, Mariamme and Drusilla, were unmarried. When the king's death became known, the people of Caesarea and Sebaste, forgetting his benefits, reviled him, seized the statues of the king's daughters, carried them to the brothels and abused them, and held public feasts, wearing garlands and perfume and pouring libations to Charon.

The dead man's son Agrippa was then living in Rome, being brought up at the court of Claudius Caesar. Claudius was eager to send him at once to succeed to the kingdom; but those about him turned him from his purpose, saying it was risky to entrust so great a kingdom to one so young. So he sent Cuspius Fadus as procurator of Judaea and the whole kingdom, ordering him to rebuke the people of Caesarea and Sebaste for their insult to the dead man. Fadus, on reaching Judaea, put down a sedition that had arisen, cleared the country of bandits, and ordered the high priest's robe to be stored in the fortress Antonia, as before. The priests and the leading men of Jerusalem did not dare to oppose him, but still asked him to allow them to send envoys to Caesar to ask that the sacred robe be kept by them; and they were allowed. When the envoys reached Rome, Agrippa's son, the younger Agrippa, who was living there, as has been said, asked Caesar to grant the Jews to keep the sacred robe. Claudius granted it, and wrote to Fadus about it. Herod too, Agrippa's brother and ruler of Chalcis, asked Caesar for authority over the temple and the sacred money and for the appointment of the high priests. He got his request, and from him the authority remained with all his descendants until the capture of Jerusalem. He removed Cantheras from the high priesthood, bringing in instead Joseph son of Camei.

## 6.13

At this time Helena, the queen of the Adiabenians, and her son Izates changed their way of life to the customs of the Jews. For Monobazus, king of the Adiabenians, whose surname was also Bazaeus, was taken with love for his sister Helena and married her. Once, lying with her when she was pregnant, he put his hand on her belly, and falling asleep he seemed to hear a voice telling him to take his hand from the womb and not to press the babe in it, who by God's providence would have a happy beginning and a happy end. Troubled by the voice, he told this to his wife. And when the son was born he named him Izates. He had another son older than him, born of Helena, and other children by other wives, but he loved Izates as if he were an only child. So his brothers envied him. His father, fearing for him, sent him to Abennerigus, king of Spasinou Charax. He received Izates gladly, made him his son-in-law by marrying him to his daughter, and gave him land. Monobazus, grown old, wished to see Izates before he died. So he sent for him, greeted him affectionately, and assigned him a district, in which he lived until his father's death.

When Monobazus died, Queen Helena sent for the grandees and the satraps; and when they came she said: "It has not escaped you that my husband wished Izates to succeed to the kingdom. But knowing that he is fortunate who receives the kingdom not from one but from the many, and those willing, I have put the matter to your judgement." They said they confirmed the king's judgement, and would gladly yield to Izates, who had rightly been preferred to his brothers in accordance with everyone's prayers; and that his brothers and kin must first be killed, so that he might rule safely. The queen advised them to hold back their opinion about killing Izates's relatives until he came and approved it with them. They urged that the men be kept in chains meanwhile until his arrival. The queen set her eldest son over affairs until his brother came back, and gave him his father's signet ring too. So Izates came, and his brother received him and stood aside from the rule for him.

While he had been abroad, a Jew called Ananias had come to know him and taught him about God and the customs of the Jews. It happened too that Helena, instructed by another Jew, had been converted to the Jewish ways. So Izates, coming and finding his kin in chains, was displeased; he freed them, but sent them away, so that they might not be under suspicion by being present, some to Rome as hostages and others to the Parthians. Learning that his mother had embraced the Jewish ways, he was eager to be converted to them himself, and was ready to be circumcised. But his mother prevented him, saying that his subjects would turn to ill will because of it, and would not bear to be ruled by a king who followed Jewish ways. He referred her words to Ananias, who was present. When he advised the same, the king was persuaded for the time; but another Jew, Eleazar, came from Galilee, and finding him reading the law of Moses, said: "You ought not only to read the words, king, but also to do what they ordain. How long will you stay uncircumcised?" He did not put off the deed, but was circumcised; and he told his mother and Ananias that the thing had been done. They fell into fear that both the king and they themselves would be in danger. But God did not allow their fear to come to pass.

Helena had a desire to go to Jerusalem and worship at the temple of God. Her son allowed it and gave her a great deal of money, and she went away to Jerusalem. Finding many there dying of famine, she brought grain from Alexandria and a cargo of dried figs from Cyprus, bought at great cost, and shared them out among the needy. Her son too sent much money to the leading men of Jerusalem, so that the starving might be helped by it as far as possible.

So much for that. Artabanus, the king of the Parthians, learning of a plot that the satraps had formed against him, came to Izates, bringing about a thousand kinsmen and servants. He met Izates on the road and said: "Do not overlook me, king, brought low by a change of fortune and become a private man instead of a king, but help me." He said this with tears. Izates, hearing the name, leapt down from his horse and said: "Take heart, king; for either I shall restore you to the kingdom of the Parthians, or I shall give up my own to you." He said this and set him on the horse, and himself followed on foot. Artabanus swore that unless he too mounted his horse and led the way, he would get down himself. Izates was persuaded and leapt onto his horse, and paid the Parthian every honour, bringing him to the palace. He wrote to the Parthians to receive Artabanus. The Parthians agreed to receive him, but said they could not give up the rule, which had already been entrusted to another; but Cinnamus, as the man who had taken over the kingdom was named, wrote to Artabanus (for he had been brought up by him and was a good man), urging him to come in trust and take back the rule. Artabanus trusted him and went. Cinnamus met him, made obeisance, hailed him as king, took the diadem from his own head and put it on his. So Artabanus, restored to his rule after six years, did not forget Izates's kindness, but repaid him.

Some time later, when Artabanus died, his son Vardanes girded on the kingdom. He came to Izates and asked him to be his ally against the Romans; but he would not be persuaded, and even advised him to give up his campaign against them and not to attempt the impossible. Vardanes declared war on Izates for not obeying. But the Parthians, learning that he meant to march against the Romans, killed him and gave the kingdom to his brother Gotarzes; when he died by a plot, his brother Vologeses succeeded him.

Izates's brother Monobazus and his kin also wished to follow Jewish ways, and carried their wish into action. What they had done became known to their subjects. They wrote to Abias, king of the Arabs, promising to give him much money if he would march against their king, and promising that they would desert Izates at the first encounter. The Arab was persuaded by this, and came against Izates bringing a large force. When battle was joined, Izates's men deserted him by agreement and turned their backs and fled. Izates, learning that the betrayal had come from the grandees, withdrew to his camp, found those responsible and punished them. The next day he engaged and won, put the Arabs to flight, and drove their king, pursued, into a fortress. He killed himself as he was being captured, and the fortress was taken and its contents plundered. Izates returned home.

The grandees of the Adiabenians wrote to Vologeses, king of the Parthians, asking him to kill Izates and set up a ruler over them from among the Parthians; for they hated their own king for having become a convert to a foreign religion. The Parthian at once set out with a very large force, and Izates encamped against him. A man sent by the Parthian told Izates how great the force of the Parthians was, and that Vologeses threatened to exact punishment from him for having been ungrateful to his masters; for not even the God he worshipped could save him from his hands. To this Izates answered that he knew the power of the Parthians, but knew that God was more powerful than men. He said this and prayed to God. That very night Vologeses received letters that enemies had invaded Parthia and were ravaging it, and at once hurried off without achieving anything. So by the providence of God Izates escaped the Parthian's threats. Some time later he died, having lived fifty-five years and spent twenty-four in his rule; he died leaving twenty-four sons and as many daughters. He left the rule to his brother Monobazus.

While Fadus was procurator of Judaea, a man

## 6.14

who was a sorcerer, named Theudas, persuaded most of the crowd to take up their possessions and follow him to the Jordan; for he said he was a prophet and could divide the river by his command; and he deceived very many. Fadus sent a squadron of horse against them and killed many, and took no fewer alive, among them Theudas himself, whose head they cut off and brought to Jerusalem. Fadus was succeeded by Tiberius Alexander, the son of Alexander who had been alabarch in Alexandria. The sons of Judas the Galilean, James and Simon, were also put to death; it was Judas who had made the people revolt when Quirinius was assessing; Alexander crucified them. Herod, who reigned over Chalcis, removed Joseph son of Cemedes from the high priesthood and gave it to Ananias son of Nedebaeus.

Cumanus came as successor to Tiberius Alexander. In the eighth year of Claudius's sole rule Herod, the brother of Agrippa the Great, died, leaving three sons; and Claudius gave his realm to the younger Agrippa. While Cumanus was procurator of Judaea, a multitude gathered in Jerusalem for the feast of the Passover. So, to prevent any revolt by the multitude, which was large, Cumanus stationed armed soldiers on the porticoes of the temple to put down any uproar that arose; those before him had done this too. On the fourth day of the feast a soldier on the porticoes uncovered his private parts and showed them to the crowds. They were enraged, since the soldier had committed impiety against God, and the bolder among them abused Cumanus. He was provoked by the abuse, and ordered the whole army to come to the fortress Antonia, which overlooks the temple. The multitude, seeing the soldiers, rushed to flee; and since the exits were narrow, many were pressed together in the flight, crushed and trampled by one another, and died, so that those who died then were counted at twenty thousand; and there was mourning instead of a festival.

This grief had not yet been laid to rest when another evil was added. Some of those who delighted in revolution robbed Stephen, a slave of Caesar, on the road and seized all his property. So Cumanus sent soldiers, ordering them to plunder the neighbouring districts and bring the most notable people to him in chains. While those places were being ravaged, a young soldier, bold and reckless, came upon the laws of Moses kept reverently in a village, and before the eyes of many tore them up, blaspheming and mocking. So the Jews went to Cumanus, begging him to avenge not them but God, whose laws had been insulted. Cumanus, afraid that the multitude would revolt again, beheaded the man who had insulted the laws and put an end to the strife.

## 6.15

The Samaritans too came into enmity with the Jews; and the cause was this. Galileans going to Jerusalem were travelling through a village of the Samaritans, and some men attacked them and killed many. So the leading men of the Galileans went to Cumanus, asking for the dead to be avenged. But he was bribed and took no thought for vengeance. The Galileans, enraged, took to arms, and set fire to some villages of the Samaritans and plundered them. Cumanus came against the Galileans with a force, killed many of them and took more alive. The leading men of Jerusalem put on sackcloth, sprinkled their heads with ashes, and urged the rebels to change their minds, throw down their arms and keep quiet; and they persuaded them. So they dispersed, but from that time the country was full of banditry.

The Samaritans went to Quadratus, governor of Syria, accusing the Jews of having burned their villages. The Jews blamed the Samaritans as the cause of the strife, and before them Cumanus, who had been corrupted by gifts and had not avenged the dead. Quadratus put off the judgement, saying he would come to Judaea and declare his decision there when he had learned the truth. So he came to Samaria, examined what had been done, and judged the Samaritans to be responsible for the disturbance; but the Jews whom Cumanus held in chains he crucified as rebels. Ananias the high priest and those with him, and Ananus the captain, he put in chains and sent to Rome to give account to Claudius of what had been done. He also ordered the leading men of the Samaritans and of the Jews, Cumanus the procurator and Celer the tribune to go to the emperor themselves, to be judged on their disputes with one another. When they had gone, Claudius sat as judge, and finding the Samaritans the authors of the evils, ordered those who had come up to him to be put to death, and condemned Cumanus to exile; but Celer the tribune he ordered to be taken to Jerusalem, dragged through the city in sight of all, and so put to death.

Caesar sent Felix to be procurator of the Jews; and he gave Agrippa the tetrarchy of Philip, and Batanaea and Trachonitis with Abila (these had been the tetrarchies of Lysanias), and took Chalcis from him, after he had ruled it four years. Agrippa gave his sister Drusilla in marriage to Azizus, king of Emesa, who was willing to be circumcised, after Antiochus Epiphanes had declined the marriage because he would not follow Jewish ways; and he betrothed Mariamme to Archelaus, the son of Helcias, to whom Agrippa their father had formerly promised her. Felix, while procurator of Judaea, saw Drusilla, who was exceedingly beautiful, was taken with love for her, and persuaded her to leave her husband and marry him. She bore him a son and named him Agrippa. It is said that in the time of Titus the woman, with her son, who had become a young man, perished at Mount Vesuvius, which is fire-bearing and then burst into fire more than ever. Berenice, another sister of Agrippa, who had been married to Herod her uncle, was joined after his death to Polemo, who was willing to be circumcised, because of the rumour that said she was living with her brother as his lover, so that she might show the slander to be false. The marriage did not last long, since Berenice left Polemo.

Claudius Caesar died, having reigned thirteen years, eight months and twenty days. The story was that he had been killed by poison by his wife Agrippina. Her father was Germanicus, Caesar's brother, and her husband Domitius Ahenobarbus, one of the notable men in Rome; when he died, Claudius married her as a widow, and she had a son Domitius, named after his father. For Claudius had earlier put to death his wife Messalina out of jealousy, by whom he had children, Britannicus and Octavius. He also had Octavia, the eldest of the siblings, by an earlier wife, and he married her to Nero; for Caesar later renamed Agrippina's son Domitius so, when he adopted him. So, to win the sole rule for him, his mother Agrippina killed Claudius with poison. But these things will be told in their proper times and places; let the narrative keep to its sequence.

## 6.16

So Nero held the rule of the Romans after Claudius; and affairs in Judaea went continually from bad to worse. The country was full of bandits and of sorcerers who deceived the crowd, many of whom Felix arrested and put to death. Felix was hostile to Jonathan the high priest, who often admonished him to govern the affairs of Judaea better, and he looked for a pretext by which to get rid of the man who was constantly troubling him; and he killed him through the bandits. They came into the temple as if to worship, carrying daggers under their clothes, mingled with the multitude and killed Jonathan. Since the bold deed went unpunished, the bandits went up without fear and killed some who were their own enemies and others for pay on behalf of others. Sorcerers and deceivers persuaded the crowd to follow them into the desert, where they would show them clear signs and wonders done by God; and Felix punished many of them. The bandits stirred the people to war with the Romans, wishing not to obey them, and they burned and destroyed the villages of those who would not be persuaded.

Syrians and Jews lived in Caesarea, and the Jews claimed the first place, since Herod their king had built the city; the Syrians admitted what concerned Herod, but said that formerly it had been a city called Strato's Tower, and that at that time no Jew lived in the city. When the people of Caesarea quarrelled over this, those in charge of the country punished the guilty with blows and lulled the uproar for a little. The Jews, who surpassed the Syrians in wealth and despised them for that reason, abused them. They, though beaten in money, took confidence because most of those serving under the Romans were from Caesarea, and for a time they too answered the Jews' insults with words; then they threw stones at each other, until many on both sides were wounded and fell; and the Jews won. Felix ordered the Jews to stop, and when they did not obey he let loose the soldiers on them; he killed many, held more alive, and allowed the soldiers to plunder houses. The more reasonable and leading men among the Jews begged Felix to call off the soldiers, to spare them, and to give them a chance to repent of what they had done. And Felix was persuaded.

King Agrippa gave the high priesthood to Ishmael, the son of Phabi. The high priests and the priests, together with the leading men of Jerusalem, were in strife with one another; they abused one another and threw stones, and there was no one to rebuke them or stop the strife. The high priests went so far in shamelessness as even to send to the threshing floors and take by force the tithes owed to the priests, so that the poor among the priests died of want.

When Porcius Festus was sent by Nero as successor to Felix, the Jews of Caesarea accused Felix before Nero; and he would perhaps have paid the penalty for his wrongs to them, had not Pallas, his brother, who had great power with Nero, begged off his anger. The Syrians in Caesarea, winning over Beryllus, Nero's tutor, with money, obtained through him a letter of Caesar declaring void the Jews' equal citizenship with the Syrians in Caesarea. From this the later evils grew for the nation; for because of this letter the Jews clung all the more to their strife with the Syrians, until the war was kindled.

## 6.17

Festus, coming to Judaea, found it harmed by bandits. For those called sicarii, who were also bandits, then gathered in greater numbers. They used curved daggers like those called *sicae* by the Romans, from which they were named sicarii. At the feasts they mingled with the multitude and easily slaughtered whom they wished, and they plundered and burned the villages. Festus sent a force against those deceived by a sorcerer who promised salvation to those willing to follow him into the desert; and those sent destroyed both that deceiver and his followers.

King Agrippa built a large room in the palace, and from it watched what was done in the temple. The people of the city were angry at this. So they raised a wall which cut off the view not only from the royal house but also from the western portico, where the Romans kept guard at the feasts because of the temple. Agrippa was indignant at this, and Festus more so, and he wished to pull down the wall. But they asked to be allowed to petition Caesar. When Festus allowed it, they sent to Nero ten of the leading men, with Ishmael the high priest and Helcias the treasurer. Nero, as a favour to his wife Poppaea, who pleaded for the Jews, ordered the building to be left. Poppaea let the others go back, but kept Ishmael and Helcias with her as hostages. King Agrippa, learning this, gave the high priesthood to Joseph called Decabi, the son of Simon, who had been high priest; then he took it from Joseph and assigned it to Ananus, the son of Ananus.

This young Ananus, having received the high priesthood, was reckless and bold. So, when Festus had died and Albinus, who had been sent by Nero as procurator of Judaea in place of Festus, had not yet reached Judaea, he assembled a council, to use Josephus's own words, and brought before it the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, whose name was James, and some others, accusing them of having broken the law, and handed them over to be stoned. Those in the city who were thought most reasonable and exact about the laws took this hard, and denounced him both to Albinus and to Agrippa. So the king took the high priesthood from him, after he had held it three months, and appointed Jesus son of Mnaseas.

Albinus, coming to Jerusalem, made efforts to bring peace to the country, and destroyed many of the sicarii. Agrippa gave the high priesthood to Jesus son of Gamaliel, removing Jesus son of Mnaseas. So strife arose among the high priests, who took the boldest as their partners, and the strife went on from insults to one another as far as stones. So from that time above all the city of Jerusalem came to be in a bad way, and everything went from bad to worse. Albinus, learning that Gessius Florus was coming as his successor, brought out the prisoners, ordered those who plainly deserved to die to be put to death, and took money and released those imprisoned on small charges. So the prison was emptied of prisoners, and the country was filled with bandits. Agrippa removed Jesus son of Gamaliel from the high priesthood and gave it to Matthias son of Theophilus, in whose time the war against the Romans began.

The high priesthood began from Aaron; after him his sons received it, and from them the honour remained with their descendants. So it was an ancestral custom among the Jews that no one should take the high priesthood, even if a king aimed at it, except those of the blood of Aaron; though the custom was not kept for all time. From Aaron down to Phinehas, who was declared high priest by the rebels during the war, there were eighty-three in all.

Gessius Florus, arriving in Judaea as successor to Albinus, filled the Jews with many evils, and became so very wicked that by the excess of his wickedness Albinus was praised as a benefactor. For Albinus hid his wickedness and was careful not to be caught in his wrongdoing, but Florus committed his crimes against the nation openly and shamelessly, as if making a display of them. And why should I count up his evils one by one? I shall show the whole by saying this much: it was Florus who forced the Jews to take up war against the Romans. The war began in the second year of Florus's procuratorship and the twelfth of Nero's sole rule.

## 6.18

From this the revolt of the Jews broke out into the open, and the war began. To tell each part of it would be a greater task than the present undertaking. I have decided to leave the rest aside, and only to give an abridgement of the capture of Jerusalem itself.

Vespasian, entrusted by Nero with the conduct of the war when Nero learned of the revolt of the Jews, did not attack Jerusalem first, but hurried to take first the cities under the mother city, and so to subdue the mother city itself. So he took Ptolemais, and there joined his son Titus, who came from Alexandria bringing the fifteenth legion. Titus had been sent by him from Achaea, where he had been appointed commander of the war by Nero; for Vespasian happened to be in Achaea when the revolt of the Jews was reported to him. He set out first against Galilee, and attacking first the city of Jotapata, and besieging it for forty days, he sacked it, and captured Josephus, who was general of Galilee and defending that city. From there he went against other forts and towns, and brought some under the Romans by agreement and others by siege. Having done this, he was preparing to engage the mother city itself, which was in a bad way, since those in it were at strife with one another and had rolled into civil fighting and mutual slaughter, and its fighting strength was being destroyed by this.

But the news that Nero had fallen from his sole rule, fled Rome in secret and killed himself checked Vespasian's impulse. Then, learning that Galba had become emperor, he sent Titus to him, to greet him and to learn what he ordered about the Jews. While Titus was still on his way, Galba too was killed. Hearing this, Titus went back to his father. And because of the uncertainty about the rule of the Romans they did not undertake the attack on Jerusalem, but stayed quiet in Caesarea. When Galba had been killed, Otho succeeded to the rule. The legions in Germany proclaimed Vitellius emperor. So Otho sent forces and made war on Vitellius. When those he had sent were defeated, Otho killed himself. Vitellius went off to Rome with the armies; for by now Otho's men too had gone over to him. Vespasian, if any small towns of the Jews were left not yet taken, sent forces and sacked these too, so that only the city of Jerusalem was now left as the Romans' target.

The city's affairs were terribly sick, as has been said. For outside, Simon and his men were more fearsome to the Jews than the Romans, and inside, those called Zealots and John their leader were harsher than both the Romans and Simon. Since the Zealots oppressed those in the city most violently, the people were forced to invite Simon and the crowd with him and bring him into the city, thinking he would perhaps free them from the Zealots' tyranny; but without knowing it they had received a worse tyrant against themselves. While this was happening in Jerusalem, Vitellius reached Rome, proclaimed emperor. When Vespasian learned this he was not pleased, and disdained to have Vitellius as master. The commanders of the legions with him, and the soldiers too, came together and proclaimed Vespasian emperor.

## 6.19

As he was about to sail, Vespasian entrusted the siege of Jerusalem to his son Titus. He gathered the forces and went off to Jerusalem, and having encamped thirty stades away, he took six hundred picked horsemen from there and went to view the city and the temper of those inside. Countless men ran out from the city against them. Most of those with Titus, seeing the frenzied onrush of the Jews, were checked from going forward, and Titus, cut off with a few of the others, was caught in the midst of the enemy. Seeing himself in danger, he turned his horse, shouted to those about him to follow, charged the Jews, and driving back his attackers with his sword, got safely to the camp; two of those following him fell.

After a day he came to Scopus (a place so called, seven stades from the city, from which the city and the temple can be seen), and ordered a camp to be built. Those in the city were always clashing with one another, but then the great war coming from outside put a stop to their quarrel. So the Jews ran out of the city and fought those building the camp, and did harm to their opponents, but suffered more harm themselves. When the war from outside eased a little, the strife inside rose again. John with the Zealots seized the temple by a trick, and many were killed; and he took heart against Simon.

Titus ordered the space from Scopus to the wall to be levelled. While this was being done, the Jews contrived an ambush against the Romans. The boldest of the rebels came out of the city, as if they had been thrown out by those who wanted peace, and huddled about the wall; others stood on the wall, as though they were of the people, shouted for peace and asked for terms, calling the Romans as if to open the gates to them. The soldiers suspected nothing and went to the task, but Titus suspected the strangeness of the invitation. For a day before, when he had invited them through Josephus to come to terms, he found them thinking nothing reasonable. So he ordered the soldiers to stay where they were. But some had already run to the gates; at first those who seemed to have been thrown out fell back, but when the Romans were between the city's towers, they ran out and surrounded them. Those on the wall shot missiles at them and hurled stones, killing many and wounding more. The Jews leapt about brandishing their shields, while Titus and the officers threatened the soldiers.

When the ground before the walls had been levelled, wishing to move the camp there, Titus drew up the strongest part of his force facing the wall; and with the Jews' sallies blocked in this way, the Romans encamped there. The city was surrounded by three walls; where the nature of the ground fortified it, it was girded with one circuit. With the city like this, an attack seemed impracticable to Titus. For the moment, then, he decided to attack at the tomb of John the high priest. He ordered his men to lay waste the area before the city and gather timber, so as to raise earthworks. They carried out the order, and when the earthworks had been raised Titus ordered the rams brought up to strike the wall.

When the rams had begun at three points, and a tremendous crash echoed round the city, a cry went up from those inside, and the rebels in fear came to agreement, settling to make common defence against the enemy. But though the rams struck, the wall did not give way under the blows; only a corner of one of the towers was shaken, and the wall was intact. The Jews, watching the Romans scattered about the camp, all ran out, bringing fire against the engines. A fierce battle took place round the siege engines, some forcing their way to set them alight, the others to stop them; and the Jews prevailed out of desperation. The fire was catching the engines, and they would have been burned up had Titus not come to help with the horsemen. As it was, about twelve of the Jews' front fighters fell, and the rest gave way and were driven into the city. One of the Jews taken alive was crucified before the wall, in case the rest might be terrified at the sight and give in. When Titus had built towers of timber, each fifty cubits high, and set them on the earthworks, the Jews no longer stopped the blows of the rams, being shot at and harmed from the towers. When the wall was already giving way to Nico (for the Jews themselves called the Romans' largest engine so), most of them lost heart and withdrew. And when the Romans climbed onto it, all fled to the second wall.

So the Romans took the first wall in fifteen days. After this they attacked the second wall. The siege engine was brought up; and when the tower against which it was striking shook, the others had fled,

## 6.20

but a sorcerer named Castor, with ten others, stretched out his hands as if in supplication and called on Titus. Titus believed him and checked the blows of the ram. Castor said he wished to come down on terms, and of the ten with him, some joined in pretending to supplicate, while others shouted that they would never be slaves to the Romans. While the time was being wasted on this, Castor let Simon know that he should take counsel about urgent matters, since he was fooling the Romans and holding back their attack. At last he was found to be dragging out the time by deceit, and he provoked the Romans to make the blows of the ram more powerful. So the second wall too was taken on the fifth day after the first.

Titus went inside and stopped his men from killing those caught, and ordered the soldiers not to set fire to the houses either; nor did he wish much of the wall to be pulled down; for he set more store on saving the city for himself and the temple for the city. So the rebels attacked the Romans who had entered the city; some shot at them in the narrow streets, some from the houses, some from the wall. The Roman guards leapt down from the towers and withdrew to the camp. The Jews, knowing the narrow streets, wounded many, fell on them and drove them out. So the Romans, having taken the second wall too, were driven out again, and the rebels' spirits were raised.

By now famine was creeping over the city and destroying many good men through want of necessities. This pleased the rebels, who thought that only those who did not want peace deserved to be saved, and that the destruction of the others was a relief to themselves. The Romans tried again to take the second wall, and the Jews prevented them; for three days they held out, but on the fourth, unable to bear the attack, they withdrew further in.

Again Titus took the wall, and at once pulled down its northern part; he put a garrison in the rest and prepared to attack the third. He divided the legions in two and began to raise earthworks. Of those inside, the rebels were unbending and unyielding, but the people were moved to desertion, and many deserted in secret. Those whom the rebels found wishing to do so, or about whom they had even a shadow of suspicion, they at once slaughtered; and fastening a false charge of desertion on the well-off, they killed them at once and plundered their property. The famine at its height increased the cruelty of the rebels. For through want of food they burst into the houses and searched them, and if they found food when the occupants had denied having any, they tortured them, and if they did not find it, they examined them more carefully, as having hidden it. They took the bodies of the wretched people as evidence of whether they had food or not. For those who still had some strength were thought to have it, while those whose bodies had wasted away were passed by. If anyone had a supply of wheat or barley, he locked his house and ate; some, under the force of the famine, even swallowed the grain unprepared. Mothers snatched the food from the very mouths of their babes, children from their fathers, wives from their husbands. Yet even eating so, they did not escape the rebels. Wherever they saw a house locked or smoke rising, they took it as a sign that those inside were eating, and breaking down the doors they brought the food up out of their throats; and there was no pity for grey hairs or for youth. On those who had managed to eat what they had first, they inflicted terrible and merciless punishments as if they were wrongdoers, blocking the passages of their private parts with vetch and cruelly driving sharp stakes into their seats. Someone would suffer things dreadful even to hear of, to make him confess to one loaf, or betray a single handful of barley meal to the bandits. To go through each of the things that happened then would be difficult or even impossible; but to put it briefly, no other city ever suffered such things, nor did any other race from the beginning of time prove more fertile in wickedness.

## 6.21

Such were the sufferings of the Jews; and Titus's earthworks went forward, though the soldiers were harmed from the wall. Those who went out to gather food were ambushed (they were not only common people, but also some of the fighters, no longer content with plunder), and when caught by the Romans, after every torture, they were crucified before the wall. To Titus the suffering seemed pitiable, since five hundred or even more were caught each day. But he judged it unsafe either to guard them or to let them go; and at the same time he hoped that the rest would give in at the sight. The rebels dragged the relatives of the deserters onto the wall, and those of the people who were eager to learn, and showed them what those who fled to the Romans suffered, lying about both the enemy and their own people.

When the earthworks had been finished, the siege engines were brought up. But the Jews from inside had dug under the space from the Antonia to the earthworks, propped up the tunnels with timber and left the earthworks hanging. Then they filled the trench with fuel and set fire to it; and when the supporting timbers burned, the mine suddenly gave way and the earthworks collapsed; and the Romans were struck with dismay and despondency at the device. Elsewhere the Romans brought up the siege engines and shook the wall; but some men rushed out recklessly, set fire to them and burned them all. With the earthworks destroyed, the Romans were despondent, and Titus took counsel with his commanders. Some urged raising others again, others to sit down before the city without earthworks and guard their exits and the bringing in of supplies, and so, they said, the city would be taken by famine; others thought it best to bring up the whole force and make an attempt on the wall, since the Jews would not bear the assault. But none of these pleased Titus; he decided to surround the city with a wall, so as to block every way out for those inside. He divided the work among the army. A rivalry fell on them for the work, and a kind of superhuman zeal, and the work was quickly built. Having shut in the city with the wall, he went round and inspected the first watch of the night himself, and entrusted the rest to others; and the guards took turns to sleep.

With the exits, every hope of safety was shut off from the Jews, and the famine fed on the people by houses and families. The roofs were full of women and babes who had collapsed, and the narrow streets of dead old men; children and young men, swollen, went round the market places like ghosts, and fell wherever each happened to give out. Those still alive had no strength to bury their kin; and many who set out to bury them died on top of those they were burying. The rebels became harsher even than the evils of the famine, robbing tombs and plundering houses. At first they ordered the dead to be buried from the public treasury, not bearing the stench; then they threw them from the walls into the ravines. Titus, going round and seeing these filled with the dead, and a thick discharge running from the rotting bodies, groaned, and raising his hands called God to witness that the work was not of his choosing. And he set about earthworks again, though the timber was hard to get; for it was brought from ninety stades away.

Many of the people deserted, some throwing themselves down from the walls, others going out as if to battle with stones and taking refuge with the Romans. Even so, most of them perished; for they were starving, and meeting plenty of food and gorging themselves greedily, they burst. Something else also happened that destroyed the deserters. Some of them who had gold coins swallowed them when they were about to desert to the Romans, so that they would not be robbed of them if caught. When they were with the Romans, they passed the coins out with the excrement of the belly, and picked them out and took them. One of the deserters was caught doing this; and when a rumour went round the camp that the deserters were coming full of gold, the wretches had their bellies cut open, so that from this a great destruction of the Jews came about; for in one night more than three thousand were ripped open. Titus, learning this, threatened the army; but Titus's anger helped the deserters little or not at all. Money was found in few of them, and the rest perished for nothing but hopes. It is said that the dead carried out through the gates of the city and thrown out, of the poor alone, amounted to six hundred thousand, and the number of the others could not be found out, while a medimnus of grain was sold for a talent.

## 6.22

With the city walled round by the Romans, as I have said above, it was not even possible to gather grass; so they searched out the old dung of animals and made it their food. The Romans had now raised their earthworks, and the wall of the Antonia was being struck by the siege engines, but it did not fall under the blows. Some of the soldiers made a roof of their shields over their bodies, dug under the foundations with crowbars, and shook out four of the stones. Night came on and stopped the fighting on both sides; and during it the wall, shaken by the rams, suddenly collapsed. But another wall was seen built up inside, which turned the Romans' joy at the fall into despondency. Titus spoke to the soldiers and roused their spirits. A man from Syria named Sabinus, holding his shield over his head with his left hand and drawing his sword with his right, went at the wall; and eleven others followed him, eager to match his courage. Those on the wall hurled javelins at them, shot missiles, and rolled down huge stones, by which some of the eleven were swept away. But Sabinus did not check his rush until he had climbed onto the wall and routed the enemy. Just when he had succeeded in the attempt, he tripped on a rock and fell headlong on it with a clash of arms. The Jews turned at the noise, and seeing him alone and lying down, shot at him from every side. He rose to his knee and defended himself, but under the number of his wounds his right arm gave out, and he was buried under the missiles. Of the rest, they killed three with stones when they had already reached the top, and the eight were carried wounded to the camp.

Two days later, at night, some men quietly climbed up through the ruins into the Antonia, slaughtered the guards there as they slept, and sounded the trumpet. The other guards fled, and Titus went up with his picked men, and the legions followed. The Jews fled into the temple, and Titus's men burst in through the tunnel that the Jews had dug under the Romans' earthworks. A fierce battle broke out about the entrances; they drew their swords and grappled, and there was great slaughter on both sides. When the Roman line was already giving way, one Julian, a centurion, an excellent man, leapt forward and alone routed the victorious Jews. The crowd fled and scattered. As that brave man pursued the scattered men, he slipped on the paving, since he had many nails in his boots, as the other soldiers did too. The Jews surrounded him and wounded him from all sides. Even lying down he defended himself, until, covered with wounds, he gave in, admired even by the enemy themselves.

So the Jews drove back the Romans and shut them up in the Antonia. Titus, after many appeals to the rebels both through Josephus and himself, when he saw them implacable, went again, though unwillingly, to war. He chose the best men and ordered them to attack the guards about the ninth hour of the night. They did not find the guards asleep, but they knew of the attack and closed with them, and at the shout the others came together too. The fighting went on from the ninth hour of the night to the fifth of the day, and the battle was evenly matched, victory weighing down on neither side. So the fighters then parted. The rest of the Roman force in seven days overthrew the foundations of the Antonia and made a broad way up to the temple. The legions, approaching the first enclosure, began earthworks. These were raised with great toil; and the Jews set fire to the part of the northern and western portico joined to the Antonia and broke off about twenty cubits, beginning to burn the holy places with their own hands. The Romans too set fire to the neighbouring portico; and when the fire had gone as far as fifteen cubits, the Jews cut away the roof. The rebels in the temple attacked the soldiers on the earthworks openly, and defended themselves with tricks.

Those who died of famine were a countless multitude. Things happened to those still alive dreadful to tell and hard for hearers to believe; of which I shall tell one. A woman from beyond the Jordan, not undistinguished in family and wealth, had fled to Jerusalem and was besieged there with the others. When she often got food for herself, the bandits in the city plundered it. Indignant at this, and driven by anger and famine, she killed the child she had at the breast, roasted it, and ate part, keeping the rest for a second meal. The rebels, when the smell reached them, were there at once, and threatened to slaughter her unless she gave up what she had prepared. She uncovered the remains of the child; and they were struck out of their wits at the sight and shuddered, and withdrew trembling, barely leaving this food to the mother.

When the earthworks were finished, the rams were brought up; but they achieved nothing because of the hardness of the wall. Others dug under the foundations, and not even so was the wall shaken down. So, despairing of other means, they brought ladders to the porticoes. The Jews were not quick enough to stop them, but fell on those who climbed up and fought them; and there was no small slaughter of them.

## 6.23

Titus, when he saw that sparing the temple was turning to the harm of his soldiers, ordered the gates to be set on fire. When the fire was brought to them, the silver with which they were plated melted and let the flame take hold of the wood, and from there it caught the porticoes. As the Jews saw the fire all round, their spirits gave way along with their bodies. That day and the following night the fire prevailed; for they had been able to set the porticoes alight part by part, not all together from every side. The next day Titus ordered part of the force to put out the fire and make a road by the gates for an easier way up for the legions, and himself summoned the six chief commanders and took counsel about the temple. Some thought it best to use the law of war and spare nothing; others advised that if the Jews mounted it and fought from it, it should be burned, since then a fortress would be burned and no longer a temple, but if not, it should be saved. But Titus said that even if the Jews mounted it and fought from it, he would not take vengeance on lifeless things instead of men, nor burn so great a work; for its destruction would be a loss to the Romans, just as it would be an ornament of their empire if it were saved.

So Titus's aim was to attack with his whole force the next day and take possession of the temple; but God, it seems, had long since decreed its destruction. For the rebels attacked the guards of the outer temple, and they, overcome by the numbers and fury of those running out, gave way. Titus, seeing this from above in the Antonia, came to help with the picked horsemen. The Jews did not stand the charge, but were shut up in the inner temple. When Titus withdrew, the rebels rested a little and attacked the Romans again. The Romans routed them and came as far as the temple. One of the soldiers snatched a piece of the burning wood, and being lifted up by another soldier, threw the fire into a golden window. As the flame rose, a cry went up from the Jews, and they ran together to defend it; and Titus, learning of it, ran to the temple to stop the fire, and with voice and right hand signalled to the fighters to put out the fire. But they neither heard him shouting nor heeded the signs of his hand. The legions, coming in and nearing the temple, pretended not even to hear Titus's orders, and urged those in front of them to throw in fire. The rebels were helpless, having given up defence, and there was slaughter and rout everywhere.

Titus, since he could not check the impulses of the frenzied soldiers and the fire was prevailing, went in with his commanders and beheld the holy place of God and what was in it. Since the flame had not yet got inside, but was spreading over the buildings round the temple, he thought the work could still be saved, and himself tried to urge the soldiers to put out the fire, and ordered one of those with him to hold back the disobedient by beating them with clubs. But they, overcome by fury and hatred of the Jews, were checked neither by respect for Titus nor by fear of the one restraining them. Hope of plunder also spurred on most of them, since they believed that what was inside was full of riches. Someone managed to throw fire into the hinges of the gate; and when a flame suddenly appeared from inside, the commanders withdrew and Titus himself, and no one any longer stopped those setting fire.

So the temple received the fire, a purging of the things impiously done in it, or a punishment of those who did them. One might wonder that the burning of the temple fell on the same month and day on which the earlier temple too had been burned by the Babylonians. From the first building, which Solomon made, to the destruction now being told, which took place in the second year of Vespasian's sole rule, there are one thousand one hundred and thirty years, seven months and fifteen days; and from the later one, which began to be built in the second year of the reign of Cyrus, to the last capture, six hundred and thirty-nine years and forty-five days.

## 6.24

While the temple burned there was plunder of whatever came to hand and slaughter of those caught. Nowhere could the ground be seen for the dead, but the soldiers ran after the fugitives climbing over heaps of bodies. The crowd of bandits pushed back the Romans and broke out into the city, and what was left of the common people fled to the outer portico. Some of the priests withdrew onto the wall, which was eight cubits thick, and stayed there. Two of the notable men threw themselves into the fire and were burned with the temple. The Romans, judging it useless to spare the buildings round the temple now that it was burning, set fire to them all; and the fire caught the treasuries too, in which a countless amount of money had been stored, and countless costly garments and other valuables. For all the wealth of the Jews had been heaped up there from every side, since those who owned it laid it up there as in a safe storehouse.

A countless crowd of the common people perished, and the cause of their destruction was a false prophet, who proclaimed to those in the city that God ordered them to go up to the temple to receive the signs of their deliverance. Many such men were put up by the tyrants to say this, so that people would desert less; and by them the wretched crowd was led astray and, as if thunderstruck, did not believe the clear signs.

There were many signs. A star like a sword stood over the city, and a comet appeared and lasted a year; and once before the war a light shone round the temple and the altar, so that it seemed bright day, and lasted half an hour. A cow brought to be sacrificed gave birth to a lamb. The eastern gate of the inner temple, which was of bronze and massive, so that it was opened and shut with difficulty by twenty men, and had very deep bars and bolts, was seen at night opened of its own accord. This showed that the security of the temple was being undone, and that the entry would be easy for the enemy. At another time a supernatural apparition was seen before sunset, chariots passing through the air over the whole country, and armed troops darting through the clouds. At the feast of Pentecost the priests who went into the inner temple felt a movement and a crash, and then heard a voice saying: "Let us depart from here."

Four years before the war, at the feast of Tabernacles, one Jesus, a countryman, came to the feast and began to cry out: "A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice against Jerusalem and the temple, a voice against bridegrooms and brides, a voice against all the people." And he went round the city crying this day and night. He was beaten for his ill-omened words, but he cried nothing else than the same words. He was brought before the Roman who was then procurator of the country, and though flayed with whips he neither begged nor wept, but turning his voice to a lament, at each blow he cried: "Woe to Jerusalem," until Albinus (for he was procurator then) judged him mad and let him go. From then until the war he lamented: "Woe to Jerusalem." At the feasts above all he cried out the gloomy omen. He did this for seven years and five months, until during the siege, going round on the wall, he again cried piercingly: "Woe to the city, and to the temple, and to the people." When at last he added: "Woe to me too," a stone from the stone-thrower struck him and killed him.

## 6.25

The rebels had fled into the city, and with the temple and everything round it burning, the Romans brought their standards into the sacred precinct and with the loudest acclamations declared Titus emperor. All the soldiers made so much money from plunder that in Syria a weight of gold was sold for half its former value. The priests who had climbed onto the wall of the temple, as has been said, held out for five days and, starving, came down begging to be spared. But Titus said that the time for pardon too had passed, and saying that since the temple was gone the priests must perish with it, he ordered the men to be punished.

The tyrants' party, unable to escape, invited Titus to a parley. He came, reproached them for their madness, and promised to grant them their lives if they threw down their arms and surrendered themselves. The bandits said they could not accept terms from him, since they had sworn never to do so, but asked to go out with their wives and children, and they would leave the city to him. Titus was indignant at this, and told them that none of them should desert any more or hope for terms, for he would spare no one, but they should fight and save themselves as best they could. He ordered the soldiers to burn and plunder the city; and they set fire everywhere. The rebels rushed to the royal palace, in which many had stored their possessions because of its strength, drove the Romans from it, slaughtered all of the people gathered there, numbering eight thousand four hundred, and plundered the money. The next day the Romans drove the bandits out of the lower city and burned everything as far as Siloam. The rebels, seeing the city burning, said with cheerful faces that they awaited their end in good spirits. They would neither bear to surrender nor were able to fight the Romans, but scattering over the outer parts of the city they slaughtered any they found wishing to desert. No place in the city was bare, but every one held a corpse either of famine or of strife. The tyrants and the bandits with them were warmed by a last hope, in the tunnels: if they fled into them, they did not expect to be searched out, and when the Romans marched away they were confident they could come out and escape. But this was only a dream; for they were not going to escape either God or the Romans. They were also at war with one another over the plunder.

Caesar, since it was impossible to take the upper city without earthworks, being surrounded by cliffs, assigned his force to the works.

## 6.26

In these days the leaders of the Idumaeans sent five men to Titus and begged him to give them terms. He, hoping that the tyrants too would give in once the Idumaeans were drawn away, granted them their safety. But Simon, learning their intention, at once killed the five who had met Titus, and seized the leaders and imprisoned them. He kept the Idumaeans under guard, and watched the wall with closer guards because of the deserters. Many were slaughtered, but more escaped. The Romans received them all, out of weariness of killing and hope of gain. For letting only the common people go, they sold the others with their wives and children, each at the lowest price, because of the number of those sold and the fewness of the buyers. Those sold off were a countless multitude, and of the common people more than forty thousand were saved. One of the priests, named Jesus, receiving an oath for his safety on condition of handing over some of the treasures, came out and handed over two lampstands, a table, mixing bowls and libation bowls, all of solid gold, and the curtains, the vestments of the high priests and many other vessels. Phinehas, the treasurer of the temple, was arrested and showed them the tunics and girdles of the high priests and many of the other treasures.

When the earthworks were finished the Romans brought their engines up to the wall. Of the rebels some withdrew to the citadel, some slipped down into the tunnels, and many defended themselves. When part of the wall had been broken away, fear fell on the tyrants too, and they were in suspense to flee. Since they no longer had those who had long been loyal (for they had scattered), and the enemy were reported to be near, they fell on their faces and lamented their own folly, and came down of their own accord from the towers, from which they could never have been taken by force, but only by famine, and fled to the ravine of Siloam, and then slipped down into the tunnels. The Romans, having taken the walls without bloodshed, slaughtered those they caught and set fire to the houses. They stopped towards evening. The next day Titus went inside and wondered at the strength of the city and of the towers, and said: "We have fought with God's help, and it was God who brought the Jews down from these strongholds." While destroying the rest of the city and razing the walls, he left these towers as a memorial of his own fortune, with which as his fellow soldier he had overcome what could not be taken.

The number of all the prisoners taken in the whole war came to ninety-seven thousand, and of those who perished during the whole siege, one million one hundred thousand. Most of these were of the same race, but not natives; for they had gathered from the whole country for the feast of Unleavened Bread, were suddenly caught by the war, and the war surrounded the city when it was full of men.

When the Romans had killed some of those in the open and taken others prisoner, they searched those in the tunnels, and breaking up the ground they killed all they came upon. More than two thousand dead were found there too. A terrible stench met those who stooped over the bodies, so that many at once withdrew. Others out of greed went in, treading on heaps of dead; for they found many of the treasures in the tunnels. Many prisoners held by the tyrants were also brought up and released.

Of these avengers, John, starving in the tunnels with his brothers, begged to receive terms from the Romans; Simon was caught later, while Titus was staying at the Caesarea called Philip's. For during the siege of Jerusalem he was in the upper city, and when the Romans got inside the city, Simon took the most loyal of his friends, and with them stonecutters and the iron tools needed for the work, and let himself down with them into one of the tunnels; and going through the old excavation he mined the earth, so that they might go further and come up in safety. But when the miners had gone a little way, their food ran out. Then he put on white tunics, pinned a purple cloak about him, and came up out of the earth at the place where the temple had formerly been. At first amazement fell on those who saw him; then they came nearer and asked who he was. Simon told them to call their commander. Terentius Rufus came when called, who had been left in command of the army. When Simon had made known to him who he was, he was seized, bound and kept under guard. His capture was reported to Titus. He was kept for the triumph, in which he was put to death, dragged with a noose in the forum at Rome, where it is the Romans' custom to kill those put to death for crimes.

This was the end of Simon son of Gioras; and John, the other fury of the Jews, was condemned to chains for life. Of the multitude of prisoners, some were sent to the works in Egypt, and others perished in the shows held in the cities, either given to fight wild beasts or killing one another. Simon's coming up out of the earth caused a great number of the other rebels too to be found in the tunnels, so that from this even the foundations of the temple were dug up.

## 6.27

Danger was brought not only on the Jews in Jerusalem, but also on those in the other cities. To tell it all would be hard work; but what happened at Antioch to the Jews living there must be told. The nation of the Jews is widely scattered over the whole world, having often been taken captive, as has already been told, and dispersed everywhere; but it is mingled most of all with Syria because it is its neighbour, and more than the other cities of Syria Antioch had Jewish inhabitants, both because of the size of the city and because the kings after Antiochus granted them safe residence in it. For Antiochus Epiphanes sacked Jerusalem and plundered the temple, but the kings after him allowed them to share in the city equally with the Greeks. So they grew in number, bringing a great number of Greeks over to their religion.

At the time when the war of Jerusalem broke out and Vespasian sailed to Syria, and hatred of the nation was at its height everywhere, a Jew named Antiochus, the son of the chief of the Jews at Antioch, came before the assembly of the Antiochenes and accused his father, and accused the rest of the Jews too, of having planned to burn the whole city; and he handed over some foreign Jews as sharers in the plan. The common people of Antioch at once burned those handed over, and rushed against the native Jews to punish them too. Antiochus, the accuser of his countrymen, saying he had given up his ancestral religion, sacrificed as is the custom of the Greeks, and urged that the others be forced to do likewise; for the plotters would be revealed by not forswearing their religion. When the Antiochenes made the test, a few gave way, and those who would not bear to become Greek were destroyed. This Antiochus also got soldiers from the Roman governor and was harsh to his countrymen, not allowing them to rest on the seventh day; and he made the compulsion so strong that not only at Antioch was the rest of the sabbath abolished, but in the other cities too this prevailed for some time.

Not only this befell the Jews in Antioch; a second disaster was added. It happened that the city's square market place was burned, with the magistrates' offices and the record offices. Antiochus blamed the Jews for the fire, and stirred up the Antiochenes, who already suspected them, against them; and all rushed as if frenzied at those accused. Some barely restrained them, advising them to refer the matter to Titus. Meanwhile some, making a careful inquiry into the matter, found the race of the Jews not guilty, but that wicked men had dared the deed through the pressure of debts, thinking that if they burned the market place and the public records they would be rid of the demands.

Meanwhile Titus arrived at Antioch. The people of the Antiochenes went out to meet him and acclaimed him, and joined to their acclamations a petition asking him to expel the Jews from the city. He then heard what was said quietly and passed on; but later, when the Antiochenes pressed very insistently for the Jews to be driven out of the city, he said: "But their own country, to which they ought to go back, has been destroyed, and no place would receive them any longer." So, failing in this request, they turned to a second, and asked for the bronze tablets on which the rights of the Jews had been written to be taken away. But Titus did not assent to this either, and left everything to the Jews at Antioch as they had it before. He himself, going away to Alexandria and seeing Jerusalem on his way, pitied the destruction of the city, cursing those responsible for the revolt as responsible for the desolation of the city, a city ancient and prosperous. Parts of its very deep wealth were still being found even in the ruins themselves. For the Romans dug up much, and the prisoners showed them more, which the owners had stored underground against the uncertain turns of the war.

## 6.28

Titus went to Egypt and reached Alexandria, and being about to sail from there to Italy, he ordered the leaders of the prisoners, John and Simon, and seven hundred other men outstanding in size and beauty of body, to be taken to Italy at once, so that they might fill out the procession in the triumph.

After Titus's arrival in Rome, Lucilius Bassus was sent as commander to Judaea. He won over the fortress at Herodium with those holding it; then, gathering all the soldiers there were there, he marched on Machaerus. This fortress was very hard to take, being a rocky hill fortified with a wall; and it had been so made by nature that it could not even be approached, for it was moated on every side by deep ravines. Strong as it was, it also had inside a palace wonderful for the size and beauty of its buildings, and many cisterns for collecting water in the most suitable places. Besides the rest, there was in the palace a rue plant worth wonder for its size; for it fell short of no fig tree in height and thickness. The story was that it had lasted from the times of Herod, and it would perhaps have lasted a very long time, had it not been cut down by the Jews who took over the place.

In the ravine on the north of the fortress there is a place called Baaras, and it grows a root called by the same name. It is like flame in colour, and about evening it flashes out a light. It is not easy to take for those who wish to, but shrinks away and does not stand still until someone pours a woman's urine or her menstrual blood on it. Even then, death is certain for those who touch it, unless someone happens to carry off the root itself hanging from his hand. It is also taken safely in another way. They dig round it, so that the part of the root hidden in the earth is very small, then tie a dog to it, and when the dog rushes to follow the man who tied it, the root is easily pulled up, but the dog dies at once; and there is no fear for those who take it after that. It is much sought after for one power. For the so-called demons, which enter into some people, it quickly drives out, even if it is only brought near the sick.

Wishing to bring this fortress over, Bassus tried to fill in the ravine on its east. The Jews shut in there separated themselves from the foreigners, forced them to stay in the lower town, and held the upper fortress themselves. They made sallies eagerly every day, and grappling with whoever they met, many of them died, and they killed many of the Romans labouring at the earthworks.

But by chance the fortress was surrendered even without the earthworks. There was among the besieged a young man, bold in daring and vigorous with his hands, called Eleazar, who, urging the many to go out and hinder the filling-in, became most conspicuous in the battles, doing the Romans much harm. Once, when the fighting had broken off, he stayed outside the gates himself and talked with those on the wall. One Rufus of the Roman camp, an Egyptian by race, suddenly ran up, lifted Eleazar with his armour and all, and got him across to the Roman camp before anyone could stop him. When the commander ordered him to be stripped and whipped in sight of those in the town, the whole town wailed together. Bassus made this a stratagem against the enemy, and ordered a cross to be fixed in the ground, as if to hang Eleazar at once. Those in the fortress, seeing it, were pained the more and wailed piercingly. Eleazar begged them not to stand by and see him die so, and to provide for their own safety by yielding to the strength and fortune of the Romans.
