They, broken by his words, and with many inside pleading for him (for he was of a large and very numerous family), gave way to pity, and sent to offer the surrender of the fortress, on condition that they might go away unharmed, taking Eleazar.

When the commander accepted this, those in the lower town, learning of the agreement made privately with the Jews, planned to escape by night themselves. When they opened their gates, word came to Bassus from those who had made the agreement. The strongest of those going out managed to break through, but of those caught inside, one thousand seven hundred men were killed, and the women and children were enslaved. Bassus, keeping his agreement with those who surrendered the fortress, let them go and gave back Eleazar.

Having done this, he hurried to the forest called Jardes; for many who had earlier escaped from the sieges had gathered there. Coming to the place, he surrounded it all with the horsemen, and ordered the foot soldiers to cut down the trees. The Jews who had fled there rushed out together with a shout and fell on those surrounding them. Since the Romans received them stoutly, no short time was spent in the battle, but its end did not turn out alike for the opposing sides. For of the Romans twelve fell and a few were wounded, but of the Jews none escaped from this battle; all, not fewer than three thousand, were taken and died.

Bassus and Laberius Maximus, who was procurator, were ordered by Caesar to sell off all the land of the Jews. To eight hundred men alone, discharged from the army, he gave a place to live in, which is called Emmaus and is thirty stades from Jerusalem. He imposed a tax on the Jews wherever they were, each to pay two drachmas yearly to the Capitol, just as they had formerly contributed to the temple in Jerusalem.

## 6.29

When Bassus died, Flavius Silva succeeded to the command. He marched against the fortress of Masada, the only one of the rebels' places still left. Sicarii held it, led by a powerful man, Eleazar, a descendant of Judas, who had persuaded many of the Jews not to submit to the registration under Quirinius. Silva at once took control of the country, and surrounded the fortress with a wall, blocking those inside from escaping. Then he turned to the siege, and having raised an earthwork where it was possible (for the fortress had been built on a high rock ringed by ravines of boundless depth), he brought up the siege engine and broke down part of the wall. But another was seen built up inside by the sicarii in its place, such as would not yield even to the blows of the engines. For it was made of timbers in two parallel rows, between which they packed earth. So the blows of the engines not only did not break it, but made it firmer, settling together with the shaking; and so Silva ordered the soldiers to hurl burning torches at it all together. The structure, being of wood, caught fire and sent up a great flame. At first a north wind blowing from above drove the flame onto the Romans, and it nearly caught the engines; then a strong south wind blew against it and drove it onto the wall, and the whole was soon burned down.

At this the Romans intended to attack the enemy the next day; but Eleazar spoke to those in the fortress and persuaded them all to kill their own wives and children and then go after them, each one. When this had been decided, they embraced their wives and hugged their children, clinging to them with kisses and weeping, and they killed their dearest with their own hands, as though it were no concern of theirs. Then they gathered all their property and set fire to it. Choosing by lot ten to be the slayers of all, each was slain by them beside his dearest. Then again the one chosen by lot killed the nine, and looking round in case anyone was left alive anywhere, when he knew all had been killed, set fire to the palace, drove his sword right through himself and fell beside his own family. They died believing that no one had been left alive; but an old woman and another, with five children, hidden in the tunnels, escaped notice. The number of the slain, with women and children, was two hundred and sixty.

The Romans attacked at dawn; but seeing none of the enemy, and great quiet inside and fire burning, they were at a loss. At last they raised a war cry, in case they might call out any of those inside. The women heard the shout, came up out of the tunnels and told the Romans what had been done; but they did not believe it. But when they went into the palace and came upon the slain, they wondered at the nobility of the men and their contempt for death.

Such was the capture of Masada. At Alexandria in Egypt too it happened that many Jews died. For those who had fled there from the faction of the sicarii persuaded many of those who received them to lay claim to freedom. If any of the Jews of standing opposed them, they killed some and called on the others to revolt. The leading members of the council gathered the Jews into an assembly, exposed the madness of the sicarii, and urged the multitude to guard against the destruction that would come from them and to hand them over to the Romans. The multitude was persuaded by what was said, and rushing at the sicarii they seized them. About six hundred were caught, and those who escaped then were captured not long after and brought back. Every torture was applied to them to make them acknowledge Caesar as master, but none gave in; all kept their resolve stronger than compulsion. Most of all the age of the children amazed those who watched; for not one of them was overcome into naming Caesar master.

The madness of the sicarii touched the cities about Cyrene too. Jonathan, a most wicked man and a weaver by trade, escaped there and persuaded some of the poor to follow him, and led them into the desert, promising to show signs and wonders. The leading men of the Jews at Cyrene reported this to Catullus, the governor of Cyrene. He sent soldiers and seized those with Jonathan. Jonathan himself escaped at the time, but was searched for carefully and caught, and brought before the governor he contrived an escape from punishment for himself, and provided Catullus with openings for unjust gain. For he said, lying about them, that the richest of the Jews had been his teachers in what had been done; and the governor eagerly accepted the slanders. Besides believing readily, he also taught the sicarii the false accusation; and prompted by him they denounced many.

Here, then, the sufferings of the Jews came to an end for that time, when Jerusalem underwent its last capture by the Romans. Again, when Aelius Hadrian ruled the Romans, the Jews revolted and took up arms against the Romans. But then too they were defeated and crushed, many tens of thousands perishing, so that very few were left; this will be told in its own place.

Since the history has mentioned the Romans and assigned them an invincible power, it is altogether necessary to tell, and to teach or remind the minds of those who read this work, who the Romans were, and from where their nation arose at the beginning, and from where it got its name, what forms of government it used, what fortunes it met, and how it advanced to the height of prosperity, so as to become master of nearly the whole world and to wreathe its power over almost all; and how, being ruled by kings at the beginning, it changed to an aristocracy, that is to dictatorships and consulships, and was transferred again to a democracy, and then came back to monarchy. So I must speak of these things too and tell them, cutting down the breadth of the narrative as far as I can and keeping it from running long, so that the affairs of the history may be easy to survey and may not escape the memory of those who read them.

## 7.2

As they grew up both were spirited and manly; but Romulus seemed superior in intelligence, and by nature more fit to command than to obey. Once, when a quarrel arose between Numitor's herdsmen and those of Amulius, the brothers beat Numitor's men and cut off a large part of the herd. Numitor's herdsmen lay in wait for Remus, when he was walking alone with a few others, seized him and took him to Numitor; and Numitor went to Amulius and asked for justice, since he was his brother and had been outraged by his men. Amulius handed Remus over to Numitor to treat as he wished. Numitor went home, and seeing the young man outstanding in size and strength, and wondering at the boldness and unbroken spirit of his soul, asked him gently who he was and where he came from. He answered boldly: "We are twin brothers, and our birth is said to be a secret, and our nurture and nursing more wonderful still, since we were fed by beasts and birds as we lay in a trough by the great river; the trough is still kept, with faint letters engraved on its bronze bands."

Numitor was led by Remus's words and his looks to think of the exposure of his daughter's children; and Faustulus, learning of Remus's capture, urged Romulus to help, then telling him plainly about his birth (for before he had only hinted at it, so that they might not think small of themselves), and himself, carrying the trough, went to Numitor full of haste and fear. He was suspicious of the guards at Amulius's gates and confused in his answers, and did not escape notice as he covered the trough with his cloak. Thinking he was carrying something stolen, they brought the trough out into the open. There happened to be present one of those who had exposed the babes; recognising the trough, he ran and told Amulius. Faustulus, questioned by the king, admitted that the children were alive, but said they were tending herds far from Alba; and that he was bringing the trough to Ilia, the children's mother, who longed to see it. Amulius, troubled by this, sent a man to Numitor to ask if he had learned anything about the children as being alive. The man sent was one of Numitor's friends. So, going off and finding Numitor embracing Remus, he encouraged him and advised them not to delay, and himself helped them. Just then Romulus too was near, bringing a large band of countrymen; and not a few of the citizens came over to him out of hatred of Amulius. With things having come together so, Amulius, having done or planned nothing for his safety, was killed.

## 7.3

Romulus and Remus assigned the rule of Alba to their mother's father, and fitting honour to their mother, and decided to be on their own; for they would not bear to be ruled, and they wished to found a city where they had been brought up. When they had set out to build the city, a quarrel arose between the brothers about the rule and about the city, and they came to a fight, in which Remus died. Another story has it that when Romulus was already digging a trench that was to be the outwork of the city's wall, Remus sometimes hindered the work and sometimes mocked it; and at last, as he leapt across it as being easy to attack, some say he fell struck by Romulus, others by someone else. From this it came to be the custom that whoever dared to cross the trench of a camp other than by the usual ways should be put to death.

Romulus buried his brother and founded the city. Yoking a bull with a cow, and putting a bronze share in the plough, he himself drew a deep furrow in a circle, and those following turned all the clods that the plough threw up inside the furrow. Where the wall was to rise, the furrow was cut, as has been said; but where they meant to set gates, they left a break in the furrow, lifting the plough over it. For they hold every wall sacred; but if they thought the gates sacred, it would not be possible to bring in some necessary things through them and send out others that are unclean.

The founding of this city was completed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, which would rather be the twentieth of April; and the Romans keep this day as a feast, calling it the birthday of their country. Romulus is recorded to have been eighteen years old when he founded Rome. He founded it around the dwelling of Faustulus; and the place was named the Palatium.

When the city had been founded, he divided the multitude of military age into army units; each unit was of three thousand foot and three hundred horse, and was called a legion, because the fighting men were picked from all; the rest he treated as the people. He named the people *populus*; from which in the law books too an action brought by the people is called *popularis*. Of the men more distinguished for birth, intelligence and choice of life he appointed a hundred councillors, naming them patricians; and the whole body he called the senate, which is the council of elders. The councillors were called patricians either because they were fathers of legitimate children, or rather because they could each show who their fathers were, being of known family, or from *patronia*; for so they called protection; for they called those who took care of others and helped them *patroni*. One would best guess Romulus's intention if one thought that by this name he meant to show that the first and most powerful men of the city ought to care for the humbler with a father's care, and at the same time to lead the people, by the name of patricians, not to resent the honours of their betters, but to be well disposed to them, thinking of them as fathers and calling them so.

When many had settled in the city, few of whom were joined to wives, Romulus took thought that they too should get wives for themselves. For being a mixed rabble, from poor and obscure families, they were scorned for marriage by the neighbouring peoples. So he planned for his citizens to take wives by seizing them, and proclaimed that he was going to hold a sacrifice, a contest and a festival show, since an altar of a new god had been found. Many came together. He himself sat in front with the best men, dressed in purple; and he gave the people as a signal for the attempt the unfolding of the purple robe and the wrapping of it round him again. When this was done, they drew their swords with a shout, rushed in and seized the daughters of the Sabines, virgins, not anyone's wives.

When the seizure had been dared, the Sabines, who were many and warlike and lived in unwalled villages because they were proud of being colonists of the Lacedaemonians, sent an embassy to Romulus, asking him to undo the work of violence and to bring about friendship and kinship between the peoples by persuasion and law. Romulus would not give up the girls, but asked the Sabines to accept the partnership; and while the others spent their time in deliberation, Acron, king of the Caeninenses, a spirited and most warlike man, rose up first and went against Romulus with a large force. When they had met, they challenged each other to fight, the armies keeping still. In the single combat between the two Romulus struck down Acron, and when battle was joined he routed his army too; and he took the city, but did no harm to those in it, only ordering them to pull down their houses and follow him to Rome, to become citizens and be granted equal rights.

Then other Sabines too fought the Romans and were defeated. After this the rest of the Sabines appointed Tatius general, marched on Rome, and took the Capitol, which was betrayed by Tarpeia, the daughter of the commander of the garrison. For she went down for water, was seized and brought to Tatius, and was persuaded to betray the stronghold, having fallen in love with the golden armlets that the Sabines wore on their left arms, and having asked to receive them as pay for the betrayal. When Tatius agreed, she opened one gate by night and let the Sabines in. Tatius, entering, ordered his men to give her what they carried on their left arms, and was the first to throw his armlet at Tarpeia, and his shield. When all did the same, she was struck by the gold and buried under the shields, and died from their number and weight. So in deed he did what Caesar and Antigonus later said in words: for the one said he loved treason but hated the traitor; and Antigonus said that he gladly received those who were betraying, but hated those who had betrayed.

## 7.4

When the citadel had been taken by the Sabines, a hard battle broke out between them and the Romans, in which many fell, and Romulus was struck on the head by a stone. As the Sabines were preparing to fight still, their daughters who had been seized held them back, appearing to them from all sides with shouting and wailing, some carrying babes in their arms, others holding out their loosened hair, and all calling on now the Sabines, now the Romans, by the dearest names. So the opponents were moved, and parted to let them stand in the middle between the lines, and weeping spread through them all. When the women had spoken, the leaders came to a parley and agreed that those of the women who wished should live with the men who had them, freed from every work and service except spinning wool; that the Romans and Sabines should live in the city in common, and that it should be called Rome after Romulus, and the Romans Quirites after Cures, Tatius's country; and that both should reign and command in common. The place in which they made the agreement is called the Comitium, that is, a place of coming together; for the Romans say *comire* for coming together. A further hundred from the Sabines were enrolled among the patricians. The kings did not take counsel together in common at once, but each first in private with his hundred; then they all gathered in one place.

In the fifth year of Tatius's joint reign with Romulus, some of his kinsmen met envoys on the road from Laurentum going to Rome, tried to take by force the money they were carrying, and when they would not give it up but defended themselves, killed them. Romulus voted that the wrongdoers be punished, but Tatius put it off and turned it aside; and this alone became a cause of open quarrel between them. The relatives of the dead, failing to get justice, fell on Tatius as he was sacrificing with Romulus at the Alban mount and killed him; but they escorted Romulus away with praises as a just man. The murder of their ruler did not disturb the Sabines, but some out of goodwill towards Romulus, others out of fear of his power, went on yielding to him. Then a plague fell on the city, bringing sudden deaths on men without illness, and failure of crops and barrenness of flocks; and the city was rained on with drops of blood. The same things befell the people of Laurentum too. So it seemed that divine wrath was pursuing the cities for the murder of Tatius and of the envoys killed by the Sabines. When the murderers had been handed over and punished, the troubles abated.

As the Romans' affairs grew strong, the weaker of their neighbours submitted, but the powerful thought they ought not to overlook it, but to cut short their growth. The first of the Etruscans to begin war were the Veientes. They engaged, lost many, and made an agreement and friendship for a hundred years, and gave fifty of their best men as hostages.

Romulus, having conquered them, held a triumph. Then, lifted up by his unexpected good fortune and taking on a heavier pride, he departed from his popular ways and changed into a monarchy oppressive and offensive in its outward show. For he wore a purple tunic, put on a toga bordered with purple, wore red shoes, and did business sitting on a throne with a back; and there were always many of the young men about him, whom he called Celeres, which in the Romans' language means "the swift"; and others walked in front keeping off the crowd with staves, girded with straps to bind those they were ordered to.

When his grandfather Numitor died at Alba, and the kingdom came to Romulus, he himself put the government into the hands of the people to court them, and appointed a ruler for the Sabines each year; and so he provoked the powerful men in Rome to seek a constitution without a king and with self-government. For not even those called patricians had a share in affairs; they had a name and an outward show, gathering in the council house more out of custom than for their opinion; then, while Romulus acted, they listened in silence, and went away having only this advantage over the rest, that they learned his decision before others. So he seemed to treat the senate with contempt; and for this reason the senate was suspected when, a little later, Romulus disappeared.

For it is said that as he was holding an assembly at the place called the Goat's Marsh, the light of the sun failed, night came on, and there were terrible thunders and blasts of wind driving a storm. Meanwhile the crowd fled, and the powerful gathered together. When the disturbance in the air had abated and many had come together again, the king was looked for; but the powerful did not allow inquiry about him, and urged all to honour and worship Romulus as having been caught up to the gods, and as one who would be a god for them instead of a good king.

The many went away persuaded by these words, buoyed up by good hopes; but some held the patricians under suspicion and stirred things up, saying that they were persuading the people of foolish things, having themselves been the king's murderers. And they would have caused trouble for the powerful, had not one of the knights, Julius Proculus, most esteemed in family, good in character and loyal to Romulus, come into the forum and said on oath that Romulus had appeared to him, fair and tall as never before, adorned with bright, blazing armour; and that he had asked: "What has befallen you, king, that you have left us under wicked charges and the whole city in mourning?" And that he had answered: "It pleased the gods, Proculus, that we should be with men so long, and then dwell in heaven again, having come from there. But farewell, and tell the Romans that by practising self-control and courage they will reach the greatest height of human power. And I shall be gracious to you as Quirinus." Because of the speaker's oath and his character, this seemed so credible to the Romans that no one spoke against it, but laying aside all suspicion and slander they prayed to Quirinus and invoked him as a god. They say that Romulus got this surname either because they named the citizens Quirites, or because the ancients called the spear-point or spear *quiris*; so that Romulus was named Quirinus as a warlike or spear-bearing god. He is said to have lived fifty-four years, and to have vanished from among men in the thirty-eighth year of his reign.

## 7.5

When this had befallen Romulus, all thought they should be ruled by a king, but a dispute and strife grew among those in Rome, not only about the man who would lead, but also about which of the two peoples would provide the ruler. For to those who had first founded the city with Romulus it seemed unbearable that the Sabines, whom they had admitted into citizenship, should force their way to rule over those who had received them; while the Sabines on the other side, since on Tatius's death they had let Romulus rule alone, claimed that the ruler should be chosen from themselves.

So both sides disputed in this way, and while the state was in suspense over this, the patricians, being a hundred and fifty, arranged that each in turn, adorned with the royal insignia, should sacrifice to the gods and do business, for six hours of the night and six of the day. For the sharing out of the times equally to each seemed well both for the rulers and for the ruled themselves; for the very quick laying down of power took away envy, since the ruled saw the same man become a private person from a king in the same day and night. I know that other things too are said about this kind of rule, but I have followed the more credible. This form of rule was named by the Romans an interregnum.

But even so disturbances arose out of suspicion, the patricians being suspected of turning the state into an oligarchy and not wishing to be ruled by a king; and from this they quarrelled. When all agreed that the future king should be chosen, the Sabines gave the Romans the first choice; and they chose from the Sabines Numa Pompilius, a man known to all for his virtue. So envoys were sent to him from Rome; for he had not moved to Rome, but was among the Sabines and lived in the city of Cures. He was the son of Pomponius, a man of good repute, and he had trained himself in every virtue by nature and education. From this he had a great name and reputation, so that even Tatius, who reigned with Romulus, made him his son-in-law by marrying him to his daughter Tatia, the only child he had; she lived with Numa for thirteen years and then departed this life. Numa, leaving the pursuits of the town, wished to live mostly in the country and spend his time in meadows and groves.

So the envoys came from Rome, calling him to the kingship when he was already in his fortieth year; but he refused. The envoys pressed him, contriving every way to persuade him, and begging him not to throw the city again into strife and civil war, since there was no one else to whom both sides would incline. In private his father too urged Numa to accept the rule as a divine gift and a service to God, which would be for a wise and good man a cause of noble and great deeds, and a bond of goodwill and friendship for his own country and the whole Sabine nation with a powerful and flourishing city.

Numa gave way to this, sacrificed to the gods and went on to Rome; and the senate and people met him with acclamations and rejoicing. When they reached the forum and the royal insignia were brought to him, he told them to wait, and said he needed God too to confirm the kingship for him. So he went up to the Capitol, sacrificed, and only then put on the royal dress and came down.

Having received the rule, first he disbanded the body of three hundred whom Romulus always had about his person; for he said he ought not to distrust those who trusted him, nor did he think it right to reign over those who distrusted him. Then he tried to make the city, from hard and warlike, softer and more peaceful. He forbade the Romans to set up an image of God in the form of a man or a beast; so they had no painted or moulded form of God, and in a hundred and seventy years, while temples were being raised for them, they made no statue with a form, since it was not holy to liken the better to the worse, nor was it possible to lay hold of God otherwise than by thought. He ordained that sacrifices be made without blood, with barley meal and libations; for the gods, being guardians of peace and justice, should be pure of slaughter; and that they should neither hear nor see anything of divine matters in passing and carelessly, but at leisure from other things and with their minds attentive, as to the greatest of actions, that concerning piety. By these and many other things, which we have passed over for their number, Numa created in the men of that time, by habit, a disposition towards the divine. They say that he himself hung his hopes so on the divine that once, when it was reported to him as he was sacrificing that enemies were coming, he smiled and said: "But I am sacrificing." The land that Romulus had won by the spear he shared out among the poor citizens, taking poverty away from them as a necessity that makes men do wrong, and turning them to farming, since this tames the people and can create a keen love of peace.

It is said that January and February too were added to the months by him, since he laid down that the year should be reckoned as twelve months by the course of the moon, while before it had been ten months, as among some of the barbarians it is three months, and among the Greeks for the Arcadians four months and for the Acarnanians six. For the Egyptians the year was a month, and then four months; so they seem very ancient though they are not, bringing in a vast number of years in their genealogies, because they set the months down as a number of years. Numa also assigned January to the beginning of the year.

When he had accustomed his subjects to justice and piety, war was removed altogether. For not only was the Roman people tamed by the king's good order and mildness, but the cities round about too began to change, and a longing flowed into all for peace and justice, to plant the land, bring up children in quiet and worship the gods. For neither war nor strife nor revolution in the state is recorded while Numa reigned, nor is any enmity or envy against him, or any gathering of men and plot from love of kingship, recorded to have arisen anywhere. Having a daughter, Pompilia, he married her to Marcius; and of her a grandson, Ancus Marcius, was born to him, who reigned after Tullus Hostilius. Numa left him five years old and died, wasting away little by little from old age and a gentle illness, having lived three years beyond eighty, and reigned forty-three years.

## 7.12

years, and so fell from his rule; and the Romans turned to Brutus and chose him as ruler. So that the sole rule might not seem a kingship, they also voted him a colleague, Tarquinius Collatinus, the husband of that Lucretia, since he was believed to be hostile to the tyrants because of the violence done to his wife. Envoys came to Rome from Tarquinius to discuss his return; and when they achieved nothing, others came again, saying that Tarquinius would give up the kingship and stop the war, if the money were given to him and his friends and kin, on which they could live in exile. When many were moved, even Collatinus, Brutus's colleague, Brutus ran out of the council house into the forum, calling Collatinus a traitor who was granting the means for war and tyranny.

The envoys, staying on in Rome on the pretext of the money, managed to corrupt some of the notable men, and with them they persuaded two sons of Brutus to join in the betrayal. When the youths had been won over, it was decided that an oath should be taken too, and for this they met in a house. The house was deserted and dark. So a slave named Vindicius was inside without their knowing, not by design but by chance, and hidden there he was a witness of what was done and heard what was planned, which was to kill the consuls and betray the city; and they sent this to Tarquinius by the envoys. When the conspirators had left the room, the slave came out and revealed everything. Those who had planned the betrayal were seized and the letters were brought; and when they were brought into the forum, they set Vindicius before them. The letters were read; and the others were downcast and silent, but Brutus, calling each of his sons by name, said: "Do you not answer the charge?" When they kept silent, he turned to the attendants and said: "The rest of the work is now yours." They seized the young men and scourged them with rods. While the others were moved by their suffering, the father neither turned his eyes elsewhere nor showed any pity, until they had cut off his sons' heads with the axe. This is not easy either to praise or to blame; for either the height of virtue set his soul beyond feeling, or the greatness of his feeling set it beyond pain; neither is small or human, but either godlike or beastlike.

When these had died in this way, Brutus was asked to give his vote about the other conspirators too. He said: "For my sons I am judge enough myself; about the others I yield the vote to the citizens, who are free." So when the vote was given, all were beheaded. Some of them were related to Collatinus, and he was angry on their account. So Brutus so provoked the people against him that they nearly killed him with their own hands. They did not do this, but they forced him to give up his office. In his place they chose as colleague Publius Valerius, who was surnamed Publicola; the name rendered into Greek means one who cares for the people, or most popular.

Tarquinius, despairing of recovering the kingship by betrayal, went to the Etruscans. They tried to bring him back with a heavy force. The consuls led out the Romans against them. As the battle began, Arruns, the son of Tarquinius, and Brutus, the consul of the Romans, fell upon each other and fought, and not sparing themselves in their fury, died together. The battle was great and many fell on both sides, and the victory was undecided. When night came on, the grove beside which they were encamped is said to have shaken, and a great voice came out of it saying that one more of the Etruscans had died than of the Romans. At the voice the Romans raised a loud and confident war cry, while panic fell on the Etruscans; and in their alarm they abandoned their camp; and the Romans took it and plundered it. When the dead of those who fell in the battle were counted, those of the Etruscans were found to be eleven thousand three hundred, and the Romans as many less one. Valerius Publicola held a triumph, the first to do so as consul.

Tarquinius, after the great battle in which he lost his son too, fighting with Brutus, fled to Clusium and begged the help of Lars Porsena, the man with the greatest power among the Italian kings; and he promised to help him. First he sent to Rome ordering them to receive Tarquinius, and when they did not obey, he came with a heavy force. Valerius Publicola, chosen to office for the second time, joined battle, was wounded, and was carried out of the battle on a litter. As Porsena pressed the city, famine took hold of the Romans. But through some chance, or rather by providence, Porsena ended the war against the Romans.

For a man named Mucius Cordus, good in every virtue and best in war, surnamed Scaevola, which means one-handed or not sound of hand, planned to kill Porsena and went into his camp wearing Etruscan dress and using a like speech. Not knowing Porsena clearly, and afraid to ask, he drew his sword and killed his secretary, who was sitting with him and was dressed much the same. He was seized and questioned; and since a brazier had been made ready for Porsena, who was then about to sacrifice, he held his hand over it, and while the flesh burned he stood looking at Porsena with an unmoved face (from this, when his hand was destroyed, he got his surname), until Porsena in wonder let him go. Scaevola outwitted the enemy in another way, and said: "Having overcome your fear, Porsena, I have been conquered by your virtue, and out of gratitude I reveal what I would not have told under compulsion. Three hundred Romans with the same purpose as mine are staying in your camp; of whom I, chosen by lot, made the first attempt, and I do not grieve at my fortune, having missed a good man, who ought rather to be a friend than an enemy to the Romans." From this Porsena became more eager for terms.

Publicola, consul for the third time, then kept challenging Tarquinius to a trial, to prove him most wicked and most justly put out of his rule, with Porsena as judge. When Tarquinius answered that he would not choose Porsena as arbiter, if he was changing sides though an ally, Porsena condemned him and ended the war. After this the Tarquins often tried to recover the kingship, fighting alongside the peoples neighbouring the Romans, but all were destroyed in the battles except the old man, who was also called Superbus, which a Greek would render as "arrogant." He too later went to Cumae in Opicia and died there.

## 7.21

This had just happened, and Marcus Furius Camillus was chosen dictator. He attacked the city, and when he achieved nothing, he dug an underground passage, beginning far off, leading into the citadel. When the tunnel was ready, since many had come over to him from Rome too as volunteers, he took them as well, attacked the city and surrounded the wall on every side; and while those inside were scattered round the whole circuit, others got inside through the tunnels without being noticed. When the city had been taken and the Romans were plundering what was in it, Camillus, watching what was being done from the citadel, groaned and wept and said: "O gods, if some retribution is owed to balance this good fortune, I pray that it may end on myself." He took out the tenth of the booty, against the soldiers' will, and dedicated it to Apollo, having made this vow before. He also dedicated a golden mixing bowl made from the women's ornaments; and in return an honour was at once voted to them, which was that they should go to the festivals in carriages, having before gone to them on foot. But the people were vexed with Camillus and resented him, partly because he had taken out the god's share of the spoils not while they were being plundered but after the time had passed, and partly because he held his triumph haughtily in other ways, and was the first of the Romans to drive in the victory procession with a team of four white horses.

The victory procession, which they also called a triumph, went like this. When some great success worth a triumph had been won, the general was at once named *imperator* by the soldiers, and he bound sprigs of laurel round the rods and gave them to the couriers announcing the victory to the city to carry. Coming home he assembled the senate and asked them to vote him the triumph. If he got the vote of the senate and the people, the title of *imperator* was confirmed for him too. If he was still in the office in which he had won, he held the procession in it. But if the time of his office had passed, he received some other name suited to it; for a private man was forbidden to hold a triumph. Dressed in the triumphal dress, taking armlets, binding on a crown of laurel and holding a branch in his right hand, he called the people together; and having praised those who had served with him, both in common and some individually, he gave them money and honoured them with decorations, giving some armlets and spears without iron, and giving crowns, some of gold, some of silver, bearing the name of each and the image of his deed of valour. For if someone had been first to mount a wall, the crown bore the form of a wall; or if he had taken a place by siege, this too was pictured. If someone had won at sea, the crown was adorned with ships; if someone had won with cavalry, something to do with horses was stamped on it. But the one who had saved a citizen from a battle or another danger or from a siege had the greatest praise and received a crown made of oak, which was held far more honourable than all, both the silver and the gold. These were given not only to individual men who had done valiantly, but also to companies and whole armies. Much of the spoils was shared among those who had served; and sometimes some even gave it out to the whole people, spent it on the festival and made it public, and if anything was left, spent it on temples, porticoes or some other public work.

Having done this, the man holding the procession mounted the chariot. The chariot was like neither a racing nor a war chariot, but was made in the shape of a round tower. He was not alone in the chariot, but if he had children or some relatives, he set the girls and the infant boys in it, and put the older ones on the horses, both the yoke horses and the trace horses; and if there were more, they rode beside the man in procession on riding horses and joined the procession. None of the others rode, but all walked crowned with laurel. A public slave rode with him in the chariot itself, holding over him the crown of gold-set stones, and said to him: "Look behind," that is, look to what is behind and what follows in life, and do not be lifted up by the present and grow arrogant. A bell and a whip hung from the chariot, showing that he too could meet misfortune, so as to be flogged or even condemned to die. For it was the custom for those condemned to die for some crime to wear a bell, so that no one coming near them as they walked might be filled with pollution.

Arrayed so, they entered the city, with the spoils and trophies going before them, and in pictures the captured forts, cities, mountains, rivers, lakes and seas, and everything that had been taken. If one day was enough for the procession of these, well; if not, it was held on a second and third day too. When these had gone ahead, the man holding the procession, carried into the Roman forum, ordered some of the prisoners to be taken to the prison and put to death, and drove up to the Capitol; there he performed some rites, brought offerings, dined in the porticoes there, and towards evening went home with pipes and flutes. Such were the triumphs of old; but factions and the power of great men brought very many innovations into them.

## 7.22

Though the people hated Camillus, as has already been told, the war against the Faliscans forced them to vote him military tribune. They defeated them in battle, but besieging a strong city of theirs called Falerii, they achieved nothing. For those in the city so despised the siege that even their children went about beside the walls with their teacher to take exercise. And the Romans would have given up the siege, had not something happened. For this teacher, plotting against the citizens, either from some anger or in hope of gain, led the children out to the wall every day, near at first, and brought them back in at once when they had exercised; but at last he took them all into the Roman outposts and told them to take him to Camillus, and standing before him said that he was handing over the whole city through the children. But Camillus, thinking the deed terrible, and saying that the great general should make war trusting in his own virtue and not in another's wickedness, ordered the teacher to be stripped and his hands bound behind him, and rods and whips given to the children, so that they might beat the traitor with them and drive him into the city. The citizens had just learned of the betrayal, and there was a rush to the walls and lamenting of men and women. While they were in this state, the children brought up their teacher naked. The Faliscans, seeing this and learning how it had happened, came of their own accord and surrendered themselves to Camillus, saying that because of his justice they welcomed defeat before freedom.

So he took money, made a treaty and withdrew. But the soldiers, who had expected to plunder Falerii, accused him of hating the people. Envied still more, he was accused of having given the public treasury no benefit from the Etruscan money, but of having appropriated it himself. They were so angry with him that they felt no pity for him in the misfortune that had befallen him; for one of his sons had fallen ill and died. When he begged his friends not to stand by while he was unjustly condemned, and they refused to help him with the vote but promised to help pay the fine if he were condemned, he would not bear it and decided to leave the city. As he went out he prayed that, if he was being driven out not justly but by the insolence and envy of the people, those same citizens might soon need him and seek him.

He moved to the Rutulians, and was condemned in his absence, and a verdict was passed against him with a fine of fifteen thousand asses, which in silver comes to one thousand five hundred drachmas.

## 7.23

The European Gauls, of whom the Asiatic Gauls are thought to be colonists, being of Celtic race, left their own land as not enough to feed them; some set out for the Rhipaean mountains, and others settled near the Alps and lived there a long time. Then, when wine was brought from Italy, they tasted it and wondered at it greatly, took up arms, brought their parents with them, and went looking for the land that yields such fruit. They marched against an Etruscan city called Clusium and besieged it. The people of Clusium fled to the Romans for help. Envoys were sent to the Gauls from Rome; the Gauls received them with honour because of the name of the Romans, stopped assaulting the wall and came to a parley. Meanwhile the people of Clusium laid an ambush and, with the envoys from Rome, attacked the Gauls. Brennus, the king of the Gauls, angry at this, left the people of Clusium alone and at once moved his army against Rome as it was, since the envoys were not handed over to him for punishment; and he moved so fast that they came upon the city before the Romans learned of their approach.

The divine, however, is said to have announced the approach to them. For Marcus Caedicius, walking somewhere at night, heard a voice saying: "The Gauls are coming." When Marcus told this to the people and the senate, they made a joke of the story and laughed, until the Gauls themselves brought the news by being near them. Then they went out in haste, fought in disorder and were most shamefully defeated. Many fell in the battle, many died caught as they fled, and very many were pushed into the river Tiber and perished; of the rest, scattered, some were able to reach Rome and others went elsewhere.

Those in Rome, learning what had happened, were helpless, and in despair they neither set a guard on the walls nor shut the city's gates; some left it and fled, others ran up to the Capitol with their wives and children. Only eighty men, whom some say were priests and others the first of the Romans in age, wealth and birth, put on sacred or most costly robes and sat in the forum on ivory chairs, awaiting the fortune to come. The Gauls came to Rome the next day, but seeing the gates open and the wall unguarded, they held back and did not go in, suspecting an ambush. On the third day they took courage, rushed in and took the city. The king of the barbarians set a guard on the Capitol, and himself, going through the forum, wondered at those men sitting in front, seeing them in their finery, unmoving and silent. Amazement at the strangeness held the Gauls, and they hesitated to go up to them. At length one dared to stand beside one of them, took hold of the man's beard, which was long, and pulled it down; and he struck him on the head with his staff. The barbarian drew his sword and killed the man. So the barbarians fell on the rest too and killed them, and sacked and burned the houses. Then they attacked the Capitol as well; and since they achieved nothing after trying for many days, some guarded the Capitol and others overran the country getting food, scattering and going about here and there, not together, since they were proud of their success; and they were tripped up by drunkenness; for coming upon much wine they drank it too unmixed, never having tasted such a drink before.

Camillus, seeing the Gauls in this state, since they were also plundering the land of the Ardeates, and the Ardeates themselves were enough in number but lacked daring through inexperience and want of training for battle, put it to the younger men that they should ascribe the barbarians' success not to their courage but to the Romans' misfortune, and he insisted that if they were eager and took heart, they would beat the enemy without danger. Having persuaded the young men in this way, and then the rest, he armed those of age, and in the dead of night he himself with the Ardeates fell on the barbarians while they were drunk. He cut most of them down there, and if some were able to escape in the darkness, horsemen caught them after daybreak and destroyed them.

When rumour quickly proclaimed the success everywhere, those of the Romans who had escaped from the first battle with the Gauls and were safe took their arms and went to Camillus, begging him to take command of them. He said he would not consent unless those safe on the Capitol first voted him the command. There was difficulty in finding someone to take the message to those on the Capitol. But one of the young men, Pontius Cominius, a lover of glory, undertook the task, slipped through the midst of the enemy unnoticed, came near the hill of the Capitol, crept up with difficulty and barely clambered to the top, and was brought by the guards to the Romans in office; he announced Camillus's victory, told what the soldiers had decided, and urged them to confirm Camillus's command. They voted Camillus dictator. He gathered the Romans outside, about twenty thousand, and many from the allies, and prepared for an attack.

The barbarians, going about after daybreak, found out where Pontius had climbed to the Capitol (they guessed it from the broken fragments of rock and the grass, of which there was much there, some pulled up and some trampled down), and planned to go up that way themselves by night. They set about the task, and with difficulty, but still they climbed, and they would have reached the outwork and attacked the guards without being noticed, had there not been geese kept about the temple of Juno, which, being by nature sharp of sense and frightened by noise, quickly perceived the Gauls' approach, and rushing at the guards with a noisy cackling, roused them all. So the Romans fell on those climbing up, killed some, pushed others down the rock, and escaped the danger.

From this the Celts were more despondent, having been worn down by the siege for seven months. So Brennus, the king of the barbarians, and Sulpicius, the military tribune of the Romans, talked about terms. It was agreed that the Romans should pay the Gauls a thousand pounds of gold, and that those who received the gold should at once withdraw from the city and the country. When the gold was brought, and the barbarians were secretly cheating over the weights, Brennus took off his sword together with his belt and put it on the weights. When the tribune asked what was happening, he said: "What else but woe to the vanquished?" At this moment Camillus with his army stood at the gates of the city; and learning what was happening, he hurried on to the Romans. Coming up, he lifted the gold from the scale and gave it to his attendants, and told the Celts to take the scale and the weights and go away, saying that it was the Romans' ancestral custom to save their country with iron and not with gold. When Brennus said he was being wronged, since the agreement was being broken, Camillus answered that the treaty was not valid, since it had been made without him when he had already been chosen dictator. Brennus, disturbed, went as far as drawing swords, but still led the Celts back to their camp; then he left the city, went sixty stades and encamped. At daybreak Camillus was upon him, leading the Romans, who had now taken heart, routed the barbarians with great slaughter and took their camp.

So Rome was taken unexpectedly and saved more unexpectedly still; and Camillus held a triumph. Since the city had been utterly destroyed, the multitude did not wish to rebuild it, being strong neither in money nor in body, and they would nearly have left it. For they were not persuaded either by those in office or by the senate, who urged and advised them not to leave the town, which had now been saved from the enemy; until, while all were deliberating about this in the forum, a centurion leading a guard and happening to pass by the assembly itself, shouted to those following him: "Halt here; for here you must stay." They thought this had been said by divine providence, and gave up moving away, and turned eagerly to the renewal of Rome, and renewed both the walls and the private houses within a year.

## 12.1

When Antoninus, who had been adopted by Hadrian and made Caesar and emperor, became sole ruler, the senate would not vote Hadrian the honours due to a hero, because of the murders of very distinguished men that he had committed. Antoninus therefore spoke to them at length, with tears, and said among other things: "Then I shall not rule you either; for everything he did, and my own appointment is one of those things, will be annulled, as the acts of a man most hateful and wicked to you." The senate, out of respect for him, and no less out of caution towards the soldiers, voted the honours to the dead man. He was named Pius because, just after he had taken the sole rule, many men were accused and some were demanded by name for execution, but he punished no one, saying: "I must not begin my care of you with deeds like these."

Through the whole of his reign he was just and good and no burden to any of his subjects, the Christians included: he not only did them no harm but even held them worthy of respect. He is said to have been inquisitive and exacting about small things, so that those who mocked him called him "the cumin-splitter". Yet he did not make money out of his subjects for all that. Once, when he was short of silver with wars pressing, he neither devised a new tax nor brought himself to ask anyone for money, but set out in the market-place all the treasures of the palace, and whatever ornaments his wife had, and invited anyone who wished to buy them. From this he raised money and paid it out to the soldiers. When he had won the war he gained many times as much, and made a proclamation that any of those who had bought the imperial possessions might give back what they had bought and receive the price. Some did so, but most declined, and he forced no one to give back what he had acquired.

He is said to have made the law that when children die without a will their parents are declared their heirs, and that children who make a will and are childless must leave the parents their lawful share.

In his reign a terrible earthquake happened about Bithynia and the Hellespont, by which several cities fell, and Cyzicus suffered most. At that time the famous temple there also fell, whose columns are said to have been four fathoms thick and to have risen to a height of fifty cubits, each made of a single stone, if anyone does not find this hard to believe; and all the rest of that building was wonderful.

It is told of this emperor that he also burned the senate's decree, made at the command of Julius Caesar, which laid down that no one might make a will unless he left a fixed share to the public treasury. Hence, it is thought, it is still written in wills to this day: "and to the imperial treasury I leave such-and-such." Antoninus Pius died an old man, by a death like a gentle sleep, having reigned alone for twenty-four years.

In his first year Telesphorus, bishop of Rome, having completed eleven years in his ministry and crowned with martyrdom, as Irenaeus has recorded, came to a most blessed end; and Hyginus was set on the throne of Rome in his place. Under him Valentinus became a heresiarch, and Cerdo the founder of the heresy of Marcion. When Hyginus died after the fourth year of his high-priesthood at Rome, Pius presided over the church of the Romans. Mark led that of the Alexandrians, after Eumenes had completed his thirteenth year in the high-priesthood; and when Mark passed to the other life after ten years, Celadion received the ministry. At Rome, when Pius died in the fifteenth year of his episcopate, Anicetus was appointed in his place. At this time also Justin, philosopher and martyr, flourished, contending for the right doctrine; he set out a treatise against Marcion and wrote a defence of the Christians addressed to Antoninus Pius. Moved by it, this emperor sent a decree to the council of Asia that no Christian should be punished for his religion, but that if anyone were accused by someone on that account, the accused should be acquitted and the accuser become liable to penalty. These things happened under Pius.

## 12.2

After his death Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, who had been adopted by him, as has been recorded, received the sole rule; and at once he made Lucius Verus Commodus, the son of Lucius Commodus, partner in his power. For Marcus was weak in body and so given to study that even as emperor he was not ashamed to go to a teacher: he studied philosophy with Sextus the Boeotian and attended Hermogenes the rhetorician, and held most to the Stoics. Lucius, being younger, was strong for hard work and suited by nature to handling military affairs. So Marcus married him to his daughter Lucilla and entrusted to him the war against the Parthians, since Vologaeses had shot down many Romans with arrows, destroyed a whole camp, declared himself an enemy of the Romans and was advancing, a terror, on the cities of Syria. Lucius came to Antioch and assigned the armies to Cassius, who engaged Vologaeses, defeated him and pursued him as far as Seleucia, burned that city and razed his palace at Ctesiphon. These things gave Lucius pride and arrogance, so that afterwards he even plotted against his father-in-law and emperor; but before he could do anything he perished by poison.

After this Cassius was appointed governor of all Asia. The emperor made war for a long time on the barbarians about the Ister, the Iazyges and the Marcomanni and others at other times, using Pannonia as his base. The Celts beyond the Rhine also drove as far as Italy; among their dead were found the bodies of women in armour. He ruled with such restraint and self-command that in such great wars he neither said anything to flatter the soldiers nor did anything out of fear. When he was not occupied with wars he sat in judgement, and he ordered more water to be poured for the orators who spoke by the water-clock, so that he might examine the justice of a case from every side. He was so hard-working that he judged even at night. He did, wrote and said nothing carelessly, thinking that an emperor ought not to do even the smallest thing carelessly, and this though his body was weak.

This emperor subdued the Marcomanni and the Iazyges in many great struggles and dangers. Against the Quadi too he waged a heavy war, and God granted him an unexpected victory. The Quadi had surrounded the Romans, who locked their shields together and defended themselves stoutly. The barbarians held off from fighting but blocked the country round about, so that the Romans could draw water from nowhere, thinking to overcome them more easily, since they would not be able to hold out against thirst and heat. When the Romans were worn down by toil, heat, thirst and wounds, clouds suddenly covered the sky and it rained heavily. This was not, as Dio has recorded, because an Egyptian magician called on Hermes and by his spells was able to bring the rain through him, but because God was called upon by the prayers of Christians and by a miracle rescued both them and the whole army. For there was in the Roman army at that time a legion all of whose men were Christians. The story is that when the emperor was at a loss and afraid for the whole army, the prefect of the guard told him that there was nothing the race called Christians could not do, and that there was a whole unit of such men in the army. On hearing this he begged them to call on their own God. When they had prayed, the enemy were struck by lightning and a rainstorm broke over the Romans. Marcus was astonished and honoured the Christians by a decree, and named that unit the Thunderbolt legion. That the legion was so named is agreed by the other Greeks and by Dio, but they do not add the reason. Eusebius also mentions this miracle in his Ecclesiastical History. Dio, however, says that while the rain was falling the Romans, busy with drinking, would almost have perished, since the barbarians then attacked them, had not violent hail fallen and the enemy been struck by many thunderbolts.

## 12.3

Cassius, while staying in Syria, rebelled. He was a Syrian, but an excellent man, such as one would pray to have as emperor. He was moved to revolt when a false report was brought to him that Marcus had died; and having once set out on the venture he did not draw back, though he learned soon after that the report was false, but prepared to hold the power by war. Marcus called the soldiers together, addressed them and encouraged them for the war. While he was making ready, news came of very many victories over various barbarians, and of the killing of Cassius: a centurion came up to him as he walked and suddenly wounded him, though not mortally, and a decurion finished the killing. So he perished, having dreamed of rule for three months and six days; and his son, who was elsewhere, was also killed. The emperor put to death none of those who had revolted with him, but treated them all with mildness. He wrote to the senate that none of Cassius's accomplices should die: "Heaven forbid," he said, "that any one of you should be executed on my account, by my vote or yours. If I do not obtain this, I shall hasten to die." So in everything he was both pious and good. A law was made at that time that no one should govern the province he came from, because Cassius had rebelled while governing Syria, where his own home was.

Marcus came to Athens and bestowed honours on the Athenians and appointed teachers in every branch of learning, who received a yearly salary from the treasury. On coming to Rome he remitted their debts to all who owed money to the imperial treasury and the public treasury. He gave money to cities, and ordered Smyrna, which had suffered from an earthquake, to be rebuilt. When the Scythian peoples stirred again, he married his son to Crispina sooner than he wished, and marched out against them. He asked for money from the public treasury, for he said that everything belonged to the senate and the people. When the barbarians had been defeated he was hailed imperator for the tenth time. Had he lived longer he would have brought everything there under the Romans; but he died, the doctors having made away with him, it is said, to please Commodus. As he was dying he commended Commodus to the soldiers, so that he should not seem to die by his doing; and to the tribune who asked for the watchword he said, "Go to the rising sun; for I am already setting." So, having ruled excellently, he died, having lived fifty-nine years less thirty-eight days and reigned nineteen years and eleven days. He was a good man by nature, and was made better still by education. Yet he did not have good fortune worthy of his virtue. One might admire him the more for this, that though he met with strange and extraordinary troubles, he himself came through them and kept the empire safe.

During his reign the holy Polycarp, high priest of Smyrna, put on the martyr's crown; and Justin, great in words and greater in confession, contended to the end, many of whose writings survive to this day. In the eighth year of the reign of this Marcus Verus Antoninus, Anicetus died, having presided over the church of the Romans for eleven years, and Soter succeeded him. When Celadion had completed his life after fourteen years, Agrippinus was entrusted with the episcopate of the Alexandrians. In the church of the Antiochenes, after Hero, Cornelius presided fourth; Eros succeeded him fifth, and Theophilus succeeded Eros sixth, who also armed himself in writing against Marcion; and Maximinus succeeded him seventh. When Soter, high priest of the Romans, departed from the things of earth, Eleutherus was brought in in his place.

## 12.4

Commodus, the son of Marcus Antoninus, though brought up and trained by his father in the best way, did not turn out according to the education he had received. He was not wicked, and was by nature far from villainy; but being cowardly, and from simplicity obeying those about him, his character was corrupted and he was led into licentiousness and bloodshed. He was nineteen years old when he took power. So he thrust aside the counsel of the best men of the senate, whom his father had set over him as guardians, made a treaty with the barbarians and went back to Rome, unwilling to toil and in love with an easy life.

For this reason many plots were made against him, and he killed a great many people, not only men but women too, and nearly all who were prominent then, except Pompeianus, Pertinax and Victorinus, so that those who wrote of these things could not account for how those men escaped death at that time. As he was entering the hunting theatre Claudius Pompeianus made an attempt on him: holding up a sword in the narrow entrance, he said, "The senate has sent you this." This man was betrothed to the daughter of Lucilla, Commodus's sister, and Lucilla herself shared his ruin, being no more reasonable or chaste than her brother. It was she who persuaded Pompeianus to attack Commodus, and she destroyed both him and herself. Commodus also put to death his wife Crispina, charging her with adultery. If anyone wished to set down exactly in writing each of those he killed, whether through false accusations, or idle suspicions, or great wealth, or brilliant birth, or eminence in learning, or a name for virtue, he would weary those who were going to read the work.

There were also wars while he was sole ruler, against the barbarians beyond Dacia, and the greatest, the British war, to which he sent Ulpius Marcellus, a man who lived with restraint and like a soldier, wholly incorruptible and sleepless by nature and still more by self-discipline. So that he should not even have his fill of bread, he ate it many days old and very stale, so that he could not eat anything beyond what was quite necessary. He did great harm to the barbarians in Britain, and for his excellence Commodus very nearly killed the man.

Perennis, the commander of the guard, was compelled to manage both military and public affairs, since Commodus was taken up with chariot-driving and debauchery. So if anything unpleasant befell the soldiers anywhere, they laid it at his door and were angry with him. The soldiers in Britain, who had mutinied and been reprimanded for it, sent fifteen hundred of their number into Italy. Commodus went out to meet them as they neared Rome and said, "Fellow soldiers, what do you want, that you are here?" They said, "We have come because Perennis is plotting against you." He believed them and handed the man over; and the soldiers maltreated him and cut him down, though he had conducted his office most incorruptibly and with great restraint.

Rid of him, the imperial freedmen, of whom Cleander was the chief, did every worst thing without fear: they sold everything, and were insolent and debauched. Cleander, raised high by fortune, gave away and sold seats in the senate, military commands, procuratorships, governorships and, in a word, everything. Some bought the rank of senator with all they had, so that it was said of Julius Solon, a very obscure man, that he had been stripped of his property and exiled into the senate. He appointed twenty-five consuls for one year, which never happened before or after. Raising money from every quarter, he gained a very great deal, and gave most of it to Commodus and his concubines.

Yet raised so high by fortune, he perished in disgrace. When a famine happened in Rome, Papirius Dionysius, who was in charge of the grain, made it worse, so that the Romans would hate Cleander and destroy him as the cause of the trouble through his thefts. A horse race was being held; and as the horses were about to compete, a crowd of children ran into the hippodrome, led by a tall and grim-looking girl, who was afterwards thought to have been a spirit. The children cried out together, and at this the people shouted and rushed to Commodus, who was in a suburb, praying for him and cursing Cleander. He sent soldiers against them, who wounded and killed some but could not hold the people back; they pressed on, trusting in their numbers and in the strength of the guards. As they drew near, Commodus, being a great coward, was so frightened that he at once ordered Cleander and his child to be killed. The child was dashed to the ground and killed; the Romans took Cleander's body, dragged it about and abused it, and his head was carried round on a spear. They also killed some others of those who had power with the emperor.

## 12.5

Commodus kept killing and doing away with the distinguished men, and was most oppressive to all the Romans, compelling them to vote him under compulsion all that they had voted his father willingly from goodwill. Among very many other honours voted to him was a golden statue weighing a thousand pounds. He decreed that all the months should be named after him, and they were counted thus: Amazonius, Invictus, Felix, Pius, Lucius, Aelius, Aurelius, Commodus, Augustus, Herculeus, Romanus, Exsuperatorius. For he gave himself all these names, and wrote to the senate thus: "The emperor Caesar Lucius Aelius Aurelius Commodus Augustus Pius Felix Invictus Romanus Hercules, high priest, holding the tribunician power for the eighteenth time, imperator for the eighth time, consul for the seventh time, father of his country, to the consuls, praetors, tribunes and the fortunate Commodian senate, greeting." Many statues were set up to him in the guise of Hercules. It was voted that the age of his reign should be called and written "golden" after him; for among his other names he was called both "golden" and "god".

Spending a great deal, he ran out of money; so he brought charges against men and women, and some he killed, while to others he sold their lives for their property. He drove chariots at home, for he was ashamed to do it in public, and fought as a gladiator: at home to the death, but in the theatre without steel and without human blood. At home he shaved the hair of some men, and cut off the noses of some, the ears of others, and something else from others. When he entered the theatre he wore the dress of Hermes, carrying a golden herald's staff. He was proud too of being left-handed. When he grew tired in his contests he drank, and the senators and knights present cried out "Long may you live!", and they were ordered to shout continually "You are lord!" and "You are first!" and "You will win the most fortunate of all victories!" and "Amazonius, you conquer!" Once he gathered together those who had lost their feet or been crippled in them by disease or accident, wound the likeness of serpents about their knees, and killed them by striking them with a club, as if he were Hercules killing the Giants.

When he was about to fight as a gladiator again, he ordered the knights and the senate to come into the theatre in the knights' dress and in cloaks, which was not the custom unless an emperor had died; and on the last day of the contests his helmet was carried out through the gate by which the dead were carried out. All thought these signs that they would soon be rid of his tyranny. And this happened shortly after. Aemilius Laetus the prefect and Eclectus the chamberlain, vexed at what he was doing, urged him not to do these things. He threatened them and was angry; and they, afraid, plotted against him and gave him poison in beef. When he was not quickly overcome by the poison, but vomited it up, suspected what had happened and began to threaten, they had him strangled by a certain Narcissus while he was bathing. He had been sole ruler twelve years, nine months and fourteen days, and had lived thirty-one years and four months. With him the house of the true Aurelii ceased to rule.

In the first year of the sole reign of Commodus, Julian was entrusted with the episcopate of Alexandria, after Agrippinus had managed it for twelve years and departed from this life. At that time Clement, the author of the Stromateis, was known, and Pantaenus the philosopher, a student and herald of our mystery. Earlier the narrative recorded that Mark led the church of Jerusalem after the bishops of the circumcision, when the city had been rebuilt by Hadrian and settled with gentiles. Cassian succeeded him, Publius succeeded Cassian, Julian Publius, Gaius Julian and Symmachus Gaius; and Symmachus departed this life in the time of another Gaius. Then another Julian succeeded to the episcopate, and his successor was Capito, and Valens followed Capito, Dolichianus Valens, and after them all Narcissus became the thirtieth bishop of Jerusalem from the apostles. In the tenth year of the reign of Commodus, Eleutherus, who had been bishop of the church of the Romans for thirteen years, departed this life, and Victor presided over the faithful there. When Julian had governed the church of the Alexandrians to the tenth year and paid his debt to nature, Demetrius was entrusted with the ministry of the episcopate. In the church of the Antiochenes, after Maximinus, Serapion oversaw those who bear Christ's name, the eighth high priest from the apostles. At that time Apollonius also, a man famous for learning and philosophy, by a martyr's end in Rome, at a decree of the senate, passed to the eternal dwellings.

## 12.6

So Commodus, having ruined the affairs of the empire, as has been said, was ruined himself; and Eclectus and Laetus chose Pertinax for the sole rule because of his virtue and rank. He, having made sure that Commodus was dead, accepted the rule, went into the camp, and won over the soldiers by Laetus's presence and by lavish promises. Then he went to the senate and said: "I have been named emperor by the army, but I resign the rule because of my age and ill health and the difficulty of affairs." When the senate praised him and chose him, he was declared emperor, and Commodus was voted a public enemy. The senate and people heaped insults on him and pulled down his images. They also wanted to drag his body about and tear it apart; but when Pertinax said that it had already been hidden in the earth, they held back from that, but called him accursed and tyrant and charioteer and gladiator and much else.

Pertinax was a Libyan from Alba Pompeia, of a father not nobly born, and had served as a tribune among the knights. He was easy to approach, listened readily, and answered as he thought fit. So Pertinax took the rule, and besides his other titles was named leader of the senate, after the ancient custom. Whatever had been in disorder was put back in good order by the emperor's management and forethought, and the disgrace of those unjustly put to death was removed by him. There was such a lack of money in the palace that only two hundred and fifty thousand drachmas were found. With difficulty Pertinax gathered silver from statues, arms, furniture and Commodus's favourites, and gave the guards what he had promised and the people a hundred drachmas each. For everything Commodus had used for luxury, gladiatorial fighting and chariot-driving he put up for sale.

Laetus praised Pertinax and insulted Commodus. Some barbarians who had received much gold from Commodus for peace, and were still on the road, he sent for and took the gold from them, saying, "Tell those at home that Pertinax rules"; for they knew the man's name from what they had suffered. Laetus did other things of this kind to discredit Commodus. But he did not stay loyal to Pertinax for long. Not getting what he longed for, he stirred up the soldiers against him. They, prevented by him from plundering, hated him and plotted with Laetus. So they agreed to make the consul Falco emperor, a man distinguished for birth and wealth. Pertinax learned of this while he was staying by the sea to arrange for the grain supply, hurried to the city, came into the senate and addressed it. When the senators were about to condemn Falco, Pertinax cried out: "Heaven forbid that any senator should be put to death while I rule, even justly."

Laetus put some of the soldiers to death as though at Pertinax's command, and the rest, afraid, were in uproar. Two hundred of the boldest drew their swords and rushed to the palace. When they were inside, his wife told him they were there. Though he could have resisted and destroyed them with the night watch and the cavalry, he did neither this nor choose to hide and escape, but, hoping perhaps to overawe them when they saw him and persuade them by speaking, he went to meet them as they came. At first they shrank back out of respect and put their swords in their sheaths; but when one of them leapt forward and said, showing his sword, "The soldiers have sent you this," and struck him, the others joined in and cut down the emperor himself and Eclectus. Then the soldiers stuck Pertinax's head on a spear and carried it round, glorying in the deed. The man had lived sixty-seven years less four months, and ruled only eighty-seven days.

## 12.7

When the murder of Pertinax was reported, Sulpicianus, who had been sent by him to the camp to settle matters there, stayed in it and worked to be declared emperor. Meanwhile Didius Julianus, a money-maker and insatiable, always eager for revolution, who for that reason had been banished by Commodus to Mediolanum, his native city, learned of the death of Pertinax and hurried to the camp. Standing at the gates, he outside and Sulpicianus inside, they bid for Rome and its rule from the soldiers, while some carried the messages and said to each, "He offers so much, and he so much; what will you add?" Since Julianus had promised the soldiers a great deal, they preferred him, fearing above all that Sulpicianus would avenge Pertinax, as his father-in-law.

Julianus was received into the camp and declared emperor, and from there went to the forum and the senate house, bringing a great many guards, so as to frighten both the senate and the people by them. He said to the senate: "You need a ruler, and I, if anyone, am the most worthy to lead you." Though he was hated for his boasting and for the soldiers who surrounded the senate house, out of fear the senate too confirmed his sole rule, and he went up to the palace.

Next day the senators came to him, so as not to be caught resenting him, but the people openly scowled. When the emperor came to the senate house they all shouted out as if at a signal, calling him parricide and robber of the empire. When he pretended not to be angry and promised them some silver, they were indignant at being bribed, and all cried out together, "We do not want it, we will not take it." Julianus ordered those who said this to be killed. The people were roused, remembered Pertinax and jeered at Julianus. Many in many parts of the city held out though wounded and killed, and taking arms they ran together into the hippodrome, where they spent a night and a day without food, calling on the rest of the soldiers, and above all on Pescennius Niger and those with him in Syria. Then, worn down by hunger and sleeplessness, they broke up and kept quiet. Julianus, having seized the rule in this way, used it slavishly, flattering the senate and anyone with influence, granting some things and promising others; he did everything to court the powerful, but was not trusted.

These things were done in Rome. The commanders of the armies, three in number, Severus governor of Pannonia, Niger of Syria and Albinus of Britain, learning about Julianus, were roused to bring him down. Severus, the cleverest of them, reckoned that if they overthrew Julianus the three would dispute the rule among themselves. He decided, therefore, to win one of them over. Since Niger was farther away from him, and he guessed that he was proud at having been called on by the people, as has been said, he turned to Albinus, and wrote to him secretly that he would make him Caesar. Albinus stayed where he was, confident that he would share the rule with Severus. Severus hurried towards Rome.

Learning of this, Julianus had the senate vote Severus a public enemy, prepared for war, and strengthened the palace with lattices and strong doors; for he thought the soldiers would never have killed Pertinax so easily had he been shut in, and he believed that if he were defeated he could survive by shutting himself up there. He also killed Laetus, and sent many men against Severus to murder him by treachery.
